en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Minor Section of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
1. The Section on Formal Acts (Kammakkhandhaka).
Discussion on the Act of Rebuke (Tajjanīyakamma).
First, in the first section on formal acts within the Minor Chapter (Cūḷavagga), [the text mentions] Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka—namely, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
And there were two among the group of six (Chabbaggiyas); those who relied upon them were likewise known as Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.
"Argue according to strength and weakness" means: respond with full strength. "More capable" means: more competent.
The discussion on the act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) is concluded.

The Discussion on the Twelvefold Set of Unlawful Acts (Adhammakammadvādasakakathā). 4. Regarding the phrases "done in the absence," etc.: it is done without the presence of the Saṅgha, the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person concerned;

it is done without having questioned the one who has been accused; it is done without that very person's admission. "In a case not conducive to confession" refers to an offense involving defeat (pārājika).

or for an offense involving a *saṅghādisesa*. Here, regarding the first three triads (*tīka*), nine phrases—beginning with "done by an illegal procedure" and "done by an incomplete assembly"—are stated, each being taken in conjunction with these [nine].
Thus, there are twelve triads in total. By way of their opposites, these same twelve triads are also stated for the bright side (*sukkapakkha*).
"By means of unsuitable associations with householders" means by means of associations with householders such as sharing their joys and sorrows, which are unbecoming for those who have gone forth.

The passage beginning "Of three bhikkhus, O bhikkhus," and so forth, is stated to show that it is permissible to carry out a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) even on the basis of each individual factor.
For while being a quarrelsome person is specifically a factor for a *tajjanīya-kamma*, [being one who causes schism is a factor] for a *niyassa-kamma* (act of demotion).

The act of constant offending is stated as the ground for the act of banishment (*pabbājanīya-kamma*) for one who corrupts families. Regarding these three factors, it is permissible to perform all of them by means of any one of them.
If this is so, then what was stated in the *Campeyyakhandhaka*—“If one performs an act of demotion (*niyassakamma*) against one deserving an act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*)...
[and so on] ...if one grants full ordination (*upasampadā*) to one deserving of it; in this way, Upāli, it is an illegitimate act (*adhamma-kamma*)”—[is explained].
[The objection that] this contradicts the statement, "And thus the Saṅgha becomes guilty of an offense for performing an act of non-discipline," is not valid.
Why? Because the meanings of the terms differ. For the meaning of the statement, "of one deserving an act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*)," is the formal determination of the act;
whereas the meaning of the statement beginning with, "Of three, monks... is the presence of the necessary factors. Therefore, when the Saṅgha has assembled...
When the formal decision has been made, saying, "We shall perform this specific legal act against this monk," then he is said to be "one deserving of a legal act.

It should be understood that for one who deserves a legal act such as *tajjanīya* (reproof) and so forth, to carry out a legal act such as *niyassa* (demotion) and so forth by means of this characteristic [of a different offense] constitutes both an illegal act (*adhammakamma*) and a non-disciplinary act (*avinayakamma*).
However, in the case of one who possesses any one of the factors among those such as being a maker of strife...

There is [a case] where the Saṅgha, if it so desires, having determined any legal act from among those acts and factors as they have been authorized, may perform that legal act after making that bhikkhu subject to the legal procedure. This is the analysis here.
In this way, what precedes accords with what follows.
In this regard, although the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) for an act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) was stated by way of one who causes quarrels,

nevertheless, when performing an act of censure against one who is foolish, incompetent, and prone to offenses, the formal proclamation must be made precisely by way of his being foolish and incompetent.
For in this way, the act is performed with a basis that is factual, and not with the basis of some other offense.
Why? Because this too has been permitted. This same method applies everywhere.
We shall explain the eighteen bases for proper conduct in the Pārivāsika-kkhandhaka.
The discussion on the group of twelve illegitimate legal acts is finished.
The Discussion on the Eighteen Points Not to Be Appeased, etc., 8.
"They shave the hair" means they have their hair shorn; the meaning is that the monks comply with them.

"They act for the sake of deliverance" (netthāraṃ vattanti): this belongs to those who are delivering themselves; it refers to those eighteen kinds of ways by which it is possible to effect a deliverance from [the offense].
The meaning is that they proceed in accordance with the right conduct (*sammāvattana*). For how long must the conduct be fulfilled? Ten or five days;
for within this section on formal acts (*kammakkhandhaka*), the conduct is indeed fulfilled by that much.
The discussion concerning the eighteen matters that should not be suspended is concluded.
The Discussion on the Formal Act of Subordination (Niyassakamma) 11.
Regarding the case of Seyyasaka—"And the monks were ordinary," "and the monks were constantly occupied"—the rest is exactly as stated in the section on Censure (Tajjanīya).
The Discussion on the Formal Act of Subordination is concluded.
The Discussion on the Act of Banishment (Pabbājanīyakamma).
21. The account of Assaji and Punabbasu is stated in the commentary on the Saṅghādisesa rules. 27.
Regarding the phrases "with bodily sport" and so forth, here "bodily sport" (kāyiko davo) means bodily play. The same applies to the other two phrases.
The same method applies here. What is called "bodily misconduct" (*kāyiko anācāro*) refers to the transgression of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed for the door of the body.

The same method applies to the other two [doors] as well. What is called "bodily harmfulness" (*kāyikaṃ upaghātikaṃ*) refers to the act of harming by way of not training in the training rules prescribed for the door of the body;
the meaning is "destruction" or "ruination. The same method applies to the other two as well. Bodily wrong livelihood (*kāyiko micchājīvo*)...
"By name" refers to things such as cooking oil or preparing medicinal tonics by means of performing medical treatments and the like, which have been rejected.
"Verbal wrong livelihood" refers to things such as receiving or announcing the teachings to householders. "Both bodily and verbal" refers to both of those together.
The remainder is exactly according to the method explained under the *tajjanīyakamma* (act of censure).
The Discussion on the Act of Banishment is finished.

Regarding the Discussion on the Act of Reconciliation (Paṭisāraṇīyakamma), in the case of the Sudhamma incident: "Without having asked for leave" means without having requested permission. "He said this": "What [do you have], householder?"
Having uncovered everything prepared for the elders and seen it, he said this:
"And there is not even one here, namely, a sesame ball (*tilasaṃguḷikā*). The meaning is that what is called a sesame roll (*tilasakkhalikā*) is not present.
It is said that in the lineage of that householder, there was once a baker at the beginning; the elder, wishing to disparage him on account of his birth, [said this].
He spoke thus: "Whatever it may be"—having thus abandoned such a vast jewel of the Buddha’s word, he uttered only this single statement regarding a sesame-cake.

By means of the illustration of the chick, he shows this: "Just as that [chick] made neither the cry of a crow nor the cry of a cock, so too by you neither the speech of a monk nor the speech of a householder was spoken."
The Discussion on the Act of Reconciliation is finished.
Regarding the Discussion on the Twelvefold Set beginning with "Acts Not in Accordance with the Dhamma": 37.
The triads beginning with "performed in the absence [of the accused]" are exactly as previously described.

39. The possession of these factors is unlike those mentioned previously. In this regard, "striving for non-gain" means that although one strives and exerts effort, one does not obtain gain in the way one would normally expect.
This same method applies to the cases of "misfortune" and so forth. Here, "misfortune" (anattha) refers to the destruction of one's welfare.
"Non-residence" (anāvāsa) means not dwelling in that place. "Disparagement of the Buddha by householders" means [speaking ill] of the Buddha in the presence of householders.
"He speaks dispraise" means he does not fulfill his promise of righteousness; that is, he does not act in accordance with what is true.
Having promised to observe the rains residence (*vassāvāsa*), he does not go, or he does something else of a similar nature.

"Of five [factors], monks," and so forth, is stated for the purpose of showing that even by a single factor one becomes subject to formal legal action (*kamma*). The rest here is of obvious meaning, and the method is the same as that explained regarding the censure transaction (*tajjanīya*).
The Discussion on the Group of Twelve [Procedures] beginning with Unlawful Acts is finished. 46.
The Discussion on the Act of Suspension for Not Seeing an Offense.
Regarding the case of Channa: "Monks, you should travel from monastery to monastery," he said; thus, you must announce it in all monasteries.

50. Regarding those beginning with "one who causes strife," after having charged him with the offense incurred by reason of such strife and so forth, the formal act (kamma) must be performed against him precisely for his failure to acknowledge that offense.

The triads are of the same type as previously described. 51. Regarding "proper conduct" (sammāvattanā), there are forty-three rules of conduct here. Among them, "he should not be reviled" means he should not be accused.
"One bhikkhu should not [be split] from other bhikkhus" means one bhikkhu should not be caused to break away from other bhikkhus. "He should not... [The sentence continues: ...not... [as before].
"The banner of householders" means that white garments with ten flower-patterned borders (*dasapuppha-dasa*) should not be worn.
"The banner of the non-Buddhist sects" means that grass-cloths (*kusacīra*) and the like should not be worn. "Should not be reviled" means should not be disparaged.
"Inside or outside" means either inside or outside the monastery (*vihāra*). The triad of terms beginning with "non-Buddhist sects" is self-evident. All the rest is in the *Pārivāsika-kkhandhaka*.

We shall explain it. The remainder is exactly according to the method stated for the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*). The act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*) for non-atonement of an offense is identical to this.
65. The account of Ariṭṭha is stated in the commentary on the *Khuddaka-vatthu*. Regarding the phrases "one who causes strife," and so forth:
the formal act should be performed precisely upon his failure to relinquish that view by which he engages in strife and the like. The remainder is as in the case of censure.
It is exactly as previously stated. For even regarding the proper conduct (*sammāvattanā*), there are likewise forty-three rules of conduct here.
The discussion on the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense is concluded.
The commentary on the Kammakkhandhaka is finished.
2. The Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsikakkhandhaka). Discussion on the Duties of One Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsikavattakathā). 75.
In the Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation—“Those undergoing probation” (pārivāsikā) means those who are living out their probation (parivāsa). Therein, it is fourfold:
Parivāsa (probation) is of four kinds: probation for what was not concealed, probation for what was concealed, probation to the end of purity, and probation by combination.

Regarding these, it is said in the Mahākhandhaka: "Monks, whoever—even if he was formerly a member of another sect—desires the going-forth and desires the full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya, probation of four months must be granted to him. Thus [it is stated].

The *titthiyaparivāsa* (probation for those belonging to other sects) is called the *appaṭicchannaparivāsa* (probation for what was not concealed). Regarding that, whatever needs to be said has already been stated.
However, this [probation] is not intended here. The remaining three types of probation are to be granted to one who has both committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense and concealed it.
Whatever needs to be said concerning them, we shall explain in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*. These, however—
This is what is intended here. Therefore, among these, those who are undergoing probation for any [of these offenses] should be understood as "those on probation" (*pārivāsika*).

Regarding "for the regular monks" (*pakatattānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ*): this refers to all others except for the most junior monk who is himself on probation, including even those subject to being sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*) and so forth.
Regarding "salutation and rising up": they consent to and accept whatever salutation and such acts those [regular monks] perform toward them.

The meaning is "they do not refuse. In that context, "proper conduct" (*sāmīcikamma*) is a designation for appropriate behavior conducive to higher practice (*ābhisamācārika*), such as fanning or providing a breeze, excluding acts like prostrating. "Offering a seat" (*āsanābhihāra*) means the bringing forward of a seat;
it refers either to approaching after taking up a seat or simply to its arrangement. The same method applies to "offering a bed" (*seyyābhihāra*). "Water for the feet" (*pādodaka*)...
"Water for washing the feet. "A footstool" means a stand for placing washed feet upon. "A foot-scrubber" means a stand for placing unwashed feet upon, or a foot-rubbing cloth.
"An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that even for one who consents on behalf of his co-resident disciples, it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing;
therefore, they should be told: "I am performing a formal act of discipline (vinayakamma); do not perform my duties; do not [insist] on my entering the village..."

"Ask for permission. If sons of good family who have gone forth out of faith say, "Venerable sirs, you may perform your disciplinary duties yourselves," and they carry out the proper conduct (*vatta*), they must still ask for permission even to enter a village;

from the time they are thus forbidden, there is no offense. Regarding the phrase "mutually according to seniority": among the monks undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*), whichever one is senior should [act] toward the other.
Therefore, it is permissible for the more junior monk to consent.
Regarding "according to seniority" (*yathāvuḍḍha*): this refers specifically to the order of seniority even when sitting with those who are not regular members of the Saṅgha (*pakatatta*).
Consequently, it is allowable to sit within arm's reach while the Pātimokkha is being recited. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it says: "Without sitting according to the text..."
It is stated: "One should sit down without releasing the hand’s reach, leaving the *pāḷi*.

When the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* is being performed, one should sit in the junior position of the Saṅgha and, while remaining seated right there, perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* according to one's own *pāḷi*.
Regarding the *pavāraṇā* as well, one should sit in the junior position of the Saṅgha and, while remaining seated right there, [perform it] according to one's own *pāḷi*.

The Pavāraṇā ceremony should be performed. When the saṅgha strikes the gong and distributes the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe), it is permissible for one to take it for oneself at the appropriate time.

"Oṇojana" refers to the distribution. For if two or three portions of *uddesabhatta* (food designated for a specific person) fall to a *pārivāsika* (one undergoing probation), and he has an expectation of receiving other private meals (*puggalika-bhatta*), he may take those in turn and say: "Venerable sir, please take the lower [portion]."
Having said, "Today I have hope for food; I will take it tomorrow," they should be released.
In this way, one is permitted to receive them on subsequent days. It is stated in the *Kurundi* that on the following day, these must be given to him first.
However, if he does not take them and does not release them, he does not receive them on the next day; this refers to the *oṇojana*.
This is specifically permitted for one who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*). Why?
Because when he sits in the lowest position in the Saṅgha at the meal hall, rice gruel, hard food, and so forth may or may not reach him;
therefore, this was specifically permitted for the sake of supporting him, thinking, "May he not suffer from a lack of alms-food."
"Bhatta" refers to the four-hall meal provided for the Saṅgha in the monastery, which must be received by those who have arrived according to their seniority;
this is what one receives according to age. However, one is not permitted to go or stand according to the order of the text (pāḷi);
therefore, having stepped back from the text and standing within arm's reach, one should extend the hand so that it is taken just as a hawk swoops down and seizes its prey.
It should be accepted. It is not permitted to have it brought by monastery attendants or novice monks;
however, if they bring it themselves, it is allowable. The same rule applies even regarding the king’s food from the great storehouse.
But as for the food from the four-hall storehouse, if one wishes to partake of it, when the alms-food has been set aside for oneself, one should say: "I have food today; I will take it tomorrow."

It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that on the following day one receives two alms-meals (*piṇḍa*). Even meals designated for recitation (*uddesabhatta*) and the like must be accepted only after they have been set aside from the formal scriptural list (*pāḷi*).
However, in a place where they serve food after having seated them, there the novices should sit with the eldest among them acting as the youngest of the community of monks (*saṅghanavaka*).

76. Now, regarding this "proper conduct" (sammāvattanā) that has been described: "one should not confer full ordination" means that having acted as a preceptor (upajjhāya), one should not confer full ordination;
however, it is permissible to confer full ordination after having relinquished the duty. Likewise, having acted as a teacher (ācariya), the formal proclamation (kammavācā) should not be recited;
yet, in the absence of another person, it is permissible to recite it after having relinquished the duty. "No dependence" (na nissayo): [this refers to the same principle].
No formal support (nissaya) should be given to newcomers. Even those who have already been receiving support by custom should be told:
"I am performing a disciplinary act (vinayakamma); receive your support from the Elder named so-and-so;
do not perform services for me, and do not ask my permission to enter the village. If they continue to do so even after this has been said, then from the time they were forbidden...
There is no offense even for those who perform [the formal act] starting from that point.
"Not a novice" means that another novice must not be taken [as an attendant]. Even novices who have been accepted by giving them the status of a pupil (upajjhā) should be told:
"I am performing a Vinaya formal act; do not perform the duties toward me, and do not ask me for permission to enter the village."
If, even when told this, they nevertheless continue to do so, there is no offense for those who continue to do so from the time they were forbidden.
The formal authorization as a teacher of bhikkhunīs (*bhikkhunovādakasammuti*) is prohibited because it constitutes a position of authority; therefore, one should say to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, I am performing a Vinaya transaction; please recognize me as a teacher of bhikkhunīs," or [one may appoint] a capable bhikkhu.
The burden must be borne. When the bhikkhunīs have arrived, they should be told: "Go to the presence of the Saṅgha;
the Saṅgha will know who shall give you exhortation," or: "I am performing the disciplinary act (vinayakamma);
go to such-and-such a bhikkhu, and he will give you exhortation."
"Regarding 'that offense': once probation has been granted for an emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*), another emission of semen should not be committed.
Or 'another similar one' refers to a grave offense (*garukāpatti*) such as physical contact (*kāyasaṃsagga*). Or 'one more serious than that' refers to an offense entailing defeat (*pārājikāpatti*);

for among the seven classes of offenses, an offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsitāpatti*) is the most serious; an offense of wrong doing (*dukkaṭāpatti*) is more serious; [and] an offense of wrong doing is [the least] serious."

The offense of confession (*pāṭidesanīya*) is more blameworthy; in this same manner, the principle should be applied to the offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*), grave offense (*thullaccaya*), offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*), and offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*).
Regarding their respective bases (*vatthu*), the base for an offense of wrong speech (*dubbhāsita*) is blameworthy, while the base for an offense of misconduct (*dukkaṭa*) is more blameworthy;

the distinction between them should be understood according to the previous method. However, in the training rules where both the formulation (*paṇṇatti*) and the fault (*vajja*) are involved, both the base and the offense are blameworthy.
In both cases of what is blameworthy in the world, the latter is more blameworthy.

"Kamma" refers to the formal act of *parivāsa* (probation). That *kamma* should not be censured with such words as "this *kamma* is not done, it is ill-done," or by such statements as "What is this so-called *kamma*?
Is it the work of a farmer or the work of a cowherd? The *kammikā* (those who perform the formal act) [should not speak thus].
Those monks by whom the formal act (*kamma*) has been performed should not be censured with such words as "fools" or "incompetent.
"One should not make them subject to being spoken to" means that one should not make them subject to being spoken to either for the purpose of creating an obstacle or for the purpose of summoning;
for if one does so for the purpose of creating an obstacle, [one says]: "I make you subject to being spoken to regarding this matter, venerable sir."
One acts thus: "Do not depart even a single step from this residence until that legal issue has been settled.

One acting for the purpose of summoning says: "I am making you subject to my word; come, let us go together into the presence of those who uphold the Vinaya. Neither of these two things should be done.
"Not a subordinate" means that one should not occupy the position of seniority in a monastery; one should not act as the reciter of the Pātimokkha or the proclaimer of the Dhamma;
nor should one exercise authority by means of even a single formal authorization (*sammuti*) among the thirteen types of such authorizations.
"Not an opportunity" refers to the opportunity for a regular monk (*pakatatta*) [to be granted] in this manner: "Venerable sir, please grant me the opportunity; I wish to speak to you."
He should not be made to perform [services]; he should not be accused of either an offense or a matter; he should not be reminded, saying, "This was a fault of yours in the past.
"He should not be associated with the monks" means that he should not be made to engage in quarrels by joining them together.
"In front" means he should not walk ahead while acting as the senior monk of the Saṅgha; [he must] leave a twelve-cubit space as a buffer zone.
One must go alone. The same rule applies to the sitting mat as well. "The limit of seats" refers to the seat for the most junior member of the Saṅgha in the dining hall and other such places;
that [seat] should be given to him, and he should sit there. "The limit of beds" means the limit of beds;
it refers to the lowest-quality bed and chair. For he is not permitted to take a bed for himself in his own allotted place according to the seniority of the rains-residence.
He receives it. Having been searched out by all the bhikkhus, the remaining inferior bedding—filled with dung and manure and bound together with rattan creepers and the like—should be given to him.

Regarding "the edge of the monastery": just as with the bedding, so too his dwelling-place within the monastery is not permitted for him in the place he has obtained through the *vassa* (rainy-season) assignment;
however, the ground covered with dust that remains after all the bhikkhus have searched and taken what they needed [is permitted].

A leaf-hut filled with owls and mice should be given to him. If all [the monks] are regular (pakatatta), tree-root dwellers, and open-air dwellers, and they do not enter a roofed dwelling, then all of them are said to have relinquished their residence. Among them, he may take whichever he desires.
On the day of entering the rains retreat, standing at one side, he is permitted to receive it as a distribution for the rainy season.

If one does not obtain a lodging, it should be taken after laying down the formal observance (*vatta*) by one who wishes to take a lodging for the fixed rainy-season residence (*nibaddhavassāvāsika*).
And it must be accepted by him: whatever limit of seats and so forth the monks assign to him, that alone must be accepted.
Regarding the phrase "with a preceding monk or a following monk": this refers to a place where relatives have offered hospitality, saying, "Come taking this many monks with you."
When invited, one should not go after making an appointment such as, “Venerable sir, a certain family has invited the bhikkhus;
let us go there,” by having other bhikkhus act as preceptors or attendants. [One should not say:
“Venerable sir, in a certain village people wish for the arrival of bhikkhus; it would be good indeed if they [were to come].”
"You should provide assistance"—it is permissible to speak thus by way of such an indirect method.
One who feels ashamed to announce [the practice] to those who come and go should not undertake the forest-dweller’s ascetic practice (āraññika-ṅga).
Even one who has already undertaken it by nature should, taking a second monk with him, cause the dawn to rise in the forest.

And one should not stay alone. Likewise, when feeling ashamed to sit at the very end of the row of seats in the refectory and other such places, one should not undertake even the alms-food-eater’s ascetic practice (*piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga*).
However, there is no prohibition for one who is already a natural alms-food eater by habit.
Nor, on account of that [practice], should one think: "Having had my meal brought out, I shall sit and eat right here in the monastery and count the nights."
For this reason—one thinking, "If I go out and see a bhikkhu and do not inform him, there might be a violation of the night-period"—one must not have almsfood brought out.

Furthermore, with the intention, "May no one know of me," meaning "May not even a single bhikkhu know of me," one does not even obtain the right to eat food prepared by novices within the monastery; rather, one must enter the village for alms.
However, for one who is ill, or occupied with duties such as those of a master builder or preceptor, it is permissible to remain in the monastery itself.
Even if hundreds of monks are wandering in the village and it is impossible to inform them,
it is permissible to go to the village residence and stay in a suitable place.
Regarding the phrase "by one who has arrived": having gone to any monastery, he should inform the monks there.
If he sees them all staying in one place, he should inform them while remaining in that very place.

But if they are staying separately at the roots of trees and so forth, he should go to each respective location and inform them. For one who intentionally fails to inform them, there is a breach of the night [of the observance].

And there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the observance (*vatta*). Now, if while searching he does not see anyone, there is only the interruption of the night; there is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the observance. Regarding "to a newcomer":
even to one who has come to his own dwelling-vihāra, whether it be one person or many, it must be announced in the manner already stated.
Furthermore, both the interruption of the night and the breaking of the observance should be understood here according to the manner already stated. If there are newcomers...
Whether they have rested for a moment or not, if they pass through the middle of the monastery, one must inform them as well.
If they depart without his knowledge, but he finds out after they have gone, one should go and inform him.

For one who is unable to reach them, there is only the breach of the night [observance], but no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the rule. This also applies to those within the monastery...

If they enter the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) without having entered the monastery itself and then depart, and [the resident monk] learns of their status as guests only upon hearing the sound of their parasols, coughing, or sneezing, he must go and inform them.
Even if he learns of it after they have already left, he must still follow after them and inform them.
For one who is unable to reach them, there is only a breach of the night-limit (*ratticcheda*), but no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the rule of conduct.

Even one who comes only at night and departs only at night creates a break in the night for him; however, because he was unaware [of the offense], there is no *dukkaṭa* for breaking the formal conduct (*vatta*).
If he performs the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) without even knowing [the offense], it is as if it were never done;
so it is stated in the *Kurundi*. Therefore, it should be performed by including the additional nights; this is the "unerring path" (*apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā*).
If, upon seeing a bhikkhu— even one traveling by boat on a river and so forth, or standing on the opposite bank, or traveling through the air,
or situated far away in mountain valleys, forests, and the like— if there is the recognition that "this is a bhikkhu," then one must either go by boat or other means,
or raise a great shout, or pursue him swiftly, and inform him; for one who fails to inform him, there is a breach of the night-period.
And there is also the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for breaking one's word.

However, if one makes the effort but is unable to reach [the person] or to inform them, there is only the interruption of the night, but no offense of wrong-doing for breaking one's word. The Elder Saṅghasenābhaya, however, speaks in terms of what is within range and what is not:
"It is said that for one who does not report it while within range, there is both the interruption of the night and the offense of wrong-doing for breaking one's word."
"But regarding what is not one's own sphere, neither [of these] exists. The Elder Karavīkatissa said: "The very determination that 'this is a recluse' is the authority;
even if it is not one's own sphere, there is no *dukkaṭa* offense for breaking the rule of speech, though there is indeed a breach of the night [of the observance].
Regarding the *uposatha*: visiting monks arrive thinking, "We shall reach the *uposatha*," even those traveling by means of psychic power (*iddhi*).

Having recognized the state of the Uposatha, they descend [into the assembly] and perform the Uposatha; therefore, on the Uposatha day, one must announce [the matter] for the purpose of purifying those who have arrived.
The same method applies to the Pavāraṇā ceremony as well. "The sick" means one who is unable to go. Regarding "by messenger":
it is not permitted to send one who has not received full ordination (anupasampanna); rather, having sent a bhikkhu, one should have him announce it.
"A residence without monks" means an empty dwelling; one should not go there for the purpose of staying where even a single monk is absent.
For in such a place, the nights spent do not count toward the required number; however, it is permissible [to stay] together with a regular (pakatatta) monk.
But in the case of the ten kinds of obstacles, even if the nights do not count, it is for the sake of being freed from those obstacles.

One must certainly go. Therefore it was said: “except in the case of an obstacle. It is not permitted to perform a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) together with those of a different affiliation (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*).
Even if one does not inform them, there is no interruption of the night; it is exactly like a residence where no monks are present.
Therefore it was said: “wherever there are monks of a different affiliation. The rest is according to the method explained in the Uposatha Khandhaka.
81. Regarding the phrase "in a dwelling with a single roof" (*ekacchanne āvāse*) and so forth: a "dwelling" (*āvāsa*) is a lodging constructed for the purpose of residing.
A "non-dwelling" (*anāvāsa*) includes a shrine room (*cetiyaghara*), a Bodhi-tree house, a refuse heap, a wooden shed, a water pavilion, a privy, a gateway, and so on.
By the third word [of the rule], both types are included. Among these, in any place whatsoever that has a single roof and is demarcated by the area where water falls from it—

One who has been suspended (ukkhitaka) is not permitted to live in a dwelling. However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that “one on probation (pārivāsika), moreover, is not permitted [to stay] even within the precincts of the monastery.
In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: “It is prohibited by way of the falling of water without distinction. In the *Kurundi*, it says:
“In these many places where five-colored canopies are tied up, for one on probation and for one who has been suspended...”

And it is said: "It was forbidden by the falling of water together with one who is of pure status (*pakatatta*). Therefore, even if they are not within each other's immediate vicinity, it is not permitted if they are under the same roof.

However, if in this case a *pārivāsika*—even one of sixty years' standing—enters and lies down afterwards, knowing that a *pakatatta* who was ordained on that very day has already entered and is lying there first, there is both a breach of the night and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for revealing the matter.
For one who does not know, there is only the breaking of the night; there is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the rule of conduct.

However, if, after that person has first lain down, a regular monk (pakatatta) enters later and lies down, and the one on probation knows [of this], there is both the breaking of the night and the offense of wrong-doing for breaking the rule of conduct.
If he does not know, there is only the breaking of the night; there is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the rule of conduct.
Regarding the instruction "one must rise and invite [the guest]": even upon seeing one who has been ordained on that very day, one must certainly rise;
and having risen, one should not go behind his back thinking, "I have had him rise while I am sitting comfortably," but must instead invite him by saying, "This is the teacher’s seat;
please sit here. However, the junior monk should not think, "I shall put the great elder to shame."
One must not go into the presence of a *pārivāsika* thera. Regarding "on the same seat": this refers to a bed or a chair belonging to one of the same seniority (*samānavassika*).

"Not when [the other] is sitting on the ground" means that one must not sit on anything higher—even a grass mat or a sandy surface—than the other person who is sitting on the natural ground as a regular monk (*pakatatta*);
however, one may sit after leaving a twelve-cubit radius around him.
It is permissible. "Walking on a single walking-path" means walking together with a companion on one walking-path.
"Walking on the ground" (*chamāyaṃ caṅkamante*)—this is the reading; or rather, this is the meaning here:
when they are walking on ground that has not been demarcated, or having made a demarcation and strewn sand [there], [they may set up] a support.
Once it has been prepared with a walkway, one should not walk even on a low one, let alone on one equipped with a foundation of bricks and surrounded by a railing!
However, if it is enclosed by a wall, provided with a gatehouse, or well-concealed within mountain clefts, forest thickets, or groves, it is permissible to walk on such a walkway.
Even if it is not concealed, it is permissible provided one leaves a space around it.

Regarding the phrase "by one who is senior": here, if the other person lies down afterwards while knowing that the senior pārivāsika has already lain down first, there is a breaking of the night for him and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of the proper conduct. However, for the senior, there is only the breaking of the night, but no offense of wrong-doing for the breach of proper conduct.
If he lies down without knowing, there is no breach of proper conduct for either of them, though there is a breaking of the night.

However, if the senior monk lies down afterwards while the junior monk who is undergoing probation has already lain down first, and the junior monk knows [of the senior’s arrival], his night-count is broken and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of duty. For the senior, there is only the breaking of the night-count, but no breach of duty.
If he does not know, there is no breach of duty for either of them, but the night-count is broken.

If both lie down, whether one after the other or simultaneously, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that for the senior there is a breach of the night [of probation], while for the other there is also a breach of the proper conduct (*vatta*).

If two monks who are both on probation have the same number of years remaining, and one has already lain down while the other, knowing this, lies down afterwards, the night is broken and there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of proper conduct. This applies to the one who lay down first.

There is a breach of the night, but not a breach of the observance. If even the one who lies down later does not know [of the other], there is no breach of the observance for either of them, though there is a breach of the night.
If both lie down without one being earlier or later than the other, there is a breach of the night for both, but not a breach of the observance.
For if two who are on probation were to dwell together, they would [be liable for] each other's transgression.
Knowing this, they might become disrespectful or remorseful, or they might commit an even more serious offense, or they might fall away from the faith;
therefore, sleeping together with them is prohibited in every respect. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated.

Furthermore, those subject to *mūlāya-paṭikassanāraha* (sent back to the beginning) and others should be understood as standing in the position of those who are *pakatatta* (of normal status) relative to the *pārivāsikas* (those on probation).

“Monks, if one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*) is the fourth member when they undergo probation, it is not permitted to perform the granting of probation or other such acts by making that person on probation the fourth member.
He does not serve as a completer of the quorum for these very acts, but he does so for other formal acts of the Saṅgha.
However, if a quorum cannot be obtained, one should have him set aside his duties and make him the completer of the quorum.”
83. Having heard this account of the duties (*vatta*), while the Elder Upāli, the bearer of the Vinaya, was in seclusion, this reflection arose in him:
"The Blessed One has prescribed many duties for one on probation (*pārivāsika*); by how many causes, then, does the interruption of the night (*ratticcheda*) occur here?
He approached the Blessed One and asked him about that matter. The Blessed One [spoke] to him...
He explained it. Therefore it was said: “Then the Venerable Upāli... [as above] ...the interruption of the night.

Therein, “living together” (*sahavāsa*) refers to living in one place with a regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhu, according to the method beginning with “under one roof,” and so forth. “Living apart” (*vippavāsa*) refers to living alone.
“Failure to announce” (*anārocanā*) refers to the failure to announce those who have arrived as guests, and so forth. By each of these three causes, there occurs an interruption of the night.
84. "They are not able" means that because of the great size of the Saṅgha, being unable to go here and there to inform everyone, they are unable to clear [the offense].
Regarding these two phrases—"I set aside the probation" and "I set aside the proper conduct"—if it is set aside by even one of these two, the probation is indeed set aside;
if both are used, it is well-set aside. The same principle applies to the undertaking [of the probation] as well.

Having thus undertaken the observances, for one who has completed the probation (*parivāsa*) and is now undertaking the penance (*mānatta*), there is no further duty to undertake the observances, as he has already undertaken them.
Therefore, the six-night penance should be granted to him; once the penance has been practiced, he is to be rehabilitated (*abbheta*).
Thus, having become free from offense and established in the pure state, by fulfilling the three trainings (*sikkhā*), he will bring an end to suffering.
The Discussion on the Duties of One Undergoing Probation is finished.
The Discussion on the Duties of One Subject to Be Sent Back to the Beginning: 86.

Regarding the statement, "Bhikkhus subject to being sent back to the beginning consent to those who are regular members," this excludes one who is junior to the bhikkhu subject to being sent back to the beginning.

[This applies] to the rest, including even those who are on probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth. For among these five—those on probation, those deserving of being sent back to the beginning (*mūlāya-paṭikassanāraha*), those deserving of the trial period (*mānatta*), those undergoing the trial period (*mānattācārika*), and those deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*)—with the exception of each person’s own junior [in seniority], all the others are indeed regular monks (*pakatatta*). Why?

Because it is permitted for them to perform salutations and other formalities toward one another according to their seniority. Therefore it was said: "to the rest, including even those who are on probation and so forth."
The characteristics of those deserving of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*) and so forth will be made clear later.

The rest here, as well as in the duties for those deserving of the trial period (*mānattāraha*) and so forth that follow this, should be understood according to the method already stated regarding the duties of one on probation (*pārivāsika*).

87. Regarding the cases such as "one who is fourth with one deserving of sending back to the beginning," just as with one on probation, these individuals also do not serve to complete the quorum for these specific disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*), but they do serve for other communal acts of the Saṅgha.
The Discussion on the Duties for One Subject to Be Sent Back to the Beginning is finished.

90. The Discussion on the Duties for One Undergoing the Trial Period (*mānatta*). Regarding the duties of one undergoing the trial period, there is this specific distinction: "One must report [one's status] daily."
92. Regarding the phrase "counting when nights are deficient": here, "a group" (*gaṇa*) refers to four or more persons;

therefore, even if one dwells with only three monks, there is indeed a deficiency of nights. The method of determination regarding the relinquishing and undertaking of the *mānatta* penance is exactly as stated [previously].
The remainder is clear in all respects.
The Discussion on the Conduct for One Undergoing the Mānatta Discipline is finished.
The Commentary on the Pārivāsika Khandhaka is finished.
3. The Samuccaya Khandhaka.
The Discourse on the Discharge of the White Cloth, 97.
In the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*: regarding the phrase "the *mānatta* penance for six days," there are four kinds of *mānatta*:
*mānatta* for unconcealed offenses, *mānatta* for concealed offenses, *mānatta* for a fortnight, and combined *mānatta*. Among these, *mānatta* for unconcealed offenses...

The *nāma-mānatta* (name-mānatta) is that which is granted as a *mānatta* to one who is eligible for *mānatta* solely on account of having committed an offense, without granting a *parivāsa* for an unconcealed offense.
The *paṭicchanna-mānatta* (concealed-mānatta) is that which is granted to one who has completed a *parivāsa* for a concealed offense.
The *pakkha-mānatta* (fortnightly-mānatta) is that which [is granted] for either a concealed or an unconcealed [offense].
Or, half a month [of probation] is given to the bhikkhunīs for an offense.

"Combined *mānatta*" means that which is given by combining [the periods] together into one. Among those, this should be understood as "unconcealed *mānatta*" because of the statement, "for six days of *mānatta* for what was unconcealed.
When giving it, if she has committed only one offense, it should be given according to the method explained here.

If he has committed two, three, or more than that, just as it was said regarding "one offense," so too should it be stated as "two offenses" or "three offenses. But if there are more than that—even if there are a hundred or a thousand—they should be stated as "many.
Even those belonging to different bases should be given together; this is the procedure for giving them.
We shall explain the granting of the *parivāsa*.

Having thus performed the formal act (*kammavācā*) regarding the offense and granted the *mānatta* penance, at the conclusion of the formal act with the words, “I hold this to be so,” one must undertake the proper conduct (*vatta*) within the *māḷaka* boundary itself, according to the method stated: “I undertake the *mānatta*; I undertake the proper conduct.”
Having undertaken the observance, one must announce it right there to the Saṅgha, and the one announcing it should announce it thus:
“Venerable sirs, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconcealed;
I [approach] the Saṅgha for six days regarding that one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconcealed.”
“I requested the *mānatta* penance; the Saṅgha granted me a six-night *mānatta* for that one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconfessed.
I am now practicing the *mānatta*; I inform you, venerable sirs:
may the Saṅgha remember me as one who informs.”
Moreover, having grasped this matter, it is indeed permissible to announce it in whatever language one chooses.

Having announced it, if one wishes to set it aside, it should be set aside in the midst of the Saṅgha according to the method already stated. Once the monks have departed from the hall, it is also permissible to set it aside in the presence of even a single person.
Having emerged from the hall, if one recovers mindfulness, [one may set it aside] in the presence of someone who is accompanying one.
It should be deposited in the presence [of the monks]. If he too has departed, it should be deposited after informing another monk in whose dwelling it has not been announced.
When announcing it, however, at the end one should say: "May the Venerable One bear me in mind as one who makes himself known.
When announcing it to two, one should say: "May the Venerable Ones bear [me] in mind"; when announcing it to three, one should say: "May the Venerable Ones..."
"May they maintain [the observance]"—this should be said. From the time it is set aside, one remains in the status of a regular monk (*pakatatta*).
If the monastery has few monks and like-minded monks are residing there, the nights should be counted within the monastery itself without setting aside the duties (*vatta*).
If, however, it is not possible to purify [the boundary], then having set aside the duties according to the method already stated, at the time of dawn...
If the monastery is enclosed, one should sit in a place hidden by a thicket or a fence, having descended from the main road and passed two *leḍḍupāta*s beyond the enclosure;
if it is unenclosed, one should sit in a place hidden by a thicket or a fence, having descended from the main road and passed two *leḍḍupāta*s beyond the spot where an enclosure would be appropriate.
Before dawn, having undertaken the duties in the manner described, one should announce them.
If another bhikkhu comes to that place for some business and sees him, or hears his voice, he must inform him.
For one who fails to inform him, there is both a breach of the night-period and a transgression of the rule of conduct (*vattabhedo*).
However, if he enters the twelve-fathom precinct and departs without the other’s knowledge, there is indeed a breach of the night-period.
However, there is no breach of the formal observance (*vatta*). From the time it has been announced, it is permissible for all except one bhikkhu to go if there is business to attend to.
When the dawn has risen, the observance must be relinquished in the presence of that one bhikkhu.
If he too goes away before dawn on some business, [the observance is relinquished] in the presence of another who has departed from the monastery or an incoming guest.
Or, having reported [the matter] to whomever he first sees and having laid down the formal duty (*vatta*), he may reside.

Since he has resided only after reporting to the group and observing the presence of other monks, there is no fault of wandering with an incomplete group nor any violation of the rule against staying apart (*vippavāsa*).
If he does not see anyone, he should go to the monastery and [report it] to the monks who have traveled with him.

"It should be deposited in the presence of one [monk]," said the Elder Mahāsumma. However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "It should be deposited after informing whichever monk one sees first; this is the exemption for one who has performed the procedure of depositing.
Having thus practiced the *mānatta* penance for six days without interruption, wherever there might be a community of twenty monks, there—
That bhikkhu is to be rehabilitated. And those who are rehabilitating him must first make him worthy of rehabilitation.

For he stands in the position of a regular (pakatatta) bhikkhu because he has fulfilled his duties; and it is not permitted to grant rehabilitation to one who is already a regular. Therefore, he must be made to undertake the duties.
Once the duties have been undertaken, he becomes worthy of rehabilitation. Having undertaken the duties and announced them, he himself must then request rehabilitation.
For one who has not laid aside the observance (*anikkhittavatta*), there is no further duty to undertake the observance.
Indeed, by the mere lapse of six days, he becomes worthy of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*); therefore, he must be rehabilitated.

In this regard, the procedure for rehabilitation stated in the Canon itself—“And thus, monks, he is to be rehabilitated”—was stated with reference to a single offense. However, if there are two, three, or many offenses...
Whether the offenses have a single basis or various bases, the formal proclamation (kammavācā) must be performed according to them.

In this manner, the penance for unconcealed offenses (appaṭicchannamānatta) is to be granted. As for the penance for concealed offenses (paṭicchannamānatta), however, since it is to be granted to one who has completed the probation (parivāsa) for a concealed offense, we shall discuss it in the section on probation itself.
102. “In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha grant a one-day probation (parivāsa) to the monk Udāyī for one intentional emission of semen,
concealed for one day,” and so on according to the method found in the Pāḷi through many [instances].

The probation (*parivāsa*) and the penance (*mānatta*) have been explained by way of their formal characteristics. Since, if the detailed exposition were to be stated for every single point as it occurs in the texts,
it would become excessively prolix like the canonical scriptures (*pāḷi*) themselves and could not be easily grasped,
we shall therefore synthesize them and present them right here.

For this "probation" (parivāsa) intended here is of three kinds: probation for concealed offenses (paṭicchanna-parivāsa), probation to the end of purity (suddhanta-parivāsa), and simultaneous probation (samodhāna-parivāsa).
Among these, probation for concealed offenses must first be granted according to the period for which the offense was concealed.
For some, there is an offense concealed for one day, as was the case with the Elder Udāyī; for others, it is concealed for two days or more.
Just as in the case of the Elder Udāyī, who was reported from abroad, some have one offense like this one,
while others have two, three, or more, as reported elsewhere; therefore, when granting probation for concealment,
the period of concealment must first be determined.
For this so-called offense is concealed in ten ways. Herein, this is the matrix: there is an offense, and one perceives it as such;
one is a regular monk, and one perceives oneself as such; there is no obstacle [to confession], and one perceives that there is none;
one is capable [of confessing], and one perceives that one is capable; and one desires to conceal it, and one conceals it.
In this context, "there is an offense and one perceives it as such" means that whatever offense has been committed remains indeed an offense, and the person there also perceives it as an offense.
Thus, if one conceals it while knowing this, it remains concealed. However, if one perceives it there as no offense, it is unconcealed;
for even when there is no offense, whether one perceives it as an offense or as no offense, it remains unconcealed by one who attempts to conceal it.
It exists. If one conceals [an offense] thinking "light" when it is heavy, or "heavy" when it is light, one stands on the side of the shameless;
however, the offense remains unconcealed. If, thinking a heavy offense is light, one confesses it, it is neither confessed nor concealed.
If, knowing a heavy offense is heavy, one conceals it, it is concealed. If one does not know whether an offense is heavy or light, [regarding] the offense...
“I will conceal it,” he conceals it, and it becomes concealed. Regarding the term “one who is in good standing”:
this refers to one who has not been subjected to the three kinds of *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (acts of suspension). If he conceals it while perceiving himself as being in good standing, it is concealed.
However, if he conceals it while perceiving himself as not being in good standing, thinking, “An act has been performed against me by the Saṅgha,” [it is not concealed].

It remains unconcealed. Even if it has been covered by one who was previously expelled, whether that person perceives him as a regular monk or does not perceive him as such, it remains indeed unconcealed.
And this has also been said:
"One incurs a grave offense with remainder..."
"He conceals it out of disrespect;
yet the nun would not incur an offense.
This question was conceived by those skilled in the wholesome."
This question was posed by one who had been suspended.

Regarding the term "one for whom there is no obstacle": if a person for whom not even one of the ten obstacles exists conceals [an offense] while perceiving it as being free from obstacles, it is considered concealed.
Even if, due to a timid nature, he does so in the dark out of fear of non-human beings or fierce wild animals...
If one conceals [an offense] while perceiving it as an obstacle, it is as if unconcealed.

For instance, when one living in a mountain hermitage must report [the offense] after crossing a ravine or a river, and there is danger from fierce beasts, non-human beings, and so forth on the way, or if pythons lie across the path, or the river is full; yet, if there is only a single obstacle and one perceives it as such an obstacle—

Having covered it, it remains uncovered. Furthermore, for one who covers [the robe] with the perception that it is an obstacle, or even with the perception that it is not an obstacle, it remains uncovered.
"Abundant" means: if someone is able to go to the presence of the bhikkhu and inform him, yet, perceiving it as abundant...

He conceals it, and it becomes concealed. Even if there is a slight boil in his mouth, or a jaw-cramp pierces him, or a tooth aches, or he has received meager alms—by that much alone he is neither able to speak nor to go;
yet he perceives, "I am not able. This is called being capable while perceiving oneself as incapable. By this...

"Even if concealed, it is unconcealed. However, for one who is unable to speak or go [to confess], whether they perceive themselves as having committed much or little, it remains unconcealed even if it has been concealed.
"He desires to conceal and he conceals"—this is of plain meaning. But if, thinking "I shall conceal it," he relinquishes his burden...

If, having committed an offense either before the meal, after the meal, or during the first watch of the night and so forth, one enters upon the state of shamefulness and reports it within the rising of the sun,
this is called "one who wishes to conceal but does not conceal.
However, for one living in a place devoid of monks, having incurred an offense, [the situation changes] upon the arrival of a fellow monk...

If, while waiting for someone of like standing or going to such a person, half a month or even a full month passes by, this is called "concealing" by one who does not wish to conceal; yet even this is considered as unconcealed.
However, he who, immediately upon committing the offense, flees in haste—like a man who has stepped into a fire—to a place where there are those of like standing...
Having gone [to him], he reveals it; this is called "not concealing" because he does not conceal it out of a desire to hide it.

However, if, even upon seeing someone who is a fellow practitioner, he does not report it out of shame, thinking, "This person is my preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya)," then the offense remains concealed. For in this context, being a preceptor and so forth is not the determining factor;
rather, merely being a fellow practitioner who is not an enemy is the determining factor. Therefore, it should be reported in the presence of one who is a fellow practitioner and not an enemy.
However, one should not report [an offense] to a preceptor who is of a different disposition and, upon hearing it, desires to proclaim it.
In that case, whether one has fallen into an offense before the meal or after the meal, by day or by night, it must be reported as long as the dawn has not yet risen.
Once the dawn has risen, the offense is concealed; on account of such concealment, [it becomes a saṅghādisesa].
And one incurs a dukkaṭa offense. However, it is not permitted to disclose [the offense] in the presence of one who has committed a saṅghādisesa offense of the same class.
If one does disclose it, the offense is disclosed, but one is not released from the dukkaṭa; therefore, it should be disclosed in the presence of one who is pure.
And when disclosing it, one should say: "I disclose one offense in your presence," or "I confess it."

Or if he says, “I announce it,” or “Know that I have fallen into one offense,” or if he speaks by way of saying, “I disclose one grave offense,” and so forth—in all such ways, it remains undisclosed; thus it is stated in the *Kurundi*.
However, if he speaks by way of saying, “I disclose a light offense,” and so forth, it becomes disclosed.
If he reports the basis [of the offense], if he reports the offense, or if he reports both, it is indeed reported in all three ways.
Thus, having observed these ten factors, one who grants probation for concealment must first ascertain the state of concealment.
Then, having ascertained the days of concealment and the offenses, if it has been concealed for one day—“I, ...”
"Venerable sir, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day.
Having had him make this request in this manner, the formal act (*kammavācā*) should be recited according to the method stated here, and the probation (*parivāsa*) should be granted.
Now, if it has been concealed for two, three, or more days—concealed for two days, three days, four days, five days, or six days—[the procedure follows accordingly].
"Concealed for seven days, concealed for eight days, concealed for nine days, concealed for ten days, concealed for eleven days, concealed for twelve days,
concealed for thirteen days, concealed for fourteen days"— in this way,
the application should be made according to the number of days up to fourteen days. For fifteen days concealed, it is "concealed for a fortnight."
Having said this, the explanation should be made. Then, from the twenty-ninth day onwards, it is "concealed for more than a half-month.
After that, [it is] concealed for one month, concealed for more than one month; concealed for two months, concealed for more than two months;
concealed for three months, concealed for more than three months; concealed for four months, concealed for more than four months.
Concealed for five months; concealed for more than five months; concealed for six months; concealed for more than six months;
concealed for seven months; concealed for more than seven months; concealed for eight months; concealed for more than eight months;
concealed for nine months; concealed for more than nine months; concealed for ten months; concealed for more than ten months.
"Concealed for eleven months" means concealed for more than eleven months; such is the construction to be made. When a year is complete, it is "concealed for one year.
Beyond that, [it is] "more than one year," "two years," "more than two years," "thirty years," "more than thirty years," "four years," or "more than four years."
"Concealed for five years... concealed for more than five years"—in this manner, the application [of the formula] should be made up to "concealed for sixty years...
concealed for more than sixty years," or even beyond that.
However, if there are two, three, or more offenses, then just as it is stated here as "one offense," [the same logic applies].
In this way, one should say "two offenses" or "three offenses. Beyond that, however, whether there be a hundred or a thousand, it is permissible to say "many.
Even when the offenses belong to different bases, one may say: "Venerable sir, I have committed many *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
one emission of semen, one bodily contact, and one lewd speech..."
“one committed by one who desires his own [benefit], one committed by a go-between, and those concealed for one day”—thus either by way of enumeration, or by way of specifying the bases:
“Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses of various bases, concealed for one day,” or: “Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses...”
Or rather, the construction should be made by way of names alone, as follows: "I committed several offenses concealed for one day.
In this context, there are two kinds of names: those shared with its own class and those shared by all.
Therein, "saṅghādisesa" is shared with its own class, while "offense" (āpatti) is shared by all; therefore, [the phrase] is "I committed several offenses concealed for one day."
In this way, it is also appropriate to speak by way of a name that is common to all.

For indeed, all these disciplinary acts (*vinayakamma*), such as probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, may be performed according to the subject matter (*vatthu*), the clan (*gotta*), the name (*nāma*), and the offense (*āpatti*).
In that regard, "emission of semen" (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) is both the subject matter and the clan; "an offense entailing suspension" (*saṅghādisesa*) is both the name and the offense.

And: "Physical contact" (*kāyasaṃsaggo*) refers both to the basis (*vatthu*) and the category (*gotta*). "An offense entailing suspension" (*saṅghādiseso*) refers both to the name and the offense itself.
In this regard, by the expression "emission of semen through physical contact," etc., as well as by the expression "those of various bases," both the basis and the category are included.
Likewise, by the expression "an offense entailing suspension" and by the expression "offenses," [both are included].

In that case, both the name and the offense were mentioned. But here, when one has committed a single offense—the intentional emission of semen—both the name and the details of the basis (vatthu) and the clan (gotta) are indeed included.

And just as it is said here, "This monk Udāyī," so too, whatever person has committed [the offense], the formal act (kammavācā) must be performed by taking that individual's name and saying, "This monk named so-and-so."

And at the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), that bhikkhu must undertake the duties (*vatta*) in the very same manner as previously described, saying within the boundary of the monastery precinct (*māḷakasīmā*): “I undertake the probation;
I undertake the duties. Having undertaken them, he should announce it right there to the Saṅgha, and he who announces it should announce it in this way:
“Venerable sirs, I committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day.
I requested from the Saṅgha a one-day probation (parivāsa) for that one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day;
the Saṅgha granted me that one-day probation for that one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day.”
“He granted me probation for one day; I am now undergoing that probation—‘Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha remember me as one who declares:
“I am declaring it. Having taken up this matter, it is indeed permissible to announce it in whatever language one chooses.
Once it has been announced, if he wishes to relinquish it, it must be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha in the manner already described. When the monks have departed from the hall...

It is permissible to deposit it even in the presence of a single person. Having emerged from the hall, one who has regained mindfulness should deposit it in the presence of someone who is accompanying him.
If that person has also departed, one should inform another to whom it has not been announced in the hall and then deposit it.
And when announcing it, at the end one should say: "May the Venerable One bear me in mind as one who makes this known."

It should be said as follows: when announcing it to two [monks], one should say, "Venerable sirs, may you bear this in mind"; when announcing it to three, one should say, "Venerable sirs, may you bear this in mind.
From the time it is set aside, he remains in the position of a regular monk (*pakatatta*).
If the monastery has few monks, but like-minded monks are residing there, he should remain in that very monastery without having set aside his duties.
The determination of the night should be made. If it is not possible to purify oneself, then having laid down the duties in the manner already stated,
at the time of dawn, together with one other bhikkhu, having crossed the boundary of the precincts in the manner described in the commentary on *mānatta*,
having descended from the main road and sat down in a concealed place, [he should perform the purification] within the rising of the sun in the manner already stated.
Having undertaken the formal observance (*vatta*), the probation (*parivāsa*) of that bhikkhu must be announced.
When announcing it, if he is junior, he should say, "Friend"; if he is senior, he should say, "Venerable Sir.
If another bhikkhu comes to that place for some business and sees him, [he should call out] a voice...
If he hears rain, it must be reported; for one who does not report it, there is both a breach of the night-period and a breach of the duty.
Now, if he enters within a twelve-fathom vicinity and departs while [the other] is still unaware, there is only a breach of the night-period, but no breach of the duty.
When the sun has risen, the duty must be relinquished. If that bhikkhu has departed on some business, [the procedure remains as stated].
When one sees another person for the very first time, one should inform that person and deposit [the object] with them.
However, if one sees no one at all, the Elder Mahāsumma said that one should go to the monastery and deposit it in the presence of a bhikkhu who has traveled together with oneself.
But the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "One should inform the person whom one sees first and then deposit it."
“This is the exemption for one who has fulfilled the duties,” he said.
Thus, for as many days as the offense was concealed, or even more than that, one should dwell in probation (*parivāsa*) for the purpose of dispelling remorse;
then, having approached the Saṅgha and undertaken the duties, one should request the period of penance (*mānatta*). For this—
When the observance (*vatta*) has already been undertaken, one becomes worthy of the trial period (*mānatta*) because the observance has been fulfilled even after it was relinquished.
However, for one who has not relinquished the observance, there is no further need to undertake it;

for he becomes worthy of the *mānatta* simply by the passing of the days during which the offense was concealed. Therefore, the *mānatta* must indeed be granted to him. This is called the "concealed *mānatta*. When granting it, if...
If there is one offense, it should be granted in exactly the manner stated in the Canon.

If there are two or three, one should observe the offenses and the days in the same manner as explained for the probation (*parivāsa*), and the application should be made thus: "I, having completed my probation, request of the Saṅgha a six-night period of penance (*mānatta*) for two or three offenses concealed for one day. One should then apply the formula accordingly.
It is also permissible to grant probation by combining an unconfessed offense with a confessed offense. How so? Having observed a one-day probation for the confessed offense, [one should say]:
"Venerable sirs, I committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day;
I now ask the Saṅgha for a one-day probation for that one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day."
I requested this, and the Saṅgha granted me a one-day probation (*ekāhaparivāsa*) for that one offense of intentional emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) which was concealed for one day.

I have completed that probation. Venerable sirs, I committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, which was not concealed. Venerable sirs, I [now] request the Saṅgha for the removal of those offenses...
“I request the *mānatta* penance for six nights for intentional emissions of semen, both concealed and unconcealed.
Then, having performed the formal act (*kammavācā*) appropriate for him, the *mānatta* should be granted.
If there are two concealed and one unconcealed, it should be said: “for the concealed and the unconcealed. If there is one concealed and [two] unconcealed...
Two [cases]: it should be stated, “of both the concealed and the unconcealed. If there are two concealed and two unconcealed, it should be stated, “of both the concealed and the unconcealed.
In all instances, having performed the appropriate formal act (*kammavācā*), the penance of probation (*mānatta*) should be granted.
And for one who has completed the penance, having performed the corresponding formal act, rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) should be granted.

It should be performed. However, here it is stated by way of a single offense. Thus, that *mānatta* which is granted at the conclusion of the *parivāsa* for a concealed offense is called "concealed *mānatta*.

In this way, it should be understood that both the *parivāsa* for a concealed offense and the *mānatta* for a concealed offense have been explained here by means of a single method of exposition. [Next is] the *mānatta* for a fortnight (*pakkhamānatta*).
We shall explain the reconciliation (*samodhāna*) and the period of penance (*mānatta*) at the conclusion of the discussion on the remaining types of probation (*parivāsa*).
For there are two remaining types of probation: the purification-end probation (*suddhanta-parivāsa*) and the reconciliation probation (*samodhāna-parivāsa*).

Regarding these, "purification-end probation" refers to that which follows the conclusion of an undharmic (*adhammika*) period of penance; as it says later: "At that time, a certain monk [who had committed many offenses]..."

In this case—where one has committed offenses involving formal meeting (saṅghādisesa), does not know the limit of the offenses, and does not know the limit of the nights—the probation (parivāsa) is permitted.
This is of two kinds: the "short purification" (cūḷasuddhanta) and the "long purification" (mahāsuddhanta).
Both of these apply to one who neither knows nor remembers the full extent or even a portion of the reckoning of the nights.
And it should be granted to one who is uncertain in that regard. As for the limit of the offenses, whether he knows "I have committed this many offenses" or not, that is irrelevant.
In this context, [the calculation] may proceed either in direct order starting from the full ordination, or in reverse order starting from the day the offense was confessed.
Or, when asked, "Do you know on such-and-such a day, or fortnight, or month, or year that your state was pure?", he replies, "Yes, venerable sir, I know; for this much time I have been pure.
The *suddhantaparivāsa* granted to him is called the "minor *suddhanta*" (*cūḷasuddhanta*).
Having taken that [period] and living in probation for as long as he knows himself to be pure, he should remove that much and live out the remainder of one month or two months.
If he took it thinking, "I am impure for only a month," but while living in probation he remembers another month, that month must also be spent in probation. Again...

There is no requirement for a formal granting of probation (*parivāsa*). Now, if one has taken up the probation thinking, "I have been impure for two months," but while on probation determines, "I was impure for only one month," then only one month must be spent in probation. There is no further requirement for a formal granting of probation.
This is indeed called "probation to the limit of purity" (*suddhantaparivāsa*); it extends both upwards and downwards.
He descends; this is its characteristic. However, regarding the emergence from other offenses, this is the characteristic:

if one performs a legal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) treating an unconcealed offense as concealed, his offense is cleared. If one performs a legal act of the Vinaya treating a concealed offense as unconcealed, it is not cleared. [Likewise] if one treats an offense concealed for a short time as concealed for a long time...
It is cleared away even for one who acts [thinking], "It was concealed long ago" or "it was not concealed long ago.
It is not cleared away for one who acts [thinking], "Having committed one offense, there are many," because without one, there can be no plurality.
However, it is not cleared away for one who acts [thinking], "Having committed many offenses, I am now committing one."
But if one who is questioned according to the method of direct and reverse order as previously described does not know the limit of the nights,
nor remembers it, or is uncertain, the *suddhantaparivāsa* granted to him is called a "great *suddhanta*" (*mahāsuddhanta*).
Having taken that [period], one should dwell in probation by counting the nights from the day it was received until the day of full ordination (*upasampadā*).

This [period] does not ascend further, but descends downwards. Therefore, if while undergoing probation one makes a formal determination regarding the limit of the nights, thinking, "A month or a year has passed for me since the offense was committed," then one must undergo probation for that month or that year.
As for the characteristics of requesting and granting probation, they are to be understood here according to the method set forth later in the text.

It should be understood that at the conclusion of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*), the undertaking of the duties, the period of penance (*mānatta*), and the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) are exactly as previously described.
This is called "probation for purification" (*suddhantaparivāsa*).

"Probation by combination" (*samodhānaparivāsa*) is of three kinds: probation by combining durations (*odhānasamodhāna*), probation by combining values (*agghasamodhāna*), and probation by combining mixed cases (*missakasamodhāna*).

In this context, "covering over by means of a throw" (*odhānasamodhāna*) refers to the probation that is to be granted after one has shaken off and wiped away the days already spent concealing an intermediate offense, and then covered over an offense committed later within the time-limit of the original offense's root date.
Regarding this, it is said further on: "Therefore, monks, let the Saṅgha [grant probation] to the monk Udāyin..."

“Having sent him back to the beginning for one intentional emission of semen offense that was concealed for five days, let him be granted a simultaneous probation (*samodhāna-parivāsa*) for both the previous offense and this one. From this point onward, the detailed account is found in the Pāḷi itself.
Here, however, is the analysis: one who, having taken probation for a concealed offense, is currently undergoing that probation...
If one who is subject to *mānatta*, or who is undergoing *mānatta*, or who is subject to rehabilitation (*abbhāna*),
commits another offense and conceals it for as many nights as the previous offense— or for fewer nights— then, by means of sending him back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*),

all those days already spent in residence and all days spent in *mānatta* are wiped out and treated as days not spent; subsequently, the later offense is [treated] within the context of the original offense.

Having combined [the periods], the probation (parivāsa) must be granted. If, for that person, the root offense was concealed for a fortnight, while the intermediate offense was concealed for less than a fortnight, then the probation must be undergone for exactly one fortnight.
