Furthermore, if the intermediate offense was indeed concealed for a fortnight, then the probation must be undergone for exactly one fortnight.
By this method, the legal determination applies up until the case where the root offense has been concealed for sixty years.

It should be understood as follows: even after having completed sixty years of probation and becoming eligible for the *mānatta* (penance), if one conceals an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) for even a single day, one must again undergo sixty years of probation.
However, if the intermediate offense was concealed for a longer period than the original offense (*mūlāpatti*), then [one must consider] what should be done in that case.
When this was said, the Elder Mahāsumma replied, "This person is incurable; one who is incurable must be dealt with after having been made to confess.
But the Elder Mahāpaduma said, "Why is he called incurable?
Is this not the Samuccayakkhandhaka, which is like the time of the Buddhas? As for an offense, whether it be concealed or unconcealed, or concealed for an equal, less, or greater duration—"
"Or rather, in this case, the authority is simply whether one is capable of joining the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*) of a Vinaya-master.

Therefore, whatever [offense] was concealed for an extended period, having treated that as a root-offense (*mūlāpatti*), one should grant probation by combining the other [offenses] with it. This is called "combination by duration" (*odhānasamodhāna*).
"Combination by value" (*agghasamodhāna*) refers to [the procedure] regarding many offenses, whether one, two, three, or several [of them].

For those offenses that have been concealed for the longest duration, having combined them according to their value, probation is granted for the remaining offenses that were concealed for a shorter duration, by way of delimiting the number of nights. This is called "combination by value.
Furthermore, later [the text states]: "At that time, a certain bhikkhu [committed] several *saṅghādisesa* offenses..."
This is indeed found in the Pāḷi in such a manner as: "He has fallen into [an offense], one offense concealed for one day, one offense concealed for two days," and so forth.

But what should be done when there are one hundred offenses concealed for ten days, and another hundred offenses concealed for ten days—thus making ten times one hundred, a total of one thousand offenses concealed for one hundred days? What is to be done in that case?
Having concealed everything, one must undergo probation for ten days. In this way, by means of a single ten-day period, even a hundred days of probation are fulfilled.
And it has been said: "Having concealed a hundred offenses—a hundred nights; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
“Having stayed for ten nights, one who is on probation would be released.
This is called “aggregation by value.
As for what is called “aggregation by mixture”: this is when various offenses with different bases are combined together and granted. In this regard, the method is as follows:
“Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
one emission of semen, one bodily contact, one lewd speech, one act of self-indulgence, one matchmaking, one building of a hut,
one building of a dwelling, one malicious injury, one irrelevant matter, and one schism in the Saṅgha, as well as one following that schism.”
"One was difficult to speak with; one was a corrupter of families. Therefore, venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for a simultaneous probation (samodhānaparivāsa) for those offenses.
Having had him request this three times, the probation should be granted by means of a formal act (kammavācā) corresponding thereto.
And in this case, it may be that he committed Saṅghādisesa offenses of different bases, or it may be that he committed Saṅghādisesa offenses [of the same base].

In this way, having combined [the details] according to the method previously stated—by way of the *vatthu* (basis), by way of the *gotta* (clan), by way of the name, and by way of the offense—it is indeed permissible to perform the formal act (*kammavācā*).

This is the "combined mixture" (*missakasamodhāna*). Furthermore, at the conclusion of every formal act of probation (*parivāsa*), the discussion regarding whether the duties (*vatta*) have been observed or not, and so forth, should be understood in the same manner as before.
The Discussion on the Parivāsa is finished.
Now, the opportunity has arrived for that which was stated: "We shall explain the fortnight-long *mānatta* and the combined *mānatta* at the conclusion of the remaining discussion on the *parivāsa*.
Therefore, it is said: "The fortnight-long *mānatta* for a bhikkhunī."
The *mānatta* (probation) must be granted. Furthermore, whether the offense was concealed or unconcealed, it must be granted for exactly half a month.
For this has been said: "A bhikkhunī who has committed a heavy offense (*garudhamma*) must undergo the *mānatta* probation for a fortnight before both Saṅghas.
Moreover, that [probation] must be undergone by the bhikkhunīs after they have cleared their own boundary (*sīma*), either within the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*) or...
If they are unable to purify it, they should assemble a quorum of four within a limited boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) at the very least, and then it should be given.
If there is one offense, it should be done on account of that one;

if there are two, three, or many—whether they share the same basis (*vatthu*) or have different bases—it should be done according to whichever [offense] they desire from among those various bases, clans, names, and offenses.
Having taken that [offense], the formal procedure (*yojana*) should be performed. Herein, this is a mere summary by way of a single offense:
having committed it, the nun should approach the Saṅgha of nuns, arrange her upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the elder nuns, and squat down.
Having sat down and extended her hands in reverential salutation, she should speak to her thus: “Venerable lady, I have committed one offense of going beyond the village boundary;
venerable lady, I ask for a half-month’s *mānatta* penance for that one offense of going beyond the village boundary.
After she has made this request three times, a competent and capable nun should inform the Saṅgha:
“Let the Saṅgha, noble ladies, hear me: this bhikkhunī named so-and-so has committed one offense of going beyond the village boundary;
she requests from the Saṅgha a half-month’s probation (pakkhamānatta) for that one offense of going beyond the village boundary.
If it seems right to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant a half-month’s probation for that one offense of going beyond the village boundary to the bhikkhunī named so-and-so. This is the motion.”
“Let the noble Saṅgha hear me: this [nun]... [as before] ... for the second time... for the third time I speak on this matter.

Let the noble Saṅgha hear me... [as before] ... grants... It has been granted by the Saṅgha that the nun named so-and-so undergo the fortnightly *mānatta* discipline for one offense committed within a village boundary.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.”

At the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*), having undertaken the proper conduct (*vatta*) and announced it to the Saṅgha in the same manner as described in the discourse on the *mānatta* penance for a bhikkhu,

she who wishes to dwell there having laid down that conduct must deposit it in the very same way as described in the presence of either a single bhikkhunī or her companion— even if other bhikkhunīs have departed from the midst of the Saṅgha. But for another...
Having announced it to an incoming bhikkhunī, it should be deposited. From the moment it is deposited, she remains in the status of one who has been restored to normal standing (*pakatatta*).
However, for one who undertakes it again and causes the dawn to rise, she is not permitted to dwell in the presence of bhikkhunīs alone;
for it is said: "The *pakkhamānatta* penance must be undergone before both Saṅghas. Therefore, her preceptors and teachers—
Having gone to the monastery, one should speak to a single elder, a Dhamma-preacher, or a monk who stands on the side of those who provide support, saying:
"There is a legal act of the Vinaya to be performed for a certain nun; therefore, noble sirs, send four monks.
It is not permissible for him to say he will not provide support; he must say, "I shall send them. [This should be done] by means of four regular (pakatatta) nuns.

Having taken the bhikkhunī who is undergoing the *mānatta* discipline, they must depart before dawn itself, go beyond two *leḍḍu-pāta*s from the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*), leave the path, and sit in a place concealed by thickets, trees, and so forth. They must also pass beyond two *leḍḍu-pāta*s from the monastery precinct (*vihārūpacāra*).
Four regular (*pakatatta*) bhikkhus must also go there. Having gone, [they should...]
However, one should not sit in the same place as the bhikkhunīs; rather, having stepped back, one should sit at a place that is not too far away.

In the *Kurundi* and *Mahāpaccarī*, however, it is said: "For the sake of self-protection, one should go taking with one either one or two experienced female lay followers (*upāsikā*) from among the bhikkhunīs, or one or two male lay followers (*upāsaka*) from among the bhikkhus. This is stated in the *Kurundi* itself.
It is said that it is permissible to release the vicinity of the nuns' quarters and the monastery, but it is not said [to release] the village.

When the monks and nuns are thus seated, that nun—having undertaken the proper conduct by saying, "I undertake the *mānatta* penance; I undertake the duties"—should first announce this to the community of nuns as follows:
"Venerable ladies, I have committed one offense of entering a village; I [submit myself] to the Saṅgha regarding that one offense of entering a village."
“I requested a half-month *mānatta* penance; the Saṅgha granted me a half-month *mānatta* for that one offense of traveling between villages.
I am now practicing that half-month *mānatta*. ‘Venerable ladies, I announce it; may the Saṅgha remember me as one who announces it.
Then, having gone into the presence of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, he should announce thus: ‘Venerable sirs, I [committed] one offense...’”
“I have committed [an offense]...pe... I am experiencing it, ladies; may the Saṅgha remember me as one who experiences it.
Here too, it is permissible to announce this in whatever language one knows.
Having announced it, one must sit in the presence of the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha alone; from the moment of the announcement, [the responsibility falls upon] the bhikkhus.
It is permissible to go. If there is danger, and the bhikkhunīs expect to return to that very place, she must remain there.
If another bhikkhu or bhikkhunī comes to that place, she must inform her as soon as she sees them.
If she does not inform them, there is a breach of the night-vow and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If she enters the vicinity without even knowing [of the danger] and then departs...
There is only a breach of the night; there is no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the routine.

If the bhikkhunīs wish to go earlier than usual in order to perform their duties toward their preceptors and others, they may do so provided they leave behind one bhikkhunī to guard against the offenses of spending the night apart, leaving the group, or crossing the boundary of a village.
When dawn has risen, that bhikkhunī must deposit the duties in her presence.
By this method, the *mānatta* penance must be observed for fifteen nights in their entirety.
However, one who has not relinquished their formal duties (*anikkhittavatta*) must conduct themselves properly in the manner prescribed in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.
This, however, is the distinction: regarding the instruction "it should be announced to a newcomer," as many [monks] as are present before or after the meal—
If monks or nuns come to that village, it must be announced to everyone.

If one does not announce it, there is both the offense of breaking the night (ratticcheda) and the dukkaṭa offense for violating the formal observance (vatta). Even if a monk enters the vicinity of that village during the night and departs, the night is indeed broken;
however, due to the factor of ignorance, one is exempt from the offense of violating the formal observance. [This is stated] in the Kurundi and other commentaries.
However, it is stated that for monks who have not relinquished their observances, it should be recited in the manner already described.
That [recitation] appears more appropriate because the observances of those on probation (*pārivāsika*) and so forth are delimited by the functional boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
It should be announced at the Uposatha ceremony, it should be announced at the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and it should be announced daily to four monks and four nuns. If there are monks...
If alms-food can be obtained in that village, one should go there. If it cannot be obtained, one may wander elsewhere and then return there to show oneself before departing.
Alternatively, one should make an appointment outside the village, saying, "You will see us at such-and-such a place.
Having gone to the appointed place, she should inform him.
If she does not see him at the appointed place, she should go to the monastery and inform [the monks]. In the monastery, she should inform all the bhikkhus.
If it is not possible to inform everyone, she should stand outside the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*) and send forth bhikkhunīs.
She should inform four bhikkhus who have been brought back by them. If the monastery is distant or dangerous, she should inform lay followers (*upāsaka*).
One must go taking both the nuns and the female lay followers (upāsikās). However, if she lives alone, she incurs the offense of staying apart at night;
therefore, a regular (pakatattā) nun should be appointed and given to her so that they may dwell under one roof.
Having thus practiced the mānatta penance without interruption, her rehabilitation (abbhāna) is to be performed by a community of twenty nuns in the manner already described.

It must be performed. If, while performing the *mānatta* penance, one commits an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), it is stated in the *Kurundi* that one should be sent back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassitvā*) and the *mānatta* for that offense should be granted.
This is called "the fortnight *mānatta*" (*pakkhamānatta*).

Furthermore, "combined *mānatta*" (*samodhānamānatta*) is of three kinds: combination by inclusion (*odhānasamodhāna*), combination by value (*agghasamodhāna*), and combination by mixture (*missakasamodhāna*).

In this regard, concerning that which was said after the Elder Udāyin had been sent back to the beginning for having committed an intermediate offense while he was undergoing probation (*parivāsa*) for an offense concealed for five days,

and while he was in the position of being subject to the trial period (*mānatta*), [the Buddha said]: "Therefore, monks, let the Saṅgha grant a six-night trial period (*mānatta*) for three offenses to the monk Udāyin."
The *mānatta* (probation) is prescribed; this is what is called "the combination by shaking off" (*odhānasamodhāna*).

For this is given by shaking off the days spent living out [the probation] through repeated sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*), and by combining them with the previous offenses; therefore, it is called "combination by shaking off.
However, in the *Kurundi*, it says: "The *mānatta* to be given to one who has completed the *parivāsa* of combination is 'combined *mānatta*' (*samodhānamānatta*)."
This has been stated. That too is appropriate by way of that method.

However, the "combination of values" (*agghasamodhāna*) and the "combined combination" (*missakasamodhāna*) refer specifically to the *mānatta* penance to be granted at the conclusion of the probation (*parivāsa*), the combined probation, and the combined probation;
that should be granted after being applied according to the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*) for probation. Up to this point—

As for what was stated in the Pāḷi by way of numerous modes, beginning with: "In that case, monks, let the Saṅgha grant a one-day probation (parivāsa) to the bhikkhu Udāyī for a single offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day," and so forth—
since the detailed exposition of that probation and the period of penance (mānatta) will be stated in their respective places as they arise:
"Like the Pāḷi, it becomes excessively prolix and cannot be easily grasped; therefore, having synthesized it, we shall present it right here.
Thus, this has been accomplished in terms of its meaning. The Discussion on the Concealed Probation (*paṭicchannaparivāsa*).
102. Now, this portion of the text that has been recited by way of one concealed offense is indeed clear in meaning. 108.

Following that, after the text has been recited by way of concealment for two, three, four, and five days, the intermediate offense is shown starting from the probation (*parivāsa*) for the offense concealed for five days.
However, because one who has committed that offense is subject to being sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraho*), [the text continues].
Therefore, for such a case, sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassana) is permitted.

However, if one who has completed the probationary period commits an offense, he does not deserve to be sent back to the beginning. Why? Because he did not commit the offense while undergoing probation; rather, he committed it while standing in the position of a regular monk (pakatatta).
Therefore, for that offense, a separate period of penance (mānatta) must be observed. This applies if the offense was concealed.

The probation (parivāsa) must also be undergone. Furthermore, when that which was called "sending back to the beginning" (mūlāyapaṭikassana) is performed, the days already spent on probation are wiped clean.

Thus, after showing an intermediate offense during probation, and then showing an intermediate offense for one who is eligible for the penance (mānatta), "sending back to the beginning" is prescribed;
when that too is performed, the days already spent on probation are likewise wiped clean.
Then, for one who has completed the probation (*parivāsa*), the simultaneous observance of *mānatta* for all three of those offenses is shown.
Next, having shown an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*) committed while practicing *mānatta*, the sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*) is stated.

When that sending back has been performed, both the days of the practiced *mānatta* and the days of the completed probation are indeed wiped away. Then, for one who is eligible for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*):
Having shown the intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), the sending back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*) was stated.
When that too has been performed, they all remain as if smeared [with guilt]. Following that, the act of rehabilitation (*abbhānakamma*) is demonstrated by combining all the intermediate offenses.
Thus, in the section on concealment, nine formal acts (*kammavācā*) are shown: five based on the duration of concealment, such as "concealed for one day," and four based on the intermediate offenses.
The Discussion on the Concealed Probation is finished.
The Discussion on the Combined Probation: 125.
Thereafter, regarding an offense concealed for a fortnight, starting from the beginning of the probation, [if it was] concealed for five days...
By way of an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), both simultaneous probation (*samodhānaparivāsa*) and simultaneous penance (*samodhānamānatta*) are demonstrated.

Furthermore, in this context, even when one has been sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassana*) for an offense committed during the period of practicing penance (*mānattacārika*) or while being entitled to penance (*mānattāraha*), all the days of the practiced penance as well as the days already completed of the probation are indeed nullified. Why? Because the intermediate offense was concealed.
Therefore it was said: "Having sent him back to the beginning and having granted him a *samodhānaparivāsa* for the previous offense, let them grant him a six-night *mānatta*.
After that, having combined all the intervening offenses and demonstrated the procedure for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), the section on the emission of semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) was concluded.
The discussion on the *samodhānaparivāsa* is finished.
The Discussion on the Emission of Semen is concluded.
134. The Discussion on the Combination of Values for Probation:
Having then demonstrated two methods—the basis of a single offense and the increase of offenses—the probation through the combination of values is shown.
Then, having shown a case where an offense was intentionally committed but not confessed,

the text is established in the manner beginning with "But here, monks," in order to show what should be done when— after an offense has been intentionally not confessed due to ignorance, lack of mindfulness, or doubt— the qualities of shame arise, or when knowledge, mindfulness, and the absence of doubt subsequently arise. Thereafter...

The text was established in that very manner to show that for those who were ignorant, who had no recollection, who were doubtful, or who had concealed their offense, there is the state of not having concealed it.
The discussion on the combination of values for the probation period is finished.
Now begins the discussion on the two-month probation period.

138. Then, having shown the case of requesting a one-month probation (*parivāsa*) for two offenses concealed for two months, [the text] now shows what should be done when—after the other month has passed and shamefulness (*lajjidhamma*) and so forth have arisen—the fact that the offenses were committed was not reported due to ignorance, lack of recollection, or doubt;
specifically, regarding the concealment of what was committed through ignorance, lack of recollection, or doubt.
The text was established in the same manner as before in order to demonstrate this.
The discussion on the two-month probation is finished.
Now begins the discussion on probation from the point of purification (*suddhanta-parivāsa*), etc.

156. Thereafter, by way of the method beginning with “he does not know the limit of the offense, he does not know the limit of the night,” the *suddhantaparivāsa* (probation until purification) is shown.
160. Following that, the text is established for the purpose of showing the practice regarding those who, having been on probation, fall away and are then re-ordained, and so forth. 165.

In that context, in passages such as “in the interval he commits numerous offenses, limited in number and unconcealed,” the meaning is that they are both “limited” and “unconcealed” by way of the delimitation of the offenses.

166. Regarding "in the last category of offenses" (*āpattikkhandha*): there is only one such category of offense; however, it is called "in the last category of offenses" because it was concealed last. The same principle applies here for the phrase "in the first.
180. "Distinguished and mixed" (*vavatthitā sambhinnā*): this is merely a synonymous expression for those that are similar and dissimilar.
The discussion on the pure end of the probation (*suddhantaparivāsa*) and so forth is concluded.
The Discussion on the Elevenfold Set Beginning with "Two Monks" (181).
Following that, the passage beginning with "two monks" was spoken in order to demonstrate the procedure for one who conceals [an offense].
In this context, "mixed" means mixed with thullaccaya offenses and so forth; "pure" means without a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
[This refers to] the category of light offenses (*lahukāpattikkhandha*) alone. 184.
Following that, in order to demonstrate the state of being impure and pure, it was said: "But here, monks, if a monk [commits] several *saṅghādisesa* [offenses]," and so forth.
Therein, nothing remains unexplained either in terms of the phrasing (*byañjana*) or the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
There is nothing [to be said] further; therefore, both that which has been stated here and all that has not been stated previously should be understood according to the Pāḷi itself.
The discussion on the eleven sections beginning with the "Two-Bhikkhu" section is finished.
The commentary on the Samuccayakkhandhaka is finished.
4. The Chapter on the Settlement of Disputes (Samathakkhandhaka). Discussion on the Resolution Face-to-Face (Sammukhāvinaya): 186–187.
In the Chapter on the Settlement of Disputes, having set forth the six matrix-headings beginning with “a person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma,” etc.
The detailed exposition is stated in the manner beginning with: “A person who speaks contrary to the Dhamma persuades a person who speaks according to the Dhamma.
In this context, “persuades” (saññāpeti) means that having spoken words resembling valid reasons and having gratified [the other], he makes them understand.

“Convinces” (nijjhāpeti) means he acts in such a way that the other person reflects upon and examines that matter. “Considers” (pekkhati) and “considers closely” (anupekkhati) mean that he... [as the other person does].
He perceives the goal and perceives it again and again; thus he acts. "He shows" and "he shows repeatedly" are merely synonyms for those same actions.

It is called "settled by what is not Dhamma" because, having deluded them by showing that which is indeed not Dhamma through such methods as "this is Dhamma," it is therefore said to be settled by what is not Dhamma.

188. "It is settled by means of the Dhamma" (dhammena vūpasammati): because one who speaks according to the Dhamma demonstrates the Dhamma itself—without confusing it—by way of such methods as "This is the Dhamma," therefore it is said to be "settled by means of the Dhamma.
The discussion on *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) is concluded. Now follows the discussion on *sativinaya* (settlement through mindfulness).
195. “Monks, there are these five legitimate grants of *sativinaya* (verdict of mind-purity).
Herein, the grant to one who is pure and without offense is one; the grant to one who has been accused is one; the grant to one who has requested it is one; the grant by the Saṅgha is one;

and the grant according to Dhamma by a unanimous assembly is one—thus there are five. However, these are not obtained by means of each individual factor alone; therefore, this is merely a formal teaching.

However, the granting of a verdict of mindfulness endowed with five factors is what is called "in accordance with the Dhamma" (dhammika) here; this is the meaning in this context. And therein, "they accuse" means they reprove.

The rest is self-evident. Furthermore, this verdict of mindfulness should be granted only to one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), and not to anyone else, not even to a non-returner (anāgāmin). Moreover, it should be granted only to one who is being reproved by another, and not to one who is not being reproved.

Once that has been granted, the charge of the accuser does not hold. Even if he continues to accuse him, he becomes subject to being dismissed with the words: "This one is an arahant who has obtained a verdict of mindfulness;
who would take your word? The discussion on the verdict of mindfulness is concluded.
The Discussion on the Resolution by Reinstatement (Amūḷhavinaya) 196. "Spoken and committed" means spoken by speech and committed by body; the meaning is "committed after having walked [upon it].
Regarding the phrase "Does the Venerable One remember having fallen into such an offense?": here, let the Venerable One remember such an offense.
"An offender": this is the meaning of "an offense of such a kind" regarding the venerable one. Alternatively, the reading is "having committed," the meaning of which is:
"May the venerable one first commit [the offense] and afterwards remember that offense.
The discussion on the verdict of past insanity (*amūḷhavinaya*) is concluded.

202. Regarding the discussion on the majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*): "To settle by means of a majority decision" refers here to that action in which the proponents of the Dhamma are more numerous; this is what is called a majority decision. 204.
Regarding the taking of voting sticks (*salākaggāha*) in an unrighteous manner: "Trifling" (*oramattaka*) means limited, insignificant, merely a matter of dispute.
“Neither gone nor gone to”: it has not been gone to two or three residences, or it has not been settled two or three times right there.
“Neither remembered nor caused to be remembered”: it has not been remembered by those monks themselves, nor caused to be remembered by others, two or three times.
“He knows”: while casting the voting tickets (*salāka*), he knows, “The speakers of what is not Dhamma are in the majority. “Perhaps indeed”: [he thinks].
As the voting sticks were being taken up in this manner, his underlying intention was: "Perhaps those who speak contrary to the Dhamma might be more numerous.
The same method applies to the other two cases as well.

Those who take [the sticks] contrary to the Dhamma are called "adhammavādino" (those speaking contrary to the Dhamma), thinking: "In this way, we shall become many," and thus they take two sticks each.

They take [the voting sticks]. "The faction takes them" means that two who speak according to the Dhamma take one voting stick for those speaking according to the Dhamma, thinking, "In this way, those speaking according to the Dhamma will not be numerous.

And they do not take them according to their own view; that is, having become speakers according to the Dhamma, they take a voting stick for those speaking contrary to the Dhamma, thinking, "We shall join the powerful side. Regarding the taking of voting sticks in accordance with the Dhamma...

This same point should be understood by reversing [the roles]. Having thus distributed the voting tickets (*salāka*), if those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma are in the majority, then that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) should be settled according to what they say; in this way, it is settled by a majority decision (*yebhuyyasikā*).
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, will follow later.
The Discussion on the Majority Decision is concluded.
The Discussion on the Further Censure begins at 207:
"Impure" means endowed with impure bodily and verbal actions. "Shameless" means [one who acts] through intentional transgression and so forth.
He is endowed with the characteristic of being shameless. "With reproach" means with censure. Thus, by way of these three factors, there are three modes of performing [the act]:
performance by the Saṅgha, and performance by a complete assembly in accordance with the Dhamma—these two together make five modes for performing the *tassapāpiyasika* (act of further penalty).
The rest here is exactly as explained in the section on the *tajjanīya* (act of rebuke) and so forth.

This, however, is the meaning of the term here: for since this is to be done by a person who is worse because of the prevalence of evil, it is called "the legal act of pronouncing one worse" (*tassapāpiyasikākamma*).
The discussion on pronouncing one worse is finished.

212. Regarding the discussion on the "covering over as with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*) and so forth: "For the sake of harshness and for the sake of savagery" means for the state of being harsh and for the state of being savage. "For the sake of schism" means for the sake of a schism in the Saṅgha.
"All together in one place" means that without bringing the consent (*chanda*) of anyone, even if they are ill, they should be brought right there and assembled together in one place.
"One should settle by means of the 'covering over as with grass'": here, this procedure is called "covering over as with grass" because it is similar to covering over with grass.

For just as excrement or urine, when trodden upon, causes distress due to its foul odor, yet that odor does not cause distress when it is well-concealed by being covered over with grass; even so, whatever legal issue [is settled in this manner]...
When a dispute is being settled by going back to the root and the sub-roots, it leads to harshness, ferocity, and schism;

however, when that same dispute is settled by this particular procedure—being concealed like excrement covered over with grass—it becomes perfectly pacified. Because this procedure is similar to covering over with grass, it is called "covering over with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*).

213. "Gross offenses" (*thullavajja*) refers to both *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa* offenses. "Connected with householders" (*gihipaṭisaṃyutta*) refers to an offense incurred in the censuring, reviling, or lawful refusal of requests by householders.
214. "And thus, monks, those bhikkhus have emerged from those offenses":

when this formal act (*kammavācā*) of covering over as with grass has been performed, at the conclusion of that formal act, however many [bhikkhus] were assembled there—even down to those who were merely asleep or in a state of meditation—[they all emerge].
Even those monks who acted otherwise— starting from the time of the ordination assembly (upasampadā-maṇḍala)—
have emerged from all those offenses, with the exception of grave offenses (thullavajja) and those connected with householders.
However, as for those who exchange views with one another, saying, "This does not please me," even if they have committed an offense together with them...
In this regard, those who have not yet arrived, or who have arrived but remain in their cells or other quarters after having given their consent, do not emerge from their offenses.
Therefore it was said: "excepting the manifestation of the view, and excepting those who are not present there.
The discussion on the covering over as with grass and so forth is concluded.
Adhikaraṇakathā 215.
“Anupakhajja” means having entered among the bhikkhunīs.

The meaning of the terms *vivādādhikaraṇa* and so forth has already been stated in the commentary on the *duṭṭhadosa*. It is called a “transaction” (*vohāra*) because it results in maturation; that is, for the sake of mental suffering.
"Vohāra" means harsh speech. "Yo tattha anuvādo" means whatever reproach there is among those who are reproaching. "Anuvadanā" is a demonstrative term for the manner [of speaking];
its meaning is "upavadanā" (reproaching). "Anullapanā" and "anubhaṇanā" are both merely synonyms for "anuvadanā.
"Anusampavaṅkatā" refers to repeatedly [engaging] in that very same [speech] with body, mind, and voice.
*Saṃpavaṅkatā*: the meaning is the state of speaking in conformity [with others]. *Abbhussahanatā*:
having made an effort, thinking, "Why should I not speak thus in blame? I shall indeed speak in blame," it is the act of blaming. *Anubalappadānaṃ*:
providing support by showing the reason for the previous statement through a subsequent statement.

Regarding the terms *kiccayatā* (the state of being a duty) and *karaṇīyatā* (the state of being what ought to be done): here, *kicca* itself is *kiccaya*; the state of being *kiccaya* is *kiccayatā*, and the state of being *karaṇīya* is *karaṇīyatā*.

Both of these are synonyms for the formal act (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha. The terms "act of notification" (*apalokanakamma*) and so forth, however, are expressions for its specific classifications.
Among these, an "act of notification" means having cleared the Saṅgha of those residing within the boundary (*sīmā*).
A formal act (kamma) that must be performed after bringing forward the consent of those entitled to give it, and announcing it three times with the approval of a united Saṅgha.
A *ñattikamma* is a formal act to be performed by a single motion (*ñatti*) with the approval of a united Saṅgha, according to the method already stated.
A *ñattidutiyakamma* is a formal act [to be performed] with the approval of a united Saṅgha, according to the method already stated...
"With one consent, one motion, and one proclamation"—thus is the formal act to be performed by means of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).

A "formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations" (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is, in the same manner as described, a formal act to be performed by means of the consent of a unanimous Saṅgha through one motion and three proclamations; thus it is by means of a motion followed by three proclamations.
In this regard, a *apalokanakamma* (an act by intimation) must be performed solely by means of intimation; it must not be performed by way of a motion (*ñatti*) or other such formal acts.
A *ñattikamma* (an act consisting of a single motion) must also be performed by establishing only one motion; it must not be performed by way of an act of intimation or other such formal acts.

However, a *ñattidutiyakamma* (an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation) may sometimes be performed after intimating, and sometimes it may not. Among these, the authorization of a boundary (*sīmāsammuti*) and the abolition of a boundary (*sīmāsamūhanana*)...

The six formal acts that are weighty—the offering of the *kathina*, the removal of the *kathina*, the designation of the site for a hut, and the designation of the site for a monastery—may not be performed after merely seeking permission;
they must be performed only after proclaiming the motion consisting of two parts (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
Furthermore, there are the remaining thirteen authorizations (*sammuti*), such as the authorization for the assigner of lodgings, the distributor of robes, and so forth; these are of such a nature.
Light formal acts (lahukakamma) may be performed even by means of a mere announcement (apalokana).

However, they must not be performed by way of a motion (ñatti) or a motion followed by a fourth proclamation (ñatticatutthakamma). A motion-and-fourth-proclamation act must be performed only after announcing the motion and the three proclamations;
it must not be performed by way of an announcement act or the like. This is the summary here.

In detail, however, the analysis of these four types of kamma has already been presented at the conclusion of the Parivāra, in the Kammavagga, by way of such methods as: "In how many ways do they fail?
and so forth. Whatever therein remains unexplained, that we shall explain specifically in the Kammavagga itself.
For if this were done here, it would not be an exposition in the appropriate place; and thus, starting from the beginning, its [proper] treatment will follow.
Because that action has been understood, it will be easy to comprehend. 216.
Regarding the questions such as "What is the root of a legal issue arising from dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*)?", these should be understood according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself. 220.

In passages such as "A legal issue arising from dispute may be wholesome," the meaning should be seen in this manner: the mental state by which they dispute is the "dispute" (*vivāda*), and it is called a "legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) because it is to be settled by means of the methods of resolution (*samatha*). Thus the sense is to be understood.
222. Regarding the statement, "A legal issue arising from an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome (akusala) or indeterminate (abyākata);
there is no legal issue arising from an offense that is wholesome (kusala)," the meaning should be understood according to what was intended by this statement.

For if a wholesome mind were a factor in a legal issue arising from an offense—such as digging the earth—then it would not be possible to say, "There is no legal issue arising from an offense that is wholesome."
Therefore, this was not said with reference to a consciousness sufficient [to constitute] a factor [of an offense]. Rather, it was said with reference to this:

whatever legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is a transgression against the world (*lokavajja*), that is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*); in that case, there is no alternative possibility such as "it might be unwholesome.
However, as for that which is a transgression against the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), since one intentionally thinks, "I am transgressing this offense,"...

Unwholesome (akusala) [kamma] occurs only for one who transgresses intentionally; however, for one who unknowingly commits an offense through such means as sharing a bed without intent, it is indeterminate (abyākata).
Therefore, with reference to this distinction between intentional and unintentional action, it was said therein:
"An offense-dispute (āpattādhikaraṇa) may be unwholesome, it may be indeterminate, but there is no offense-dispute that is wholesome."

If, however, one were to say, "That which a person with a wholesome mind commits is called an offense-originated legal issue (āpattādhikaraṇa) that is wholesome," then even for those offenses originating from woolly sheep’s hair, footprints, or *sodhamma* [cloth], a wholesome mind would have to be present;
yet a wholesome mind existing therein is not a factor for the offense. Rather, it applies to those actions set in motion through bodily or verbal intimation (*viññatti*).
It is either one or another factor of body or speech, and because it is included within the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), it is indeterminate (abyākata).

Regarding the phrase "one who knows," etc., the meaning is as follows: that consciousness which is a factor for the offense—knowing the basis (vatthu) by means of that [consciousness], and knowing and perceiving it together with the mode of transgression, thinking "I am transgressing this"—by way of the volition of transgression...
Having intended and planned it, crushing by means of an effort, having overcome [the resistance], and having sent forth a mind free from apprehension,
whatever transgression of an offense-formal issue (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) one commits—
this transgression resulting from such a transgression is called "an unwholesome offense-formal issue."
In the section on the indeterminate (*abyākatavāra*), regarding that consciousness which constitutes a factor for an offense: by its absence, one does not know;
and by not knowing the mode of transgression, one does not recognize it. By the absence of the volition of transgression—which is a factor for the offense—one does not intend it.
By the absence of deliberate crushing, one does not willfully direct it. Without sending forth a mind free from apprehension, whatever legal issue of an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) there may be—
He commits a transgression; that which is the transgression from such a transgressing is called "an indeterminate legal issue arising from an offense" (*āpattādhikaraṇaṃ abyākataṃ*). 224.

In phrases such as "this dispute is not a legal issue," the meaning should be understood as "not a legal issue" because it lacks the quality of being something to be settled by the means of reconciliation (*samatha*).
The Discussion on Legal Issues is concluded.
**The Discussion on the Settling of Legal Matters (Adhikaraṇavūpasamana-samatha-kathā)** 228.

Regarding the phrase "as many bhikkhus as are competent for the formal act": here it should be understood that for a formal act performed by a quorum of four, four bhikkhus are competent; for one performed by a quorum of five, five; for one performed by a quorum of ten, ten; and for one performed by a quorum of twenty, twenty bhikkhus are competent. 230.
"Well-attended" means it should be accepted after having been properly attended to. Having accepted it...
Furthermore, for the sake of restraining pride, one should let a few days pass, thinking: "Today we shall wash our requisites; today we shall bake our bowls; today there is some obstacle.
231. "Infinite discourses arise" means that immeasurable words emerge here and there.
“Bhāsāni” is also a reading; it has this same meaning. He should be appointed by a committee (*ubbāhikā*);

that is, he may be appointed either by a mere motion (*apalokana*) or by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), as will be stated later. Once appointed, those monks should sit down separately or within that very assembly and announce: “Nothing should be said by others who have not been so appointed.”
That legal case must be adjudicated. 233. *Tatrāssa* means "in that assembly.
*Naiva suttaṃ āgataṃ* means it has not come down in the Sutta; *na mātikā āgatā* means it has not come down in the Mātikā.
*No suttavibhaṅgo* means the Vinaya is not well-mastered. *Byañjanacchāyāya atthaṃ paṭibāhati* means that the mere letter obstructs the meaning.

Having grasped the meaning, he refutes it. Seeing monks who are experts in the Vinaya being made to incur an offense for accepting gold, silver, fields, or land, he says: "Why do you make them incur an offense?
Has it not been stated in the Sutta, 'He abstains from accepting gold and silver,' that there is merely an abstinence mentioned here, and no offense exists in this case?"
Another Dhamma-preacher, because it is so stated in the Sutta, says regarding those who put on their lower robe while letting it hang down:
"Why do you charge them with an offense? Is it not simply stated here that 'the training is to be observed thus: "I shall wear the lower robe all around"'? There is no offense here."
234. Regarding the phrase "more numerous bhikkhus": even with just one more person they are "more numerous," so what need is there to mention two or three?
The discussion on the methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
The discussion on the taking of ballots (*salākā*) in three ways.

235. "For the purpose of persuasion" means for the sake of making [the assembly] understand. Regarding the terms "in secret" and so forth: a secret ballot (*salākaggāha*) should be conducted before an assembly consisting mostly of shameless persons;
an open ballot (*vivaṭaka*) before an assembly consisting mostly of conscientious persons; and a whispering in the ear (*sakaṇṇajappaka*) before an assembly consisting mostly of fools.
"Having made marks and counter-marks" means having assigned signs and tokens to the ballots of those who speak according to the Dhamma and those who speak against the Dhamma.
They should be made dissimilar from one another. Then, having placed all of them within the folds of the robes, they should be distributed according to the method already described.
Regarding the instruction "if it is wrongly taken, it should be withdrawn": having said, "The voting sticks have been wrongly taken," they should be taken up again and distributed up to three times.

Regarding the instruction "it should be announced that it is rightly taken": even if there is only one person in excess among those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma, [it should be announced that it is rightly taken].
"Voting sticks must be announced. "The legal case should be settled according to what those who speak according to the Dhamma say.
Then, if even up to the third time the speakers of non-Dhamma remain in the majority, they rise saying, "Today is not the right time;
we shall know tomorrow," and for the sake of breaking the faction of the shameless ones, they search for a faction of those who speak according to the Dhamma on the following day.
A voting by lot (salākaggāha) should be performed. This is the secret voting by lot.
However, when the "whispering-in-the-ear" method is employed, it should be said:

"In this matter, if the senior of the Saṅgha takes a voting stick that speaks against the Dhamma, he should be thus enlightened: 'Venerable sir, you are advanced in years and have reached old age; for you..."
"This is not appropriate; however, this is the voting stick for those who speak according to the Dhamma.
Thus he should be shown the other voting stick. If he takes that one, it should be given to him. If, however, he does not understand, he should then be told, "Do not tell anyone.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. *Vivaṭaka* means simply one whose meaning has been revealed.
The Discussion on the Threefold Taking of Votes is finished.
238. Regarding the Discussion on the Vinaya Procedure of Further Exasperation (*tassapāpiyasikā*):
"Near to a *pārājika*"—here, that which is near to a *pārājika* offense regarding sexual intercourse is a *dukkaṭa*.
In cases such as taking what is not given, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). "One who unravels" means one who unravels by saying, "I do not remember.
"One who overwraps" means one is overwrapped by such words as, "Come now, venerable sir. "I indeed remember, friend," he thus admits for the sake of concealing a defeat (*pārājika*).
Being further overwrapped by him, after giving his admission that "I indeed remember," [he says], "Now me..."
Out of fear that they would destroy him, he said, "For sport's sake," and so forth. Against him, a *tassapāpiyasikā* (act of further penalty) should be carried out.
If he is virtuous, then by fulfilling his duties he obtains the cessation [of the offense];
if not, he remains one who has been destroyed. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The Discussion on the *Tassapāpiyasika* Method of Settling Disputes is finished.
The Commentary on the *Samatha-kkhandhaka* is finished.
5. The *Khuddakavatthu-kkhandhaka*.

243. Discussion on the Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukathā). In the Section on Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka): “Boxers” (*mallamuṭṭhika*) refers to professional boxers. “Village dandy” (*gāmamuddava*) refers to city-dwellers devoted to grooming their bodies and adorning themselves with cosmetics.
There is also a reading *gāmamoddavā*; it has the same meaning. “Pillar” (*thambha*) refers to a pillar erected by being driven into the ground at a bathing place.
"He hews" means he hews either brick, stone, or wood.
"Bathing at a *aṭṭhāna*"—here, a *aṭṭhāna* is a bathing place where they carve out a site like a tree-trunk or a plank, cut lines in the shape of a checkerboard pattern, and bury it;
there, people sprinkle powder and rub their bodies. "With a *gandhabbahatthaka*" [refers to] at the bathing place.
With a wooden hand that has been set up; it is said that people take powder with it and rub their bodies.
"A bundle of *kuruvindaka* beads" refers to a cluster of pills made by binding *kuruvindaka* stone powder with lac;
they take hold of it at both ends and rub their bodies. "They perform the preparatory service while quarreling."
They rub body against body with one another. What is called a "shell" (*mallaka*) is made by cutting shark-teeth and shaping them like the base of a shell;
this is not permitted even for one who is ill. 244.
What is called an "unmade shell" is made by not cutting the teeth; this is not permitted for anyone except one who is ill. A fragment of brick...
However, a fragment of a skull is also permissible. "Ukkāsika" refers to a cloth roll; therefore, it is permissible for anyone bathing to rub the back with a roll of a bathing cloth.
"Puthupāṇika" refers to hand-massage; therefore, it is permissible for everyone to perform back-massage with the hand.
245. *Vallikā* is a designation for ear-hangers, pendants, and the like protruding from the ears;
and it is not only *vallikā* that is forbidden, but no ear-ornament whatsoever—even a palm leaf—is permissible.
*Pāmaṅga* refers to any kind of hanging thread. *Kaṇṭhasuttaka* refers to any kind of neck ornament. *Kaṭisuttaka* refers to... [a waist-belt].
"Any waist-ornament," including even a mere thread; "an ankle-bracelet" means a bangle.
Bracelets and so forth are well known; any ornament below the wrist-joints on the arms is not permitted.
246. "Two months' growth or two finger-breadths": here, if the hair reaches two finger-breadths within two months, [it is permissible].
It must be cut [repaired] within two months. It is not permitted to let it exceed two finger-breadths [in length].

Even if it is not long, it is likewise not permitted to let it exceed two months by even a single day; thus, this is stated as the maximum limit in both respects, for there is no such thing as a "new" status once that period has passed.
“Rubbing with a brush” means having rubbed with a brush, they cause it to settle. “With a comb” means with anything made of ivory and so forth.
“With a hand-comb” means performing the function of a comb with the hand itself, rubbing it with the fingers.
“With honey-wax oil” means with any sticky substance such as honey, wax, resin, and so forth. “With water-oil” means...
With oil mixed with water. For the purpose of adornment, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in every case;

however, for the sake of smoothing down the hair that grows upward, one may moisten the hand and wipe the head. It is also permissible for those whose heads are covered in dust from being heated by the sun to wipe them with a wet hand. 247.
"Monks, [one should not look] in a mirror or in a bowl of water"—here, this includes bronze bowls and other such items in which the reflection of the face [can be seen].
Everything becomes as if reflected in a mirror. Even sour gruel and the like become as if in a bowl of water.
Therefore, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for anyone looking at anything [in this way]. Regarding "on account of illness":

it is said that it is permissible to look for the purpose of knowing whether one's wound has healed or not yet healed, and also for the purpose of observing the formations of life (*āyu-saṅkhāra*) by thinking, "Am I old or not?"
“They smear their faces” means they smear them with face-pastes that produce a clear complexion and luster.
“They massage” means they massage with various unguents. “They powder” means they dust the face with facial powder.
“They mark the face with red arsenic” means they make marks such as *tilaka*s on the face with red arsenic; even using yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) and so forth for these is not permitted.
Body ointments and the like are already evident. In all such cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). 248.
Regarding the rules beginning with "Monks, one should not go to see dancing," etc.: for one who goes to see any kind of dance whatsoever—even a peacock’s dance—there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For one who dances oneself, or causes another to dance, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing. The same applies to singing.

Whatever there may be—whether the singing of actors, the singing of virtuous men, or even the gnashing of teeth—if they produce sounds at the outset while thinking, "We shall sing," this is not permitted.
For one who sings oneself or causes others to sing, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Playing any kind of musical instrument is likewise not permitted. However, if one is spitting or standing in a place of danger, the snapping of fingers...
If he snaps his fingers or strikes with his hand, there is no offense in that case. There is no offense for one standing within the monastery grounds who sees [the act].
There is indeed an offense for one who goes from one dwelling to another dwelling with the thought, "I will see. If he sits in the assembly hall and sees it, there is no offense.
There is an offense for one who stands up and goes with the thought, "I will see. Standing on the path, [turning] the neck...
Even for one who looks after having turned [the bowl] over, it is indeed an offense. 249.
*Sarakuttiṃ* means the act of juggling. *Bhaṅgo hoti* means he is unable to produce what has not been obtained, nor can he attain what has been obtained.
*Pacchimā janatā* means that even our teachers and preceptors sang in this way; thus, it is "the last generation."
People follow what they have seen and sing in that very same way.
Monks, regarding the phrase "not with drawn-out [intonation]," here "drawn-out" refers to that which proceeds by breaking the respective rhythmic rules (*vatta*) and destroying the syllables.

Now, in the Dhamma, there is the rhythmic rule for the Suttantas, there is the rhythmic rule for the Jātakas, and there is the rhythmic rule for the Gāthās; having destroyed those, [to recite] too long—
It is not permissible to do so. The words and phrases should be presented with a square gait and a circular gait.
*Sarabhañña* means reciting with a melodic tone. It is said that in *sarabhañña* there are thirty-two types of gait, such as the wave-gait, the washed-gait, the galloping-gait, and the flowing-gait;
among these, one may employ whichever one desires. [This applies to] the words and phrases of all [recitations].
The characteristic is simply the wearing [of the robe] in a square manner, in accordance with the suitability for a recluse, without tearing or altering it.
Regarding "wool with the nap outside": they put on a woolen cloak having placed the woolly nap on the outside;

for one who wears it in that way, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). It is permissible to wear it with the nap inside. The discussion on what is appropriate for a recluse has been stated in the commentary on the training rule concerning plants and seeds (bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada).
251. “Monks, regarding ‘one’s own private parts’: for one who cuts off only the private parts, there is a *thullaccaya* offense.
However, for one who cuts off anything else—such as the ear, nose, finger, or other limbs—or for one who inflicts similar pain [on another], there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
But there is no offense for one who cuts off [limbs] or causes blood to flow in cases such as being bitten by a snake or insects, or for the purpose of treating another ailment.”
"252. 'A sandalwood knot has appeared' means a sandalwood casket has appeared.

It is said that after having nets cast both upstream and downstream, he was playing in the river Gaṅgā; as he was being carried away by the current of the river, a sandalwood knot came and became snagged in the net.
His men brought it and gave it to him; thus it 'appeared. This is a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*)."

Vessels are not permitted for use by an individual alone; however, they are permitted for use by the Saṅgha or if they are discarded items belonging to a householder.
"Even a bowl made of copper is not permitted, but a platter is permitted"—all of this is stated in the *Kurundi*.
Regarding the phrase "made of gemstone," this refers to those made of sapphire (*indanīla*) and other such gems. Regarding the phrase "made of bronze" (*kaṃsamaya*), here—
Even one made of round metal is included. 253.
"Engraved" is said for the purpose of making it thin. "Ordinary bowl-rim" refers specifically to a bowl-rim cut with makara-teeth. 254.
"Having turned over" means having struck one another. Regarding "a bowl-rest," here [the text says] "by means of ivory, creepers, rattan, and so forth..."
"In the *Kurundi*, it is stated: 'When there are three earthenware stands, it is permissible to place two wooden stands one on top of the other.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: 'On an earthenware stand, there is no room for three bowls; it is permissible to place two.
The same rule applies even when wooden stands or staff-stands are well-prepared. [A stand] resembling the edge of a lathe..."
However, a wooden rack bound with three pegs, or a peg-stand, provides no space even for a single bowl;
having placed it there, one must sit while holding it by hand. But on the ground, it may be placed overturned so that it stands alone.
"At the edge" means at the edge of a porch, a veranda, and so forth. However, if, after being turned over, it remains standing right there, [it is permissible].
It is proper to place [the bowl] on such a broad mat. "At the edge" (*paribhaṇḍante*) means at the edge of a thin mat made on the outer side.
The detailed explanation here should be understood in the same manner as that stated for the mat.
"A cloth" (*coḷakaṃ*) is that which is spread out upon which the bowl is placed; but in its absence, on a wicker stool or a wooden board.
It is permissible to place it on ground that has been plastered with clay, or on ground where it does not get dirty, or on such sand.
However, for one who places it on dusty soil or rough ground, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
It is permissible to construct a bowl-shed (pattamaḷaka) either of bricks or of wood. A "bowl-basket" (pattakuṇḍolikā) is a small wicker container shaped like a large-mouthed bowl.
It is said: "Whoever should stick it on"—for one who sticks it anywhere, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). It is not permitted to tie it even to a robe-stand and leave it there.

Whether it was made for the purpose of storing goods or for the purpose of sitting or lying down, for one who places it anywhere—on a bed or a chair—there is an offense of wrong-doing; however, [it is permissible] along with other goods...
It is permissible to tie it and set it aside. It is permissible to tie it to a crossbar and hang it, but even after tying it, it is not permissible to place it on top [of other items].

However, if a bed or a chair has been lifted and placed upon a robe-rod or similar support so that it is covered by a canopy, it is permissible to place it there. With a shoulder-padded cloth, [on] the shoulder...
It is permissible to place [food] on one's lap. It is not permissible to place even a single *bhattapūra* (a full bowl of food) on a parasol, nor even a leaf held on the shoulder.
However, anything placed together with one's belongings—either tied up or set upon a stand—is permissible.
255. Regarding the term "one with a bowl in hand": it is not only the case that one who has a bowl in his hand is "one with a bowl in hand"; it is not...
Moreover, he is not permitted to open the door-panel alone; rather, provided there is a bowl anywhere on his body—
whether in his hand, on his back, or on his foot— he may open the door-panel with his hand,
his foot, his head, or any other part of his body, or lift the bolt with a needle using a key.
One is not permitted to open it. However, having hung the bowl from the shoulder, one is permitted to open it as desired.
"A gourd-vessel" refers to a vessel made of a gourd; it is not allowable to carry that about. But having obtained it, it is allowable to use it for a limited time.
The same rule applies to a jar-vessel (*ghaṭikaṭāha*). "Jar-vessel" means a jar-fragment. *Abhuṃ*...
"Meti" is a word meaning "fear. Regarding "one who uses only rag-robes": here, both robes and bedding (mattresses and stools) may be rag-robes;
however, as for food to be swallowed, only that which has been given [as alms] should be accepted.
"Cakes" refers to scraps of meat thrown away after being chewed. "Bones" refers to the bones of fish and meat. "Leftover water" refers to...
Water for rinsing the mouth: for one who empties any of these [liquids] from the bowl, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
One may not wash one's hands even after having used the bowl as a receptacle. It is not permitted to pour water used for washing hands or feet into the bowl and then empty it out.
It is not permitted to take a clean bowl that has not been soiled with food waste with a hand that is soiled with food waste.
In this case, however, one may pour water with the left hand, take a mouthful of water, and it is permissible to hold it with the soiled hand;
for at that point, the bowl becomes soiled. But after rinsing the hand with water on the outside, it is permissible to take it.
When eating fish, meat, fruits, or other such foods, whatever bone...
If one wishes to discard either a bone or a piece of flesh, one is not permitted to place it in the bowl. However, if one wishes to chew it, one is permitted to place it in the bowl.
As for bones, thorns, and the like, it is permissible to leave them right there, pull them out with the hand, and eat them.
But if one wishes to eat again anything that has been removed from the mouth, that may be placed in the bowl.
One is not permitted to leave it [there]. Having bitten off pieces of ginger or coconut, one is permitted to leave them again.
256. *Namataka*: a piece of cloth used for wrapping a knife. *Daṇḍasatthaka*: a knife made by attaching a handle, such as a pepper-cutter or any other stick.
*Kaṇṇakitā hontī*: they become stained with grime. *Kiṇṇena pūretun*: to fill with powdered rice-flour (*kiṇṇacuṇṇa*). *Sattuyā*: with parched grain.
"With flour-dust mixed with turmeric. "Saritaka" refers to stone powder; the meaning is that I authorize [the use of] it for filling.
"To refresh with honey-dregs" means to smear with honey-dregs. "The refreshed [sheath] breaks open" means that the sheath smeared with honey-dregs breaks.
"A refreshed sword-sheath" refers to a cloth sheath made of honey-dregs; [this is] for a sword-case sheath.

However, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that [the cloth] is "in accordance with" a well-polished wooden board. "Kathina" refers to either a ladder or any one of the mats, straw mats, or reed screens to be spread thereon.
"Kathina-rope" is that by which they sew the double-layered robe and also bind the robe to the kathina frame.
"The kathina is not sufficient" means that the kathina made according to the measurement of a tall monk is [insufficient] for a short one.
When a monk’s robe, while being spread out, does not suffice, it remains inside [the frame] and does not reach the crossbar—this is the meaning.
“A crossbar-frame” (daṇḍakathina) means: I allow him to fasten another ladder in its middle according to the measurement of the other monk. “Bidalaka” means:
folding back the edges of the matting to the measurement of the crossbar-frame and making it double-layered.
"Salākā" refers to a pin for inserting between the two layers of a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*).
"Binding rope" (*vinandhanarajju*) refers to the rope used to bind a small ladder together with a large ladder.
"Binding thread" (*vinandhanasutta*) refers to the cord used to bind the robe to the small ladder. "Having bound it, one sews the robe" means that by means of that thread, one sews it there.
Having dyed the robe-cloth, [he should] sew it. "They become uneven" means some are small and some are large.
"A *kaḷimbhaka*" refers to anything such as a palm leaf used for making a mark to indicate measurement.
"False thread" refers to making a mark with turmeric thread on wood, like carpenters do with black thread. "Receiving with the finger" means receiving the needle-end with the finger.
They receive it in a finger-ring (aṅgulikosaka). 257.
"A workshop box" (āvesanavitthaka) means any small container such as a bowl for betel-nut and so forth.
"On a high base" means that I allow one to make it on a high base by scattering earth [over it]. "Having plastered over it, one should make it smeared inside and out" refers to the roof-covering.
"Having shaken it out and made it a thick-staffed [roll], one should smear it with clay both inside and out"—this is the meaning.
"With a cow-horn-shaped [tube]" means having inserted a bamboo or a wooden staff inside, one should roll it up together with that—this is the meaning.
"A binding cord" refers to the binding cord for that which has been rolled up in such a manner.
258. A "ladle-sieve" (kaṭacchuparissāvana) is one made by tying [cloth] around three sticks.
259. "He who would not give": an offense applies to one who does not give to someone who lacks a sieve.
However, if someone asks while a sieve is already in their own hand, one need not give it against one's will. A "stick-sieve" (daṇḍaparissāvana) is...

Just as with the alkaline straining-cloth of washermen, one should tie a cloth to a ladder fixed at its four feet and pour water onto the middle crossbar; it then flows through, filling both sections.
What is called a "filter" (*ottharaka*) is that which is spread out in the water so that water is drawn up by means of a jar; for in that case, the cloth [is placed] upon four sticks.

Having tied [the raft] together, having sunk four stakes into the water, and having fastened it to them, they release all the edges from the water, pile up [the wood] in the middle, and take up water with a jar. "A mosquito-hut" refers to a robe-hut.
260. "With bodies overflowing" means with bodies overflowing with phlegm and other humors. A "door-lintel" (aggaḷavaṭṭi) is one that is exactly equal in measure to the door-posts.
The "bolt-post" (aggaḷatthambha) is so called because three or four holes are made there into which bolts are inserted.
The "monkey-head" (kapisīsaka) is the bolt-socket (aggaḷapāsaka) inserted there after piercing the door-jambs.
The "bolts" (sūcikā) are those inserted through a hole made in the middle of that [socket]. The "knobs" (ghaṭikā) are those fixed on top. "To make it circular" means to have a low base.
To build. "Smoke-hole" means an opening for the exit of smoke. "To scent" means to scent with fragrance.
"Water-place" means a place for keeping water; having placed water there in a jar, it should be used from a basin.
"Corner" refers to a door-corner. 261. Regarding "three coverings": here, the covering for the sauna (*jantāghara*) and the covering for the water are the preparatory work.

It is permissible only for one who is actually performing [the act]; it is not permissible for the others, such as those merely paying homage and so forth. A lower garment (*vatthapaṭicchādi*) is permissible for all formal acts. "There is no water" means there is no bathing water. 262.
*Tula* refers to a scale for carrying water, like those used by vendors. *Karakatako* is said to be that which is yoked to oxen...
"Dragging it with the hands" means pulling it along by means of long leather straps and so forth. "A water-wheel" (cakkavaṭṭaka) refers to a pulley system for drawing water.
"A leather vessel" (cammakhaṇḍa) is a leather container that is to be fastened either to a balance-beam or to a hook. "It is exposed" means it is not enclosed by a fence.
"A water-wiper" (udakapuñchanī) may be made of bamboo, horn, or wood; it is permissible [to use any of these]. Of that—
If there is no cloth, it is permissible to scoop out the water even with a small rag.
263. "Watercourse" (*udakamātikā*) means the channel by which water flows. A "broom-house" (*nillekhajantāghara*) is called a house with curved side-walls;
this is the name for a gabled roof constructed by placing side-walls on a circular frame above the rafters.
"Regarding 'the four-month period with the sitting mat' (nisīdana): the meaning is that one must not stay apart from the sitting mat for four months.
264. "In places strewn with flowers" means in places covered with flowers. A "namataka" is made of sheep's wool and is unwoven;
it should be used in the same manner as a piece of hide. An "āsittakūpadhāna" is [a bowl-rest] made of either copper or silver.
This is a designation for a box that has been made; however, because it is rejected [as a container], even one made of wood is not permitted.
A *maḷorikā* is called a staff-holder. Staff-rests, leaf-rests, and the backs of small baskets are also included herein.
From the point when they come under the category of "rests," whether they have holes or not, or are pierced or unpierced, they are indeed permitted. Regarding "a single vessel":
In this regard, if one monk takes fruit or cake from the vessel and departs, when he has gone, it is permissible for the other to eat what remains.
For the other as well, it is permissible to take more once that [remaining portion] is exhausted. 265.
Regarding the phrase "with eight factors": here, even if one possesses only a single factor, whether within the boundary (*sīmā*) or outside the boundary (*nissīma*)—
It is indeed proper to overturn [the bowl] in rivers and such places. Once the bowl has been overturned in this manner, no gift should be accepted from that person's house;
one should send out [messengers] to other monasteries as well, saying, "Do not accept alms in the house of so-and-so.

At the time of righting it, however, after having had the request made up to three times and having had [the person] move beyond arm’s reach, it should be righted by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma).
268. *Purakkhatvā* means having placed [him] at the head. *Saṃharantū* means let them be gathered. *Celapaṭikaṃ* means a cloth-spreading.
It is said that he spread it with this underlying intention: "If I obtain a son, the Blessed One will step upon my cloth-spreading.
Yet, he was incapable of obtaining a son; therefore, the Blessed One did not step on it. Had he stepped on it, afterwards...
One who does not obtain a son might form the view that "this one is not omniscient. This, first of all, is the reason for the Blessed One’s not stepping over [the threshold].
Furthermore, since even monks who do not know [of this] might step over it, they would become despised by householders;
therefore, he laid down the training rule (sikkhāpada) in order to protect the monks from such contempt. This is the reason for the promulgation of the training rule.

"By one who is requested for the sake of an auspicious occasion": whether she has recently given birth or is heavily pregnant, it is permissible to step on such places when one is requested for the sake of an auspicious occasion.

"A place where the feet have been washed" means a rug or covering spread out in a foot-washing area for the purpose of stepping upon after the feet have been washed; it is permissible to step on that.
269. *Kataka* is a foot scrubber shaped like a lotus seed-vessel (*padumakaṇṇika*), made by driving in thorns.
Whether it is circular or of other shapes such as square, it is strictly prohibited because it involves indulgence in luxury.
It is neither permitted to accept nor to use. "Gravel" refers to stone; it also includes stone-foam (*pāsāṇaphenaka*).

It is permissible. A "fan" (*vidhūpana*) is called a *vījanī*. As for a palm-leaf fan (*tālavaṇṭa*), whether it is made of palm leaves, or of bamboo, ivory, or reeds, or of peacock feathers, or of leather products—all are permissible.
A mosquito fan (*makasabījanī*) with a handle made of ivory or horn is also permissible;
this includes fans made of wool, or of *ketaka* shoots, *kuntāla* leaves, and so forth.

270. "An umbrella for one who is ill": here, for anyone who suffers from a burning sensation in the body, an excess of bile, weak eyesight, or any other ailment that arises without an umbrella, an umbrella is permitted whether in a village or in the forest.

Furthermore, during the rainy season, it is permitted for the purpose of protecting one's robes, and in times of fear from wild beasts or thieves, also for the purpose of protecting oneself. [This refers to] an umbrella made of a single leaf.
However, it is permissible in all cases.
*Asissāti* means "he will eat. *Vijjotalatīti* means "it shines forth. Regarding the "authorization for a staff" (*daṇḍasammuti*):

here, only a staff of four cubits (*hattha*) that is appropriate in measure should be authorized and given. Anything shorter or longer than that is permissible for everyone even without such authorization. A carrying-net (*sikkā*).
However, it is not permitted for one who is not ill; even for one who is ill, it should be given only after formal authorization. 273. Regarding "for one who chews the cud":
here, except for the actual ruminator, there is an offense for those who swallow the regurgitated matter that has come up by holding it in the mouth.

But if it goes down the throat without being held in the mouth, it is permitted. "Whatever is being given" means: whatever is being given by donors and falls outside the receiving bowl—that I authorize the monk to take himself and consume; this is precisely what is described in the *Bhojanavagga*.
274. "I shall cause agitation" means: "I shall make a noise. There is no offense in cutting the nails with the fingernails and so forth;
however, nail-cutting was permitted for the purpose of protection. "Polished twenty times" means they have them polished twenty times on each nail.
"Merely the dirt" means: "I authorize [the removal] of merely the dirt from the nail"—this is the meaning.
275. *Khurasipāṭika* means a razor-case. *Kappāpentī* means they have the beard shaved with a razor.
*Vaḍḍhāpentī* means they have the beard made long. *Golomika* refers to the sheep’s wool-like beard placed long upon the jaw.
*Caturassa* means four-cornered. *Parimukha* means the removal of hair from the chest. *Aḍḍhaduka*—
Regarding "the planting of a line of hair on the abdomen": for all cases such as having a beard trimmed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"On account of illness" refers to the abdomen [being affected] by conditions such as boils, wounds, or blood.

"With scissors" refers to cases where it is done on account of illness such as boils, wounds, blood, or diseases of the head. There is no offense in having nose-hair removed with pebbles or similar objects.
However, for the purpose of preservation, a pair of tweezers is permitted. Regarding the rule, "Monks, one must not have grey hair removed":
here, it is permissible to have removed any hair—whether grey or not grey—that has grown on the eyebrows, the forehead, or the beard and stands in a repulsive manner.
277. *Kaṃsapattharikā* means bronze-vessel merchants. *Bandhanamattaṃ* means merely the binding of items such as a waist-cloth, a knife, or a staff.
278. Regarding the rule, "Monks, [one should not go] without having fastened one's waist-band": here, if one departs without having fastened it, one must fasten it wherever one remembers.
It is permissible to go with the intention, "I will fasten it in the assembly hall. Once one has remembered, one must fasten it before leaving.
One must not go for alms [with such items]. A *kalābu* is one with many cords. A *deḍḍubhaka* is shaped like the head of a water-snake.
A *muraja* is made by wrapping it into the shape of a drum-head. A *maddavīṇā* is shaped like a *pāmaṅga* (a type of lute).
Not even a single one of these is permitted, let alone many. Regarding the phrase "a strip of cloth (*paṭṭika*) or a pig’s entrails (*sūkarantaka*)," here the natural state is as follows:
Either a fish-bone needle-case or a strip of cloth is permitted; other types, such as those shaped like an elephant's trunk and so forth, are not permitted.
What is called a *sūkarantaka* has the shape of a key-case or a sheath. However, a single-stringed lute and a waist-band made of dates conform to the *sūkarantaka*.
"I allow you, monks, the *muraja* and the soft *vīṇā*"—this refers only to the ten [types of musical instruments].
It is permitted. Furthermore, a girdle (*pāmaṅgada*) that exceeds four [fingers] in width is not allowed. "Sobhaṇa" refers to sewing around the edge of the mouth after wrapping it.
"Guṇaka" refers to sewing in the shape of a drum (*mudiṅga*); for when the edges are sewn in this way, they become firm. "Pavananta" is said to mean the border (*pāsanta*). 280.
"Elephant-trunk style" (*hatthisoṇḍaka*) refers to wearing the lower robe by making a hanging loop from the base of the navel in the shape of an elephant's trunk.
It is like the lower garment worn by the women of Coḷa. That called *macchavāḷaka* is worn by draping it so that it bites on one side and hangs down on the other.
That called *catukaṇṇaka* is worn by displaying four corners—two above and two below.
