That called *tālavaṇṭaka* is a lower garment worn by draping a cloth in the shape of a palm-leaf fan. That called *satavalika*...
It is worn by repeatedly folding a long robe and making it into a waist-wrap (*ovaṭṭika*),
or by wearing it so that continuous folds appear on the left and right sides. However, if only one or two folds are visible starting from the knees, it is permissible.
"Putting on the *saṃvelliya* (the wrapped robe)" means they put it on by tying a waist-knot, like laborers and the like.
It is not permitted to wear it in this manner even for one who is ill or traveling on a road.

Furthermore, when traveling on a road, if they lift one or two corners and hang them over the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*), or if they do so with a single saffron robe inside, [it is likewise not permitted].
Having put on one [robe] inside, they put on another outside; all of this is not permitted.

However, one who is ill may, after showing the waist-wrap (*ovaṭṭika*) of the saffron robe inside, put on another over it. One who is not ill, when putting on two robes, should put them on so that they are folded together (*saguṇa*).
Thus, having avoided everything that is prohibited here and everything mentioned in the commentary on the *Sekhiya* rules, [one should act].
One should wear the lower robe evenly all around, concealing the three circles without making any alteration.

One who makes any alteration does not escape a *dukkaṭa* offense. "Monks, one should not wear the robe like a householder"—having thus rejected the householder’s manner of wearing it, one should not wear it in that way;
rather, having made both corners equal, the wearing of the robe is called "wearing it evenly all around," and that is how it should be worn.
In this context, whatever is worn by those dressed in white cloth, those dressed as wanderers, those wearing a single robe, those with matted hair,
those dressed as palace attendants, those dressed as great elders, those entering huts, those dressed as brahmins, or those wearing the *pāḷikāra*—
all such dress that deviates from the characteristic of being wrapped all around is called "lay dress. Therefore, [one should not wear it].
Just as the white-robed Aḍḍhapālaka Nigaṇṭhas wrap themselves, and just as some wanderers (paribbājaka) expose their chests and place the cloak over both shoulders,
and just as single-clothed people, having covered their backs with one end of the wrapped cloth,
place both corners on both shoulders, and just as those addicted to liquor and the like [do].
Wrapping their necks with a cloth, they let both ends hang down over their bellies, or they throw them over their backs;
just as women of the royal harem wear a veil after showing only the whites of their eyes,
or as the Mahājeṭṭhās, having put on a long robe, cover their entire bodies with one end of it, or just as farmers do.
When entering the field-shed, they wrap the cloth around it, tuck it under both armpits,
and cover their bodies with one end of it; and just as the brahmins insert the cloth between both armpits and tuck it over the tops of their shoulders,
and just as a monk who wears the robe over one shoulder covers his left arm with that single-shoulder draping.
Having opened the robe, he places it over one shoulder.
Thus, having dressed without such faults, and having avoided all these and other defects in the manner of dressing, one should dress evenly and without alteration.
Likewise, having dressed in this manner, for one who acts with any alteration whatsoever out of disrespect—whether in the monastery or within a house—a *dukkaṭa* offense is incurred.

281. *Muṇḍavaṭṭī*: the intended meaning is like the people who carry the requisites for a king wherever he goes. *Antarākājaṃ*: a load that is to be carried by two [persons] after being suspended in the middle.

282. *Acakkhussaṃ*: it is not beneficial to the eyes; it produces deterioration. *Nacchādeti*: it is not pleasing. *Aṭṭhaṅgulaparamaṃ*: measured by the standard finger of humans, it is no more than eight fingers in length. *Atimaṭāhakaṃ*: too small.

283. "Setting fire to a grove" means they set fire to grass, forests, and so forth. "Counter-fire" means a fire set against [the main fire]. "Protection" means protection by means of clearing away vegetation or by digging a trench.
In this case, however, if there is one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), one is not permitted to set the fire oneself;
if there is no such person, one is permitted to set the fire even after cutting the ground and removing the grass.
One may dig a trench, break off green branches, and even extinguish a fire; one may likewise extinguish the fire whether the bedding or bowl has been reached or not.
However, this must be done with water that is *kappiya* (permissible), and not otherwise.
"When there is a task to be done" means when there is a necessity for taking dry wood and so forth. "A man’s height" (*porisiya*) means the measure of a man.

"In times of distress" means: having seen wild beasts and the like, or being lost on the road, or desiring to look toward the directions, or seeing a forest fire or a flood approaching—in such calamities as these, it is permissible even to climb an exceedingly high tree.
(285) "Possessing beautiful speech" means having a sweet voice. "One should commit to verse" means [one should compose] in the Pali language, just like the Veda.

We shall cause it to be entered into the path of recitation. Regarding the phrase "in one's own language" (*sakāya niruttiyā*): here, "one's own language" refers to the Magadhi idiom as spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One. 286.

"Lokāyata" refers to the teaching of the non-Buddhist sectarians (*titthiya*) associated with meaningless reasons such as: "all is vomit," "all is not vomit," "a crow is white," "a crane is black," and so forth, based on such [absurd] causal arguments.
288. *Antarā ahosi* means she was in between, hidden, or concealed. 289.
*Ābādhappaccayā* means that for which garlic is the medicine for a certain ailment; the meaning is "on account of that. 290. *Passāvapādukaṃ*:
here, a footrest may be made of bricks, stone, or wood. The same rule applies to a toilet footrest (*vaccapādukā*). *Pariveṇaṃ* refers to the interior space enclosed by the walls of the latrine hut.

293. "He should be dealt with according to the rule" means that he should be dealt with for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by way of an offense of wrong-doing, and for an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) by way of an offense of expiation.
"A weapon" (*paharaṇī*) refers to anything made for the purpose of striking;
this is a designation for whatever is reckoned as a weapon. The meaning is: "With the exception of that, I permit all other metal utensils. "The *kataka* and the *kumbhakārika*"—[and so forth].
In this regard, the *kataka* has already been explained. "And a potter's [hut]" refers to any hut made entirely of clay belonging to Dhaniya.
The rest is clear throughout.
The discussion on minor matters is concluded.
The commentary on the Khuddakavatthu-khandhaka is finished.
6. The Senāsanakkhandhaka: The Discussion on the Permission for Monasteries.
294. In the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*: "Not laid down" means not permitted. A "vihāra" is any dwelling other than an *aḍḍhayoga* and so forth.
An *aḍḍhayoga* is a house with a curved roof like a garuḍa’s wing. A "pāsāda" is a long palace. A "hammiya" is a gabled chamber situated on an upper terrace; it is a type of palace.
A "guhā" is a cave made of brick, a rock cave, a wooden cave, or an earthen cave. [It is for] those who have come and those yet to come...
“Of the Saṅgha of the four quarters” means: of the Saṅgha of the four quarters whose movement is unimpeded in the four directions, both those who have arrived and those who have not yet arrived.
295. In the verses of thanksgiving—“cold and heat”—this is stated by way of the discordance of the seasons. “And rain in the cold season as well.”
Here, "cold" refers to the wind that has touched [the body]. "Rain" refers specifically to rain from upright clouds.
All these should be construed with the phrase "he wards off.

"Is warded off" means it is warded off by the monastery (vihāra). "For the sake of shelter" means for the sake of taking refuge. "For the sake of comfort" means by way of the absence of dangers such as cold and so forth.

"For the sake of dwelling in happiness" (*sukhavihāratthaṃ*). The two phrases "to meditate" (*jhāyituṃ*) and "to attain insight" (*vipassituṃ*) should also be connected with this very phrase "for the sake of happiness.
For this is what is meant: the gift of a dwelling is for the sake of happiness; what kind of happiness?
It is for the sake of that happiness which consists in meditating and attaining insight. Alternatively, it may also be connected with the subsequent phrase: "and to meditate..."

And the gift of a monastery for the purpose of insight meditation: the Buddha has praised the gift of a monastery as the foremost among gifts to the Saṅgha by one who gives with the thought, "They will meditate here and practice insight. For it is said: "He is a giver of all who gives a dwelling place.
And because it is praised as the foremost, there is the verse: "Therefore, a wise person... and so on, ending with "...should provide lodging for those of great learning."
In this monastery, one should dwell with those who are learned in the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and those who are learned through realization (*paṭivedha*).
To them—meaning to those who have become upright and whose minds are not crooked—one should give all that is suitable for them: food, drink, clothing, and bedding such as beds and chairs.
"One should give" means one should bestow it; and that indeed, with a serene mind.
Without violating the clarity of mind with their thoughts, they teach the Dhamma to one whose mind is thus serene...
[and so on] ...he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints. 296.
Regarding "the hole for drawing in" and "the rope for drawing in": here, as for the "rope," even if it were made from a leopard's tail-hair...
If it has been made, it is indeed permissible; nothing whatsoever is impermissible. "Three locks" means three keys. Regarding "a mechanical needle":
whatever one knows [how to operate] is a mechanical device, and it is permissible to make a needle for opening it.
A "balcony window" is like a balcony on a cetiya. A "lattice window" is one fitted with a lattice. A "slat window" is—
"Thambhakavātapānaṃ" means a window with a frame. "Cakkalikaṃ" means that I allow [the use of] a cloth foot-wiper to be tied there;
this is the meaning. "Vātapānabhisī" means that I allow a mattress to be made and tied according to the dimensions of the window; this is the meaning. "Miḍḍhaṃ" means a bolster.
"Bidalamañcakaṃ" means a cane bed; or one woven from bamboo slips.

297. *Āsandika* refers to a square chair. Because it is stated that even a high one is called an *āsandika*, it should be understood that while only a long chair with legs eight finger-breadths in height is permitted on one side, a square *āsandika* is permitted even if it exceeds the standard measurement.
A *sattaṅga* is a bed made by providing supports on three sides; this too—
It is permissible if it exceeds the standard measurement. A "Bhaddapīṭha" is said to be a chair made of cane. A "Pīṭhikā" is simply a chair bound with cloth.
An "eḷakapādapīṭha" is called a chair made by placing the feet upon a wooden plank, like a food-tray.
An "āmalakavaṭṭikapīṭha" is a multi-legged chair constructed in the shape of an *āmalaka* fruit. These...
These are the types of benches mentioned in the text. However, the rule here is that any bench made of wood is permissible.
As for the "cocoon" (koccha), it is made either of *usira* grass or of *muñja* or *pabbaja* grass.
Regarding the phrase "the bed-legs shall not exceed eight finger-breadths," the "eight finger-breadths" here refers specifically to the human finger-breadth (*mānusa-aṅgula*).
*Cimilikā* is said to be a covering spread over prepared ground for the purpose of protecting the skin.
*Rukkhatūla* is the cotton of any tree whatsoever, such as the *simbali* tree. *Latātūla* is the cotton of any creeper whatsoever, such as the milk-vine (*khīravallī*).
*Poṭakitūla* is [the cotton] of any species of grass whatsoever, such as the *poṭaki* grass.
Even the cotton of sugarcane, reeds, and so forth is included. By these three, all categories of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) are comprised.
For there is no other category of living beings apart from the species of trees, creepers, grasses, and shrubs;

therefore, the cotton of any such category of living beings is permitted for a bolster (*bimbohana*), but once it reaches the stage of a mattress (*bhisi*), all of it is called "unallowable cotton" (*akappiyatūla*). And this is not the only case.
Regarding this stuffing, cotton is indeed permitted; furthermore, the feathers of all birds such as swans and peacocks, as well as the hair of all four-footed animals such as lions, are also allowed.
However, any kind of flower, such as the *piyaṅgu* or *bakuḷa* flowers, is not permitted.

Pure *tamāla* leaves alone are not permitted, but those that are mixed with other materials are allowed. Regarding mattresses, the five kinds of stuffing authorized—wool and so forth—are also permitted.
"Half-body-sized" means measuring half the size of a body; those [robes] which, starting from the waist, reach up to the head.

"Head-sized" means that when measured across the three ears, the distance between two ears is one cubit (*vidatthi*) and four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), while the middle part is a fist-measure (*muṭṭhiratana*). As for the length, however—
"Either one and a half cubits or two cubits," so it is stated in the *Kurundi*. This is the maximum limit for the size of the head;
more than this is not permitted, but less is allowed. For one who is not ill, only two things are permitted:
a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet. For one who is ill, however, it is even permissible to lie down after spreading out bolsters and placing a coverlet on top.

"It is permissible," said the Elder Phussadeva. "Furthermore, even a large bolster made with those five types of allowable stuffing (kappiyatūla) that have been authorized for bolsters is permissible. However, the Elder Vinayadharūpatissa said:
"For one who makes a bolster by putting in either allowable or unallowable stuffing with the intention, 'I shall make a bolster,' only the [prescribed] measurement is permissible."
"Five stuffed cushions" (*pañca bhisiyo*) refers to cushions filled with wool and so forth. Their number is stated here according to the count of the stuffing material.
In this context, by the mention of "wool" (*uṇṇā*), not only sheep's wool is included;
rather, with the exception of human hair, all the feathers or fur of birds and quadrupeds—whether of a permissible or impermissible kind—is included here under the term "wool."

It is permitted. Therefore, it is allowable to make a mattress by using either one of the six kinds of cloth or one of the six kinds of compliant cloth as the outer covering, and then placing all of that inside.
However, even if woolen fibers are not added, but only a fourfold or fivefold layer of woolen blanket is placed inside, it still counts as a woolen mattress (*uṇṇabhisi*).
A cotton mattress is one made by gathering any kind of new or old cotton and either stuffing it or placing it inside;
a reed mattress is one made by stuffing any kind of reed; a grass mattress is one made by stuffing any kind of grass;
and a leaf mattress is one made by stuffing any kind of leaf except for pure *tāla* leaves.
This should be understood. As for the *tamāla* leaf, it is permissible only when mixed with something else, but not when pure.

There is no fixed rule regarding the dimensions of a mattress; having observed what is appropriate for a bed-mattress, a chair-mattress, a floor-covering mattress, a walking-path mattress, or a foot-wiping mattress, the size should be determined according to one's own preference. Furthermore, as for this fivefold stuffing of wool and so forth—
A mattress is permitted; regarding this, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that "it is also permitted [to use] a bolster.
By this, it is established that it is permissible to use a bolster.
"Spreading a bed-mattress on a bench" means they spread the bed-mattress upon the bench; they bring it for the purpose of spreading it.
It is appropriate. "Without making a ceiling" means without providing a matting underneath. "To sprinkle" means to apply droplets on top with dye or turmeric.
"Plastering work" refers to plastering work over the outer bark of a *bhisī* plant. "Hand-plastering" refers to a five-fingered pattern of plaster.
298. "Resin" means either the exudation of a tree or gum-resin. "Flour-paste" means a lump of flour. "Mud from a bowl" means...
*Kuṇḍakamissakamattikaṃ*: clay mixed with dregs. *Sāsapakuṭṭaṃ*: crushed mustard seed (mustard flour). *Sitthatelakaṃ*: honey-dregs that have melted. *Accussannaṃ hoti*:
it remains as drop after drop. *Paccuddharituṃ*: to wipe away. *Gaṇḍumattikaṃ*:
clay from the excrement of earthworms. *Kasāvaṃ*: the decoction of *āmalaka* and *harītakī*.
299. Regarding the rule, "Monks, a decorative painting (*paṭibhānacitta*) [is not permitted]," here it is not only the forms of women and men that are prohibited;
even the forms of animals, down to the form of a boil or a pimple, are not allowed for a monk to make himself, nor to tell another, "Make this.
It is not even permissible to say, "Lay follower (*upāsaka*), act as a doorkeeper. This applies to gifts and other such acts that are unlike those found in the *Jātaka* collection.
However, it is permissible to have others perform inspiring or world-weariness-inducing tasks. It is also permissible for one to perform tasks such as weaving garlands oneself.
300. *Aḷakamandā* is a single courtyard crowded with people. Regarding "three chambers," here a *sivikā-gabbha* (palanquin chamber) is a square chamber.
A *nāḷikāgabbha* is a long chamber whose length is two or three times its width. A *hammiyagabbha* is a gabled-roof chamber or a flat-roofed chamber on the upper level of a building.
A *kalaṅkapādaka* is a wall-footing made by boring into a tree trunk, driving stakes into it, and constructing [the support] there; it is an imported type of wall-footing.
The meaning is: "I authorize [it] to be fixed to the ground for the purpose of supporting the feet of one whose old matting is worn out.
A *parittāṇakiṭika* is a small shed for the purpose of protection from the rain. *Uddasudha* is clay mixed with cow-dung and ashes.
An *āḷinda* is called the porch. A *paghana* is that which [is used] by those entering and exiting on foot.
"Hananti" is a designation for that place where, at the door of a dwelling, the walls have been removed on both sides;
it is also called "paghāna. "Pakuṭṭa" refers to a surrounding enclosure made around the middle of a cell;
"pakuṭa" is also a reading. "Osāraka" refers to a roofed entrance made by inserting a bamboo pole in a dwelling that lacks a porch and then hanging down rafters from it.
A "saṃsāraṇakiṭika" is a wheeled cart used for transporting goods.
(301) A "pānīyabhājana" is a vessel for giving water to those who are drinking. A water-scoop (*uḷuṅka*) and a shallow bowl (*thālaka*) are accessories for a water jar.
(303) An *apesī* is a door-bolt made by inserting a long wooden post into a stump and binding it with thorny branches. A *paligha* is a wheeled door-bolt, similar to those found at village gates.
305. *Assatarīhi yuttā rathā* means chariots yoked with mules; thus, *assatarī-rathā*. *Āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā* means those who have put on jeweled earrings; thus, *āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalāni*.

*Parinibbuto* means completely extinguished by the extinction (*parinibbāna*) of the defilements (*kilesa*). *Sītibhūto* means become cool due to the absence of the heat of the defilements. *Nirūpadhī* is said to be "without substrate" because of the absence of the substrate of the defilements (*kilesūpadhi*).

*Chetvā sabbā āsattiyo* means having cut off all attachments, whether toward objects such as forms or toward all states of existence. *Hadaye daranti* means having removed the distress of the defilements from the heart—that is, from the mind. *Veyyāyikaṃ* is said to mean the act of making wealth.
307. “His words are to be accepted” means that many people consider his speech to be worthy of being adopted and heard.
“They built monasteries” means that those who possessed wealth built them with their own money;
to those who had little wealth or were destitute, he gave money. Thus, having given one hundred thousand kahāpaṇas and goods worth one hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas], he...
Having established monasteries at intervals of one *yojana* throughout the forty-five *yojana* journey, he proceeded to Sāvatthī.
"He had it spread with a layer of ten million" means that he laid down ten million coins against each ten million [of the ground].
Taking the measurement of the circumference of whatever trees or lotus ponds were there, he [did the same] in another place.
Having spread it out, he gave it away. In this way, his treasure of eighteen crores went to exhaustion.

"It occurred to the prince" means that, seeing the serene expression on the face of the householder even as he was giving away such vast wealth, this thought arose in him. "He had a gatehouse built" means he had a seven-storied palace-gatehouse constructed.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had monasteries built at Jetavana... [and so on] ...he had pavilions built; by other [means as well].
He had these monasteries and other structures built at a cost of eighteen crores on a piece of land measuring eight *karīsas*.
For the Blessed One Vipassī, the householder Punabbasumitta purchased a piece of land one *yojana* in extent by covering it with golden bricks and had a monastery constructed there.
However, for the Blessed One Sikhī, the householder Sirivaḍḍha [purchased] a piece of land three *gāvutas* in extent by covering it with golden rods.
For Vessabhū, the householder Sotthija [laid it out] with a layer of gold ploughshares measuring half a yojana;
for Kakusandha, however, the householder Accuta [laid it out] with a layer of golden elephant’s footprints measuring one gāvuta;
for Koṇāgamana, the householder Ugga [laid it out] with a layer of golden bricks measuring half a gāvuta; and for Kassapa, the householder Sumaṅgala...

"Having purchased land measuring eight karīsas from our Blessed One’s householder Sudatta by spreading it with gold coins, he had a monastery built upon a golden tortoise-skin spread over an area measuring twenty usabhas.
Thus, as success gradually declines in this way, it is enough to become dispassionate toward all success; it is enough to be liberated.
308. *Khaṇḍanti* means a broken place. *Phullanti* means a cracked place. *Paṭisaṅkharissatīti* means he will restore it to its original state.
However, a monk who has received new work assignments should not perform the work himself by taking up tools such as axes, hatchets, or chisels;
rather, he must ascertain what has been done and what remains to be done.
310. "Going behind, behind" means that the Elder, it is said, used to come at the very end while looking after the sick and supporting the aged and the elderly;
this was his custom. Therefore it is said: "going behind, behind.

"The foremost seat" refers to the seat of the Elder. "Foremost water" refers to the water for the ritual offering (dakṣiṇodaka). "Foremost alms-food" refers to the alms-food of the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
"Having placed it between the thighs" means having placed it between the four feet.
"He established [the gift]" means that after making a renunciation worth eighteen koṭis, he established it. In this way, he renounced all fifty-four koṭis.
The discourse on the authorization of the monastery is concluded.
The Discussion on Obstructing Seating, etc. 316.

Regarding "one who has finished eating": a monk eating anywhere—whether in a village, in a monastery, or in the forest—must not be made to rise as long as his meal is not yet concluded. If one arrives later in a village and takes alms food...
One should go. If people or monks say, "Please enter," one should say, "If I enter, the monks will have to rise.
However, when told, "Come, venerable sir, there are seats," one may enter.
If no one says anything, one should go to the assembly hall and stand in a suitable place, not too close.
Once space has been made and he is told, "Enter," he should enter.
However, if a seat has fallen to his lot and a monk is already sitting there not eating, it is permissible to ask him to rise.
But as for one who is sitting while drinking or eating anything—such as rice gruel or fresh food—even if his hands are empty, [he should be asked to rise] until another person arrives.
It is not permissible to have [the meal] completed. For he remains one whose meal is still unfinished.
"If he has it completed" means if he indeed has it completed even after the time for the offense has passed.
"And he is one who has already invited [himself]" means that while the one he has had complete the meal is such a person, this monk must be told: "Go, bring some water."

For this is the only way to command a more senior monk. If he does not even fetch water, then, showing what must be done by one who is junior, [the Buddha] said, "Thoroughly [prepare] the rice," and so forth.
Regarding "a suitable bed for one who is ill": here, one who is ill with coughs, fistula, dysentery, and so on, [should have] spittoons, chamberpots, and the like.
They must be excluded. If one is a leper who defiles the lodging, a separate lodging—such as a lower story of a palace, a leaf-hut, or similar structure—should be given to him.
Even for one who dwells there without defiling the lodging, a superior bed should indeed be provided.
Also, regarding any medicinal treatment such as oil-drinking, purgatives, or nasal medication...
If [the illness] occurs, everyone is indeed considered ill; having observed this as well, a suitable dwelling-place should be given to him.

"By way of a slight pretext" means by even a minor affliction such as a headache and so forth. "Having counted the monks" means having ascertained the limit of the monks in the monastery, thinking, "There are so many monks.
The discussion on the refusal of seats and so forth is finished.

318. Discussion on the Allocation of Lodgings (*Senāsanaggāhakathā*): "Lodging" (*seyyā*) refers to the places for couches. "By means of the lodging" (*seyyaggena*) means by way of the delimitation of the lodging;
the meaning is: "I authorize [the Sangha] to announce the time on the day of entering the rains retreat and to assign one couch-place to one bhikkhu. By means of the lodging...
"They cause to enter" means they are being caused to enter by means of the demarcation of the bedding. "They raised up the bedding" means that there were extra bed-places.
The same method applies to the upper parts of the monastery and so forth. "To give another portion" means to give yet another share.
For when the monks are very few, two or three cells should be given to each individual monk. "It should not be given unwillingly."

It should not be given against one's will. In that regard, if the share was taken on the day of entering the rains retreat, that share must not be given to those who arrive later if it is against the giver's own inclination.
However, if the person by whom it was taken gives that share—or even the first portion—of their own accord, it is permissible.
“Standing outside the boundary” means standing outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*). However, it is indeed permissible even for one standing at a distance within the precinct boundary.
“Having taken up a dwelling” means having taken it up on the day of entering the rains residence (*vassūpanāyika*).
“Barred at all times” means they are barred even during the season following the end of the four months. Regarding the three ways of taking up dwellings: the first and the last...
And these two verses are fixed.
Regarding one who dies in the interval, this is the analysis: In a certain monastery there is great gain and lodging.
The owners of the lodging, having attended upon the monk who has entered the rains retreat with all requisites and having invited him [to leave], at the time of his departure—
They give many requisites for the ascetics. Even from afar, the great elders come on the day of the entry into the rains retreat;
having taken possession of them and lived there in comfort, they depart after the rains have ended and have received their share of the offerings.
The resident monks think, "We do not receive the offerings arising here; the visiting great elders always receive them. They themselves will come and look after them."
Even as it was being destroyed, they did not look back. For the sake of looking after it, the Blessed One said:
"When the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) has passed, a temporary dwelling (antarāmuttaka) should be assigned for the purpose of the upcoming rains residence.
When assigning it, the Elder of the Sangha should be addressed: "Venerable sir, please accept this temporary lodging."

If he accepts it, it must be given to him. If not, then by this same method, starting from the most senior monk down to whoever accepts it—even if it be a novice (sāmaṇera)—it must be given to him. He must maintain that lodging for eight months.
Whatever part of the roof, walls, or floor is broken or dilapidated, all of that must be repaired. [He should attend to] recitation, interrogation, and so forth.
It is permissible to spend the day [there] and stay there during the night. It is also permissible to stay at the pariveṇa during the night and spend the day there.
It is likewise permissible to stay right there for both day and night. Those who are elders and have arrived during the appropriate season must not be turned away.
However, when the day of entering the rains retreat has arrived, if the Saṅgha Elder...
If he says, "Give me this lodging," he does not receive it.

Having said, "Venerable sir, this [lodging] was taken as a 'rain-breaker' (antarāmuttaka) and has been maintained by a single bhikkhu for eight months," it must not be given; it belongs solely to the bhikkhu who maintained it for those eight months.
However, in the case of a lodging where they provide requisites twice a year, at the end of every six months...
That which is "released in the interim" (antarāmuttaka) must not be included. Or, in a case where they give three times, each time after the lapse of four months;
or in a case where they give four times, each time after the lapse of three months—that too is "released in the interim" and must not be included.
For that maintenance will indeed be obtained through the very requisites themselves. However, in a case where many requisites are given all at once within a single year...

"Friends, this should be understood as the 'intermediate release' for taking up a dwelling. This, then, is the account of the taking up of lodgings as it appears in the Canon regarding the day of entering the rains residence during the rainy season.
Now, this so-called "taking up of lodgings" is twofold: that at the appropriate time (*utu-kāla*) and that during the rains residence (*vassa-vāsa*). Of these, regarding the appropriate time:
In this regard, some incoming bhikkhus may arrive before the meal, some after the meal, or during the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night;
whenever they arrive, the bhikkhus should rise and give them lodgings immediately.
There is no such thing as an "inopportune time. Furthermore, the one who assigns lodgings must be wise.
One or two bed-places should be set aside. If one or two elders arrive at an improper time, they should be told:
"Venerable sirs, if we were to be made to rise starting from the beginning, all the monks would become dispossessed of their belongings;
therefore, please stay right here in our dwelling place."
But when many have arrived, after having them enter, it should be given out in order. If each individual cell (pariveṇa) is available, it should be given to each individual cell;
in that case, the fire-hall, the long hall, the circular pavilion, and so forth, all belong to that same person.
If this is not sufficient, it should be given by way of the palace (pāsāda). If the palaces are insufficient, [it should be given] by way of the rooms (ovaraka).
It should be given. If the inner rooms are insufficient, it should be given starting from the beds. If the beds are insufficient, it should be given according to the space for couches.
If the space for couches is insufficient, it should be given according to the space for a single chair. However, one must not allow even the mere space where a monk stands;
for that is not considered "lodging" (*senāsana*). But if the space for chairs is insufficient, [one may assign] a single space for a couch.
Or, taking turns by rotation, one should give the seat or the bench to three people, saying, "Venerable sirs, rest.
For it is not possible to remain in the open air all night during the cold season.
After the Elder has rested during the first watch, he should go out and say to the second Elder, "Friend, please enter here. If...
The senior elder is heavy with sleep and does not know the time; having coughed and knocked on the door, he should say: "Venerable sir, the time has come; the cold is biting.
He must go out and give him space; he is not permitted not to do so.
The second elder, too, having rested during the middle watch, should give space to the other in the same manner as before. [If] heavy with sleep...
He should be made to leave in the same manner already described. Thus, for one night, a single bed and a single place should be given to three [monks].

However, some monks in Jambudīpa say: "As for lodgings, whether it be a bed or a bench, whatever is suitable for one person may not be suitable for another; therefore, whether guests arrive or not, the lodging should be [assigned] daily."
They take possession [of the lodgings]. This is what is called the taking of lodgings during the season.
However, regarding the rains residence (*vassāvāsa*), there is the duty for newcomers (*āgantuka-vatta*) and the duty for residents (*āvāsika-vatta*).
First, concerning the newcomer who wishes to leave his own place and go elsewhere to dwell, he must not go there on the very day of the commencement of the rains (*vassūpanāyikā*).
For in that place, the dwelling might be cramped, alms-gathering might not succeed, or one might therefore fail to live in comfort.
Therefore, thinking, "In about a month, the commencement of the rains retreat will take place," one should enter that monastery.
While staying there for about a month, if one is seeking formal instruction, one should observe the excellence of the instruction.

If one whose practice is centered on a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) observes that it is conducive to that subject, or if one who requires material requisites observes that they will be obtained there,
he may dwell comfortably during the rains retreat.
When going there from his own place, he should not pass through the village where he seeks alms, nor should he speak to the people there.
—“In dependence upon you, there is no longer any provision of tickets for meals, or rice-gruel and snacks, or the rainy-season gift;
this is the property of the cetiya, this is the property of the Uposatha hall, and this is for your monastery: accept these gongs and needles.
Having thus maintained the lodgings and put away the wooden and earthenware utensils...

Having fulfilled the duties of a departing monk, one should go. While traveling in this manner, one should not go by way of the village gate making oneself visible—having young novices lift up their bowls and robes, have them take oil-flasks, walking-sticks, and so forth, and having taken up an umbrella;
rather, one should travel by a concealed forest path. If no forest path exists...

One should not go while crushing clumps of earth and the like; rather, having fulfilled the duties for one going on a journey, having cut off discursive thought, and with a pure mind, one should go according to the proper conduct for traveling.

However, if the path passes through a village gate, and people see him going along with his retinue, they might think, "He is like our own Elder," and run toward him, saying, "Where are you going, venerable sir? All your requisites—"
“Take [these goods] and go,” they say. Among them, if one person says, “This is the time for entering the rains retreat;
monks go to those places where, during the rains, fixed alms-rounds and shelter for goods are available,” and having heard him, those people say, “Venerable sir, in this village too, people eat and—”
Having said, "Wear [these robes] and do not go elsewhere," he summoned his friends and kinsmen;

after consulting them all, he established a regular routine for the monastery, provided meals by ticket and so forth, and offered the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gifts, saying, "Venerable sirs, please stay right here.
It is permissible to accept all of this, for all of it is both allowable and blameless.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is said: "When asked, 'Where are you going? one should say, 'To such-and-such a place.
When asked, 'Why are you going there? one should explain the reason. Both of these, moreover, are blameless because they arise from a pure mind.
This is called the duty for a guest (*āgantukavatta*).
This, however, is the duty of the resident monks: the monastery must be maintained by the residents beforehand. Cracks and dilapidations must be repaired, and plastering must be done.
The night-quarters, the day-quarters, the privy-huts, the urinal areas, the meditation hall, the dwelling, and the path—all these must be looked after.
Furthermore, whitewashing the shrine, oil-anointing the brick altar, and the maintenance of beds and chairs must be performed.
All this should also be done [with the thought]: "May those who wish to dwell for the rains come and dwell in comfort, engaged in recitation, interrogation, and application to the meditation subject.
From the fifth day of the bright half of Āsāḷhī, those who have performed the preliminary work should ask for the *vassāvāsika* (rains-bathing robe).
Where should it be asked for? From wherever it is normally obtained. However, from those by whom it has not been given before, [it must be asked].
It is not proper to ask them. Why should one ask? Because people sometimes give, and sometimes they do not give due to being afflicted by famine and other such calamities.

In that regard, if those who would not give were not asked and the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robes were taken anyway, it would create an obstacle to the gains of the monks who have already received them;
therefore, one must take them only after asking. When asking, [one should say]: "The time for you to receive the *vassāvāsika*..."
It should be said, "It is near. If they say, "Venerable sir, this year we have been afflicted by drought and other calamities;
we are unable to give," or "We shall give less than what we gave previously," or "Now cotton is easily obtained;
we shall give more than what we gave previously," one should take note of that.
In accordance with that principle, the rains-residence fee (*vassāvāsika*) should be assigned to the monks in their respective lodgings.
If people say, "Whoever receives our rains-residence fee should provide drinking water for the three months,
maintain the path to the monastery, maintain the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard, and pour water on the Bodhi-tree," [it should be accepted].

It should be assigned to whoever it reaches. However, if there is a village two or three *yojanas* away, and families there have deposited goods as a trust and are giving the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season residence fee) to the monastery, then even if one has not asked those families, the *vassāvāsika* should be collected for one who stays in their lodgings after performing the proper duties (*vatta*). If...
However, if a paṃsukūlika monk is staying in their lodging, and upon seeing him arrive they say,
"We shall give you the rains-residence gift," he should inform the Saṅgha. If those families do not wish to give it to the Saṅgha, but instead say,
"We shall give it to you alone," then a monk who shares the same affiliation should say, "Perform the proper service and then receive it."
It should be asked. However, this is not permitted for a paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearer); thus, the donor people regarding the gift of faith must be asked.
But regarding what arises on the spot, the stewards (kappiyakāraka) must be asked. How should they be asked? "Friends, will there be cloth for the Sangha's requisites?
If they say, "Yes, Venerable Sir, there will be nine handspans [of cloth] for each person..."
If they say, "We shall give you a cloth; please accept it as a gift for the rainy season residence," it should be accepted. Even if they say, "There is no cloth, but there is the value for one;
please accept it, venerable sir," it is indeed permissible to accept it even when only the value exists.
For from whatever suitable item has been given into the hands of the stewards with the instruction, "Use this as a permissible article," all that which is permissible [may be used].
It is permitted to consume [these things].

However, whatever is given here specifically for the purpose of alms-food or as a requisite for the sick, that should be offered for the robe by those who offer it, having first obtained the consent of the Saṅgha for the welfare of the community.
That which is given specifically for the purpose of lodgings is considered heavy property (garubhaṇḍa).

There is no requirement for a formal act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) for those who offer robes or the four requisites when what has been given was already provided by way of robes or the four requisites.
Furthermore, when performing an act of notification, it must be done with respect to the individual alone and not with respect to the Saṅgha.
An act of notification is also not permitted on account of gold or silver, nor on account of raw grain. It is permitted, however, on account of allowable goods (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*).

It is permissible [to offer] by way of robes, rice, and so forth. However, it should be done in this manner: “At present, food is abundant and alms are easy to obtain, yet the monks are distressed for lack of robes;
would the monks accept such a portion of rice as being sufficient to make robes?
Or: “Requisites for the sick are easily obtained and there are no sick monks; would the monks accept such a portion of rice as being sufficient to make robes?”
Having thus observed the requirements for robes, when the time for lodgings has been announced and the Saṅgha has assembled, an assigner of lodgings (senāsanaggāhaka) should be appointed.
It is said that two should be appointed; for in this way, a junior monk may assign [lodgings] to one who is senior, and a senior monk may assign them to a junior.
However, in a large monastery such as the Mahāvihāra, three or four [should be appointed].
Persons should be appointed. However, it is stated in the *Kurundi* that "it is permissible to appoint eight or even sixteen persons.
Their appointment may be carried out either by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*) or by means of a motion (*apalokana*).
The monks appointed by them must designate the lodgings: the shrine room, the Bodhi-tree house, and the assembly hall.
The broom-house, the wood-shed, the privy, the brick hall, the mason’s hall, the gatehouse, the water-booth, the road, and the lotus pond—these are not lodgings.

The monastery, the lean-to, the mansion, the gabled house, the cave, the pavilion, the foot of a tree, and the bamboo thicket—these are lodgings; these should be assigned. And when assigning them, first...
The monks should be made to draw lots according to the method stated here: "The monks should be counted; having counted the monks, the lodgings should be drawn.

If there are two requisites for robes—namely, those belonging to the Saṅgha and those given through faith—if the monks wish to take one first, then after that has been drawn, the other should be drawn starting from its position.
However, the Elder Mahāsumma said that if, when lodgings are being distributed by way of the *pariveṇa* due to a shortage of monks,
one particular *pariveṇa* yields great profit such that ten or twelve robes are obtained, that [profit] should be divided and added to other residences where there is no gain,
and then distributed among the other monks as well. The Elder Mahāpaduma...

But he says: “It should not be done in this way; for people give requisites for the purpose of maintaining their own dwellings, therefore other bhikkhus should enter there. If, however, the Elder Mahāthera objects here:
“Friend, do not take it thus; act according to the instruction of the Blessed One, for this was said by the Blessed One: ‘I allow...’”
“Monks, you should distribute it by way of the *pariveṇa*. If, instead of standing firm in his refusal, he is persuaded by saying, “Venerable sir, there are many monks and the provisions are meager;
it is appropriate to show consideration,” then it must indeed be distributed.
And the monk appointed to distribute it should go before the senior elder (*mahāthera*) and speak thus: “Venerable sir, …”
“The lodging for you has arrived; take it and accept the requisites. “Friend, the requisites from such-and-such family and the lodging have arrived for me.
“They have arrived, Bhante; please accept them. “I accept them, friend. It is thus accepted.
But if, when it is said, “Bhante, they have been accepted by you,” he says, “They have been accepted by me,” [it is also accepted].
When it is asked, "Will you take it, venerable sir? and he replies, "I will take it," the Elder Mahāsumma said, "It has not been taken.

However, the Elder Mahāpaduma said: "Whether it be a statement regarding the past or the future, or a statement regarding the present, the mere arising of mindfulness and the mere forming of the intention are here the criteria; therefore, it has indeed been taken."
Even if a monk who wears rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*) takes up a dwelling and relinquishes the requisites, he must not have them placed in another residence.
It is permissible to have them taken by someone else in that very same courtyard, in the fire-hall, in the long hall, or at the foot of a tree.
The rag-robe wearer will maintain the dwelling with the thought, "I am staying here," while the other [will maintain] the requisites...
“I take it,” thinking thus, the lodging will become better tended by these two reasons.
However, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*: “When one who wears rag-robes takes a lodging for the purpose of dwelling, the assigner of lodgings should say:
‘Venerable sir, there are requisites here; what should be done with them? He [the wearer] should reply: ‘Have another assigned below.’”

It is permissible [to accept it]. However, if he stays without saying anything at all, and they give him a robe-cloth after he has completed his rains-residence and placed it at his feet, that is permissible.
Or, if they say, "We give you the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence gift)," it belongs to the monks who have spent the rains-residence in that monastery.
But for those who have no lodging and give only requisites, their requisites...
It is permissible to assign the rain-retreat dwelling (*vassāvāsika*) to a monk.
When people build a stupa (*thūpa*) and offer the rain-retreat dwelling, the stupa itself is not a dwelling place;
therefore, the assignment should be made by tying it to a tree or a pavilion in the vicinity of that stupa. That monk must maintain the shrine (*cetiya*).
The same principle applies to the Bodhi tree, the Bodhi-hall, the sitting-hall, the broom-house, the charcoal-house, the latrine, the privy, the door-tower, the water-shed, and the tooth-stick shed.
However, the dining hall is indeed a lodging; therefore, it is permissible to assign it to one person or to many after apportioning it.
All of this has been stated in detail in the Mahāpaccarī.
However, the assigner of lodgings must assign them starting from dawn on the first day of the fortnight until the next dawn breaks;

for this is the proper time for the assignment of lodgings. If, after the lodgings have been assigned early in the morning, another monk who wanders about with discursive thoughts arrives and requests a lodging, one should say:
"Venerable sir, the lodgings have already been assigned; the Saṅgha has entered the rains residence."
"It is a pleasant dwelling; you may stay wherever you wish, such as at the foot of a tree or elsewhere," he should be told.

Once the monks have entered the rains residence, after establishing the fixed duties for the duration of the rains, those monks who have entered the rains residence should be told, "Bind together the brooms.
If sticks and splinters are easily available, each person should prepare six or five handfuls of brooms.
Two or three bamboo brooms should be tied together. If these are difficult to obtain, two or three fist-brooms should be tied together with one bamboo broom.
Novices should grind five pieces of fire-sticks each. A plastering of decoction-wood ash should be made in the dwelling place.
Furthermore, those performing the duties [of the Saṅgha] should think: “We must not recite [the Pāṭimokkha], nor cause it to be recited;
we must not engage in private study, nor give the going-forth, nor confer full ordination, nor grant formal support, nor listen to the Dhamma;
for all these are conceptual proliferations (*papañca*). Being free from proliferation, we shall perform only the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*)”; or else, “All [these]...”
One should not establish such unrighteous rules as these: "Let them undertake the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga);
let them spend their time standing or walking without preparing a bed; let them take a vow of silence; and even those who have gone on a seven-day mission should receive shared requisites.
Rather, it should be done in this way: "The Dhamma of the scriptures establishes the Triple Gem in its entirety."
Therefore, teach with care, cause others to teach, and engage in recitation. While residing in the meditation hall, do not cause disturbance;
sit within the monastery and teach, cause others to teach, and engage in recitation.
Make the hearing of the Dhamma successful. When ordaining, ordain only after purifying [the candidate]; when conferring full admission, confer it only after purifying [the candidate].

Having purified yourselves, grant me your formal support (*nissaya*); for even a single son of noble family, having obtained the going-forth and full ordination, can establish the entire Dispensation.
According to your own strength, undertake as many ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) as you are able.
During this very rainy season, you must remain heedful throughout the entire day and during both the first and last watches of the night.
Vigor must be exerted. Even the ancient great elders, having severed all worldly attachments, fulfilled the practice of wandering alone during the rainy season;
knowing the proper measure for discourse, it is fitting to deliver discourses on the ten bases, the ten kinds of foulness, the ten recollections, and the thirty-eight objects of meditation.
One should perform the duties for visiting monks and grant leave to those who have gone on business for seven days after obtaining their permission.
"It is proper" means that such a duty (*vatta*) should be performed.
Furthermore, the monks should be exhorted: "Do not speak contentious, slanderous, or harsh words;
day by day, recollecting the precepts (*sīla*), never neglecting the fourfold protection, dwell with abundant attention. This is the duty regarding the chewing of tooth-sticks.
It should be explained: one who is bowing to a shrine or the Bodhi tree, offering perfumes and garlands, or putting the bowl into its bag should not engage in conversation;
rather, the proper conduct for the alms-round should be explained:
"Within the village, one should not engage with people in talk concerning requisites or in improper conversation; with the sense faculties guarded..."
"Such numerous discourses leading to liberation as 'one must become [virtuous]' and 'the duties of the Khandhaka and the duties of the Sekhiya must be fulfilled' should be explained.
Furthermore, on the day of the later entry into the rains retreat, if the Saṅgha has assembled after the time has been announced,
and someone brings a ten-cubit cloth and offers it as a gift for the rains residence (*vassāvāsika*), if the visiting monk is the senior of the Saṅgha, then to him—
It should be given. If [the recipient] is a junior monk, the appointed monk should say to the senior of the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sir, if you wish, please set aside your first portion and take this cloth. If he does not set it aside, it should not be given.
But if he sets aside what was previously taken and takes [this], it should be given. By this same method, from the second senior...
Having counted them starting from the beginning and rearranged them, they should be given to the newcomer at the appropriate place.

If those who entered the rains retreat first received two, three, four, or five robes, then each robe received should be distributed by this same method until the amount is equal to that of the newcomer.
Once it has become equal with his, the remaining surplus should be shared.
It should be given to the senior seat. When there is a present gain, it is permissible to make an agreement to take possession by means of a standing rule (*ṭhitikā*).
If there is a famine, and the monks who have entered the rains retreat during both the two periods of entering the rains find themselves exhausted from begging for alms, they may say:
"Friends, while staying here we are all exhausted; it would be well if we were divided into two groups, [one] for those whose places are invited by their relatives..."

If they say, "There is [something here]; having stayed there, come for the Pavāraṇā ceremony and take your own *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe)," then for those among them who stay there and return for the Pavāraṇā, the *vassāvāsika* should be given after asking their permission.
For even though they consented, they are not the owners of the *vassāvāsika*; and even though the residents have exhausted it, they are not [the owners].
They obtain [the robe] without having given it. However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*: “A formal agreement (*katikavatta*) should be made:
‘If there is not enough rice-gruel and alms-food for all of us here, stay in a common place and then return; you will receive your rainy-season robe.
If one person objects to this, it is well objected; if he does not object, the agreement is properly established.”
"Afterwards, when they have stayed there and returned, it should be given to them after taking leave; at the time of taking leave, it is not permitted to refuse.

Furthermore, it is said: "If, while some monks who have entered the rains residence find that their *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence) portion is not being distributed, they make an agreement: 'The *vassāvāsika* for those whose rains residence was interrupted, as well as the *vassāvāsika* that will now arise..."
“Once an agreement has been made in this way—‘It is pleasing to give to these [monks]’—it is just as if they had already received it;
whatever arises should be given to them.
Having provided drinking water for three months and having cleared the monastery path, the shrine courtyard, and the Bodhi courtyard, [he attended] at the Bodhi tree.

Even one who has departed after pouring water [over the bowl] or one who has gone away (vibbhamta) still receives the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe). For he has performed the act of "entering into service" (*bhatiniviṭṭha*).
However, even one who has gone away during the rains retreat receives that which was taken after performing a formal act of consultation (*apalokanakamma*) regarding property belonging to the Sangha.
But they say that what was taken by way of personal requisites (*paccaya*) is not received.

If a monk who has completed his rains residence and is traveling abroad takes some allowable article from the hand of a resident monk and, having said, "I have received my rains-residence fee at such-and-such a family;
please take it," then departs for another place and disrobes there, the rains-residence fee becomes the property of the Saṅgha.
However, if he goes after having caused the people to accept it in their presence, [it remains his].
He receives it. When it is said, "We give this rainy-season residence robe to the bhikkhu who has stayed in our lodging," it belongs only to him from whom it was taken.

However, if the owner of the lodging, out of a desire to please [the bhikkhu], brings many robes such as for his sons or daughters and gives them, saying, "We give them to our lodging," then only one [robe] belongs to the one who entered the rains retreat there.
One robe-cloth must be given; the remainder belong to the Saṅgha and should be distributed according to the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) allotment.
In the absence of such an allotment, they should be distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder.

The same rule applies even when many robes have been brought forth out of faith in a monk who has entered the rains residence at that monastery, and given with the thought, "We give these to the dwelling."
But if, having placed it at the base of his feet, they say, "We give this to this bhikkhu," it belongs to him alone.
In one man's house there were two rains-retreat gifts: the first portion was taken by a novice, and the second for the seat of the elder.
He sent one robe of ten cubits and one of eight cubits, saying, "This is the rains-retreat gift for the bhikkhus who have received it."
Having thus investigated and assigned the superior portion to the novice, the remaining portion should be given to the elder’s seat.
However, if both are brought to the house, fed, and he himself places [the gift] at the feet of each, then whatever is given to whom belongs to that person alone.
Hereafter follows the method as it appears in the *Mahāpaccarī*: “In one person’s house, the rainy-season gift for a young novice...”

If it reaches [the recipient], and he asks, “To whom has our *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-offering) been given?”—without saying, “It was for the novice,” one should say, “You will know at the time of distribution. On the day of distribution, one should have a senior elder (*mahāthera*) sent to have it brought out.
If the person to whom the *vassāvāsika* was given disrobes or passes away, and people ask [about it]:
—“To whom does our *vassāvāsika* bowl belong?”—it should be explained to them as it truly is.
If they say, “We give it to you,” it accrues to that monk.
If they give it to the Saṅgha or to a group, it accrues to the Saṅgha or to the group. If those who have entered the rains residence are exclusively pure *paṃsukūlikas*...
“...they should be brought back and used to provide for the rainy-season bedding and requisites, or pillows and such should be made.
This is the duty of the resident monks.
The discussion on the allocation of lodgings is finished.
The Story of Upananda 319. Regarding the account of Upananda:
"In that case, O foolish man, what was taken by you there has been relinquished here;
what was taken by you here has been relinquished there. Herein, this is the meaning: that lodging which was taken by you there has been relinquished by you.
While one is still grasping here, it becomes released. But when one says, "Now, friend, I release this," it is released even there.
Thus you are excluded from both.
This, however, is the analysis here: by grasping, grasping is pacified; by grasping, attachment is pacified.
Through clinging, grasping is stilled; through clinging, clinging itself is stilled. How so?
Here, someone, having taken up lodgings in one monastery on the day of entering the rains retreat, goes to a neighboring monastery and takes up lodgings there as well.
By this act of grasping, his previous grasping is stilled. Another thinks, "I shall dwell here."
Having made a mere attachment [to his current dwelling], he goes to a neighboring monastery and takes up lodgings there;

by this taking up, his previous attachment is pacified. Another, thinking "I shall dwell here," either takes up lodgings or makes an attachment, and having gone to a neighboring monastery, makes an attachment [there] thinking, "Now I shall dwell right here"; thus, by means of that attachment...
Either the taking [of a dwelling] by means of attachment ceases through attachment, or in all cases it remains in the final taking or attachment.

However, for one who goes thinking, "Having taken a lodging in one monastery, I will dwell in another," the taking of the lodging ceases upon crossing the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*). But if... there...
"If it will be comfortable, I shall stay; if not, I shall return. Having gone there and knowing that it is not comfortable, he returns;
this is permissible. Regarding the phrase "within three years": here, one who is "within three years" means one who is either two years senior or junior.
However, one who is one year senior or junior, or one who is of the same age, [is also included].
In this regard, there is nothing at all that needs to be said. All these [seats] may be used by two persons each to sit upon, whether it be a bed or a bench.
Whatever is capable of supporting three people—whether it be portable or not portable—even on such a mere wooden plank, it is permissible to sit together with one who is not yet ordained.
“Elephant’s claw” refers to that which is fixed upon an elephant’s frontal globe; it is said that this is the name given to such a thing.

Regarding “all the furnishings of the palace”: doors, beds, chairs, fans, water-jars made of gold or silver, water-basins, and whatever else is decorated with artistic work—all of these are permitted.
“The male and female slaves of the palace, the fields and lands, the cattle and buffalo... [and so forth].
When they say, “We give this,” there is no need for separate acceptance; once the palace has been accepted, it is already accepted.
It is not permitted to spread out woolen rugs (*gonaka*) and so forth upon couches or chairs in either a communal monastery or a private dwelling and use them.
However, such items may be used on a Dhamma-seat under the principle of what is offered by laypeople; even there, it is not permitted to lie down.
The Story of Upananda is concluded. The Discussion on the Subject of What Is Not to Be Given (Avissajjiyavatthu). 321.
“These five” refers to five by way of groups; however, by way of their individual forms, they are many. Among them, *ārāma*...
A flower garden or a fruit garden. A park site (*ārāmavatthu*) is a plot of land set aside and demarcated for the purpose of those very gardens;
or, when those gardens have fallen into ruin, it is their former ground area. A monastery (*vihāra*) is any dwelling such as a palace and so forth.
A monastery site (*vihāravatthu*) is the location where that [monastery] is established. A couch (*mañca*) is—namely, a *masāraka*...
A bedstead is one of the four types previously mentioned: the *bundikābaddha*, the *kuḷīrapādaka*, or the *āhaccapādaka*.
A chair (*pīṭha*) is one of the four types of chairs beginning with the *masāraka*. A mattress (*bhisi*) is one of the five types beginning with the woolen mattress (*uṇṇabhisi*).
A bolster (*bimbohana*) is one of the various types of bolsters already described. An iron cauldron (*lohakumbhī*).
A *kumbhī* is a pot made of black iron, copper, or any kind of metal whatsoever. The same principle applies to the *lohakaṭāhaka* (iron cauldron) and so forth.
Here, however, *bhāṇaka* refers to a water-pot (*arañjara*), while *vāraka* refers to a jar (*ghaṭa*). A *kaṭāha* is simply a basin.
Regarding the axes and such, as well as the creepers and such, there is nothing that is difficult to understand. Thus—
Two have two factors, the third has four;
the fourth has nine divisions, and the fifth has eight parts.
Thus, with these five groups, he whose eyes are the fivefold purity—
The Lord has declared twenty-five kinds of heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Regarding this, the following is the analytical exposition: for all these heavy goods are here "not to be disposed of" (*avissajjiya*), as stated in the *Kīṭāgiri* case as "not to be divided" (*avebhaṅgiya*). However, in the *Parivāra*, it is said:
"Five things not to be disposed of and not to be divided were spoken of by the Great Seer."
“There is no offense for one who gives it away or uses it;
this question was pondered by those skilled in the Dhamma.

Thus it has come down. Therefore, while it is not to be given away or shared out by way of cutting off the root, there is no offense for one who gives it away or uses it by way of exchanging it; such is the intended meaning here.
In this regard, here is the sequential explanation: first of all, it is not permitted to offer these five kinds of things for the sake of robes, almsfood, or medicine.
However, it is permitted to exchange durable goods for durable goods, and valuable goods for valuable goods.
As for durable goods, such as fields, building sites, ponds, or irrigation channels, they may be managed by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.

It is not permissible to accept, receive, or consent to [these things] directly; however, it is permissible for them to be treated as allowable articles once they have been processed by a kappiyakāraka (one who makes things allowable).
Furthermore, it is permissible to exchange four types of property: an ārāma for an ārāma, an ārāmavatthu for an ārāmavatthu, a vihāra for a vihāra, and a vihāravatthu for a vihāravatthu.
Herein is the method of exchange: if the Saṅgha’s coconut grove is located far away, or if there are too many kappiyakārakas...
They eat it. Even when they do not eat it, they give the cart-hire and take only a small amount.
However, there was a grove near the monastery belonging to other people living in a village not far from that monastery;
those people approached the Saṅgha and requested that monastery by means of their own grove, and the Saṅgha, having obtained permission with the words, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha," [granted it].
It should be accepted. Even if there are a thousand trees belonging to the monks and five hundred men [belonging to the laypeople], one should not say, "Your park is small.
For although this may be small, it nevertheless yields more income than the other.
Even if it yields exactly the same amount, one may still enjoy it whenever one wishes.
It must certainly be accepted as "Sakka. However, if there are more trees belonging to the people, one should say, "Are not your trees more numerous?
If they say, "May our merit be even greater; we give them to the Saṅgha," it is permissible to accept them after making this known.
[In this case], the trees belong to the monks and bear fruit, while those belonging to the people...
Trees do not yet bear fruit; even though they do not yet bear fruit, one must simply accept that they will bear fruit before long.
Trees bear fruit for people, but trees do not yet bear fruit for monks. One should say, "Do your trees not bear fruit?
If [the other] says, "Take them, Venerable Sir; it will be merit for us," [then one may take them].
Having informed the other [monastery], it is permissible to accept [the gift]; in this way, one monastery may be exchanged for another monastery.
By this same method, a monastery site, a monastery, a monastery site, or a monastery may be exchanged for a monastery.
And by means of a large or small monastery site, a monastery, a monastery site, a monastery, or a monastery site may be exchanged.
How should one dwelling be exchanged for another dwelling? Suppose the Saṅgha has a house within a village and people have a mansion in the middle of the monastery;
both are equal in value. If the people request that house in exchange for the mansion, it is permissible to accept it.
If, however, the monks’ house is of greater value, [the rule is: "That which is of greater value..."

When they say, "This is our house," one should say, "Although it is more expensive, it is unsuitable for those who have gone forth; it is not possible for renunciants to live there. But this [other place] is suitable, so please accept it.
In this way, it is permissible to accept. However, if [the other house] is expensive for people, one should say, "Is your house not expensive?"
But when it is said, “Let it be, Bhante; let there be merit for us; please accept it,” then it is proper to accept it.
In this way, one monastery should be exchanged for another monastery. By this same method, a monastery site, a monastery, an arama, or an arama site should be exchanged for a monastery.
And by means of a monastery site—whether of great or small value—one may exchange monasteries, monastery sites, aramas, and arama sites.
Thus, first of all, the exchange of durable goods for durable goods should be understood.
Regarding the exchange of heavy goods for heavy goods, however, whether a bed or a chair be large or small—
even if it has legs only four finger-breadths high, or was made by village children playing in sand-houses— it belongs to the Saṅgha.
From the moment it is given, it becomes heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Even if kings, royal ministers, and others were to give a hundred or a thousand beds all at once, all these allowable beds (*kappiyamañca*) should be accepted;
having accepted them, they should be assigned according to seniority with the words, "Use these for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha," and not on an individual basis.
They should be given. It is also permissible to place the bowl and robes on an extra couch after arranging it in the storehouse or similar locations.
A couch that was given outside the monastery boundary with the words, "We give this to the Saṅgha," should be given to the senior monk of the Saṅgha for his dwelling place.
If there are many couches there, one need not be used; rather, it should be placed where there is work to be done in the dwelling place of whichever monk requires it.
It should be given with the words: “Make use of this as communal property of the Saṅgha.
If one obtains another bed worth a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand [coins] in exchange for a bed worth a high price, it may be accepted after bartering.
It is not only beds that may be exchanged for beds; monasteries, monastery sites, dwellings, dwelling sites, stools, couches, and pillows may also be exchanged.
It is permissible to exchange them. This same method applies to stools, couches, and pillows as well;
for regarding these, the distinction between what is allowable (*kappiya*) and what is unallowable (*akappiya*) is exactly as stated. Among those, what is unallowable must not be used;

what is allowable may be used through communal ownership (*saṅghika-paribhoga*). Alternatively, having exchanged what is unallowable or what is valuable—even if it is allowable—one should take the aforementioned items.
However, there is no such thing as a mattress or pillow made of heavy goods.
As for the iron pot, the iron vessel, and the iron cauldron—these three, whether large or small, even if they hold only a *pasata* measure of water—are indeed heavy goods.
Furthermore, regarding the iron bucket, it may be made of black iron, copper, round iron, or bell-metal.
Whatever is made [of metal] that occupies a "foot" (pāda) in the island of Siṃhala must be distributed. A "foot" measures five *nāḷis* by the Magadhan measure;
anything exceeding that is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*). These, first of all, are the metal vessels mentioned in the Canon (*pāḷi*).

Furthermore, even those not mentioned in the Canon—such as water-pitchers (*bhiṅgāra*), receiving-bowls (*paṭiggaha*), ladles (*uḷuṅka*), wooden spoons (*dabbikaṭacchu*), bowls (*pātitaṭṭaka*), cups (*saraka*), caskets (*samugga*), charcoal-bins (*aṅgārakapalla*), incense-burners (*dhūmakaṭacchu*), and so forth—are included.
Whether small or large, all heavy articles [are included]. However, these are items to be distributed: the alms-bowl, a bronze vessel, and a copper vessel.
An item fashioned from bell-metal, iron, or brass is permissible for communal use by the Saṅgha or as a gift from a layperson, but it is not permissible for individual use.
Even if a vessel made of bell-metal or similar materials has been given to the Saṅgha...
Indeed, it is not permissible [to use] a personal ornament (*pārihāriya*). It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that "it should be used only in the manner of a household item.

However, with the exception of articles made from vessels, among other allowable metal objects—such as a collyrium box, a collyrium stick, an ear-cleaner, a needle, a leaf-needle, a small pair of scissors, a small awl, a small thorn-remover, a key, and so forth—[these may be used].
A gong, a kattara-stick, a piercing tool, a nose-ornament, a spear-head, an iron hammer, an iron chisel, an iron ball, an iron lump, an iron wheel,
and any other broken iron utensil that is subject to distribution; furthermore, smoke-pipes, iron lamps, tree-lamps, hanging lamps, wall-hanging lamps, images of women, men, or animals—
whether these or others— to be placed upon walls, ceilings, doors, and so forth, starting from an iron peg.

All metal vessels are indeed heavy articles (*garubhaṇḍa*); even those obtained by oneself must not be used for personal consumption after having accepted them, but are permitted for use belonging to the Saṅgha or as gifts from householders.
The same rule applies to vessels made of tin. Vessels such as plates and bowls made of stone or clay are also indeed heavy articles.

However, a small oil-jar is indeed a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa) from the moment it is taken up. Vessels made of gold, silver, bronze, brass, or crystal are not permitted even if they belong to a layperson;
how much less so if they belong to the Saṅgha or are used for personal use.
But in the case of using furniture for lodgings, everything is permitted, whether it has been consecrated (āmāsa) or unconsecrated (anāmāsa).
Regarding axes and other tools: an axe by which one cannot perform any great work other than cutting a handle-stick or stripping sugarcane is "to be shared" (*bhājanīya*).
An axe larger than that, whether made in any manner whatsoever, is indeed "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Furthermore, an axe—even one used by physicians for venesection—is indeed heavy property. A hatchet is similar to an axe.

Such is the decision. However, that which is made by way of a collection of weapons is not to be touched. A pickaxe—even if it is only four finger-breadths in size—is indeed a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa).

Whether a chisel has a square face, a scoop-shaped face, or is curved or straight—even down to the handle-piercing for a broom—if it is attached to a handle, it is indeed a heavy object. [The same applies to] the tool for carving the handle of a broom.
However, that which is merely a fruit without a stalk—such as can be placed in a small box and carried about—is "to be shared" (*bhājanīya*).
Even the tip [of the fruit] is included by the very act of piercing it.
Those people who have given axes and other tools to the monastery, when their house has been burnt down or plundered by thieves, [should say]: "Venerable sir, give us back our implements."

If they say, “We shall restore them to their original state,” they should be given back. If they bring them back, they should not be refused; nor should those who do not bring them back be reproached.

For smiths, carpenters, coppersmiths, reed-workers, jewelers, bowl-binders, and others, all iron implements—such as hammers, tongs, pliers, scales, and so forth—become heavy goods (garubhaṇḍa) from the moment they are given to the Saṅgha.
This also applies to the tools of tin-smiths, goldsmiths, and leather-workers.
The same method applies here. However, this is the distinction: among the tools of the tipu-smelter, the small knife for cutting tipu;
among the goldsmith’s tools, the small knife for cutting gold; and among the tanner’s tools, the small knife for cutting prepared leather—these are items that may be shared.
Among the barber’s and tailor’s tools as well, with the exception of the large knife and the large pair of scissors.
The *mahāpipphalaka* (large pepper) and all items that are to be distributed are [light property]. The *mahākattarī* (large knife) and so forth are heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Among creepers and the like, any creeper such as the *vettavalli* (bamboo-creeper) measuring half an arm’s length—if it has been given to the Saṅgha, or grows there [on Saṅgha land], or has been protected and guarded—constitutes a heavy good.
If, when work for the Saṅgha or work for a *cetiya* has been performed, there is a surplus of it...
It is permissible to include it even among one’s personal property; however, that which is unprotected does not constitute "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

Ropes or cords made of thread, cotton, bark, coconut husks, or leather—whether single-stranded or double-stranded, made by twisting together cotton, bark, coconut husks, or leather—become heavy goods from the moment they are given to the Saṅgha.
However, thread that has not been twisted, as well as cotton, bark, coconut husks, and [leather], [are not heavy goods].
And they are worthy of being used. However, those by whom these ropes, cords, and so forth were given should not be prevented from taking them away for their own business.
Any bamboo whatsoever—even if as small as an eight-finger-width needle-handle—that has been given to the Saṅgha or grown there [is likewise theirs].
Or, heavy goods that have been guarded and protected—even those may be given for personal use once they have been used for Sangha-work or work for a shrine (cetiyakamma) and there is a surplus.
Furthermore, oil-tubes for massaging the feet, walking sticks, sandals with handles, umbrella handles, and umbrella ribs—these are the items here that are subject to distribution.
When people leaving a burnt house take these things and depart, they do not...

[The bamboo] must be returned. One who takes bamboo that has been protected and guarded must, whether it is of equal value or more than that, perform a compensatory act (*phātikamma*) by providing something stable, even if only of equivalent value.
One who takes it without performing a compensatory act must use it right there;
when departing, he should leave it in the communal dwelling (*saṅghikāvāsa*) and then go. If one has taken it and gone away through forgetfulness...
Having sent it, it should be given. By one who has gone to another region, it should be placed in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha that has been reached.
"Grass" means any grass whatsoever, excluding *muñja* and *pabbaja*. However, where there is no grass, they cover [the ground] with leaves;
therefore, leaves too are included under "grass. Thus, among *muñja* and the rest, anything whatsoever—
