Even a mere handful of grass, or even a single leaf from among palm leaves and the like, if it has been given to the Saṅgha, or if it grows there naturally, or if it is grass grown within the monastery grounds that was originally part of the Saṅgha’s grass-land and has been protected and guarded—it is considered "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa).

Even such property, when used for the business of the Saṅgha or for the business of a shrine (cetiya), may be given after the work is completed for use in personal business. [This applies to] people whose houses have been burnt down.
Those who go taking it with them should not be stopped. Even a blank book measuring only eight finger-breadths is indeed a heavy object.

As for clay—whether it be natural clay, five-colored clay, lime, or anything among Sajjurasa, kaṅgu, *uṭṭha*, *silesa*, and so forth—if it has been brought from a place where it is scarce, or given there, or produced locally, or protected and guarded even if it is only the size of a ripe palm fruit, [it is a heavy object].
It is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*). Even that may be given for a personal task once the work for the Saṅgha and the work for the shrine (*cetiyakamma*) have been completed.
However, asafoetida, vermilion, yellow orpiment, realgar, and collyrium are items to be shared out (*bhājanīyabhaṇḍa*).
Regarding wooden articles (*dārubhaṇḍa*), any wooden article even as small as a needle-handle eight finger-breadths long may belong to the Saṅgha in places where wood is scarce.
The *Kurundi* states: "Whether it has been given [to the Saṅgha] or grown there [on its land], and is protected and guarded—this constitutes heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*).

However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, having included all manufactured items such as wood, bamboo, leather, and stone within the category of wooden property (*dārubhaṇḍa*), the determination of wooden property is explained starting from the passage:
"Now at that time, a chair (*āsandika*) had arisen for the Saṅgha."

In this regard, the summary of the meaning is as follows: a high-backed chair, a seven-limbed throne, a *bhaddapīṭha*, a bench, a bench with sheep’s-leg feet, a bench with a rounded frame of *āmalaka* wood, a plank, a wicker stool, and a straw mat—among these, whatever is small or large, if it has been given to the Saṅgha, it is considered "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
And here, by the mention of the "straw mat," benches made of plantain leaves and so forth are also included.
These are included. Even a tiger-skin rug, though covered with the forms of wild beasts and sewn with jewels, is indeed a heavy article.
A curved board, a long board, a board for washing robes, a rubbing board, a rubbing mallet, a knot for cutting tooth-sticks, a staff-mallet, a water-strainer, a dye-vat, and a water-receptacle.

Whether made of wood, ivory, or bamboo—whether with feet or without feet—a casket, a chest, a box larger than the size of a foot-hold, a water-tub, a water-basin, a ladle, a spoon, a drinking-cup, or a conch-shell for water:
whatever among these is heavy property given to the Sangha is [considered such]. However, a conch-shell bowl is to be distributed.
Likewise, a wooden water-pot;
a foot-stool, a spittoon, or a circular seat—whether made of wood or of cloth, leaves, and so forth—all such items are "heavy goods" (garubhaṇḍa).
A bowl-rest, a bowl-cover, a palm-leaf fan, a fan, a broom, a basket, a stick-broom, and a hand-broom [are also included].
Among these as well, whatever—whether small or large—is made of wood, bamboo, leaves, hide, or any other material, it is indeed "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Whatever house-furniture there may be, whether made of wood or stone, such as pillars, scales, steps, planks, and so forth;
any kind of bedstead; any kind of floor-covering; and any kind of unallowable hide—all this belongs to the Saṅgha.
A heavy article that has been given may be used as a floor-covering.
However, sheepskin falls under the category of bedspreads, and it too is a heavy article. Appropriate hides are to be shared out.
But in the *Kurundi*, it is stated: "Any hide the size of a bed is a heavy article."
The mortar, pestle, winnowing fan, grindstone, small grindstone, stone trough, stone basin, spinning wheel, shuttle, and so forth—
all these articles of the weaver and others, all the tools of the plowman, and all vehicles equipped with wheels are indeed heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Among these, such things as the leg of a bed, the frame of a bed, the leg of a stool, the frame of a stool, and the handles of axes, hatchets, and so forth— whatever [is included therein]...
Woodwork for which the carving has been partially completed but not yet finished is *bhājanīya* (common property); however, once carved and polished, it becomes *garubhaṇḍa* (heavy property).

Furthermore, among items permitted for a resident, there is no offense regarding a staff, a handle for an umbrella, a leaf-fan, a walking stick, sandals, a set of fire-sticks, a water-strainer, a bowl for washing the feet that is not oversized, a jar for *āmalaka* fruit, a vessel for *āmalaka* fruit, or a gourd-vessel.
A gourd-pitcher, a horn-vessel, and so forth—all these are "vessels" (*bhājanīya*); anything larger than those is "heavy property" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

An elephant tusk or any kind of horn that has not been carved, remaining exactly as it was produced, is a "vessel"; the determination regarding bed-legs and other items made from them is the same as before.
Even if carved and finished, a casket for asafoetida, a casket for collyrium, or a toggle is [treated as heavy property].
The collyrium box, the collyrium stick, and the water-wiper—all these are indeed items to be shared.
Among earthenware vessels, everything used for human enjoyment and utility—including jars, pots, and other clay vessels;
bowls and basins; charcoal basins; incense burners; oil lamps; lamp-stands; lamp-shades; and roof-tiles—is [to be shared].
The *thūpika* (the spout) has been heavy property since the time it was given to the Saṅgha.

However, from the time it is used for washing the feet, a water-pot (*ghaṭaka*) that is not of excessive size, as well as a bowl (*patta*), a dish (*thālaka*), a golden vessel, and a water-flask (*kuṇḍikā*)—these here are items belonging to the category of divisible property.
And just as with earthenware vessels, so too among metal vessels, the water-flask belongs exclusively to the category of divisible property; this is the sequential explanation in this matter.
The Discussion on Non-Transferable Objects is concluded.
323. Regarding "by the mere placing of a pigeon-nest":
this refers to the mere attachment of a pigeon-nest above the doorposts. Regarding "by the mere plastering of the borders": [this refers to...]
"By the mere act of smearing with cow dung and plastering with clay.

"Smoke-time" means that as long as the smoke from its funeral pyre is still visible, they give the monastery, having completed it after obtaining permission during that period of smoke, saying, "This monastery belongs to him alone.
"Incomplete" here means incomplete so long as the rafters have not yet been set up. Regarding the rafters...

But once they have ascended [into the building], it is considered "much done"; therefore, from that point on, nothing more should be given, as he will have them do whatever little remains by means of persuasion.
Having inspected the work in a small vihāra, one should give five or six years' worth; having inspected the work in a four-cubit vihāra, four years' worth;
in a five-cubit one, five years' worth; and in a six-cubit one, six years' worth. [This applies to] a half-yoga.
However, because it is seven or eight cubits [in height], it is therefore stated here as "seven or eight years old.

But if it is nine cubits, it should be given even when it is nine years old. Furthermore, for a large dwelling or palace that is ten or eleven cubits [in height], one that is ten or eleven years old should be given. But for one that is twelve cubits...
Even for a building larger than that, such as one resembling a bronze palace, only twelve years' worth [of materials] should be given, and not more than that.
If a *navakammika* (work-assigning) monk obtains that residence during the rainy season, he may not be obstructed during the [subsequent] seasons.
If that residence falls into decay, it should be reported to the owner of the residence or to someone born in his lineage.
—“Your dwelling is falling into ruin; look after this dwelling! If he is unable to do so, the monks should have his relatives or attendants encouraged to look after it.
If they too are unable, it should be looked after using the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha.
If even that is not possible, one dwelling should be relinquished and the remainder looked after. Having relinquished many, [the rest should be maintained].
It is indeed permissible to maintain even one [monastery].

When food is scarce and monks have departed, all monasteries will perish; therefore, having relinquished one, two, or three monasteries, those who consume the rice gruel, alms-food, robes, and other requisites from there must certainly maintain the remaining monasteries.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is said: "If there are no requisites belonging to the Saṅgha, one monk should be told:
'Take one bed-place and look after it. If he desires more, even if only a third part or a half is given, he should be made to look after it.
Then [if others say], 'Only the mere posts remain here; much work must be done'..."
If he does not wish to do so, one should have him maintain it [thinking]: “Let this be made yours as personal property;
for in this way, there will be a place for the Saṅgha’s belongings and a dwelling place for the novices. When maintained in this manner, while he is alive, it remains his personal property;
when he has died, it belongs solely to the Saṅgha. If he wishes to give it to his co-residents, he should look at the work [required].
"Having made it one-third or one-half [of the property] personal (*puggalika*), he should have it looked after. For in this way, he is permitted to give it to his co-residents (*saddhivihārika*).
But when there is no one to look after it, he should have it looked after by the method beginning with 'having assigned one dwelling place,' and so forth.
And this other point is also stated in that very same place: "Two monks, having taken and cleared a piece of land belonging to the Saṅgha..."
They construct a dwelling place. Whichever person first took possession of that site is the owner. If both parties claim it as their own private property (*puggalika*), he alone is the owner.

If he makes it the property of the Saṅgha while the other makes it his private property, if there is another abundant site suitable for a dwelling, even one who makes it his private property should not be prevented.
However, if no other such suitable place exists...
Having set that aside, it must be made into property belonging to the Saṅgha. However, whatever value-work has been done on it there must be paid back.
But if, in the constructed dwelling or at the site where the dwelling was built, there are shade-providing or fruit-bearing trees, they should be removed after obtaining permission.
If they belong to an individual, the owner must be asked; if they do not give them, [the matter ends there].
After asking for permission up to three times, they may be removed [from the site] with the thought, "We shall provide the value of the trees.

However, if someone, without taking even a single creeper belonging to the Saṅgha, builds a private dwelling on land belonging to the Saṅgha using requisites brought from elsewhere, half belongs to the Saṅgha and half belongs to the individual. This applies if it is a palace.
The lower story belongs to the Saṅgha; the upper story belongs to an individual. If he desires the lower story, it belongs to him.
If he desires both the lower and the upper, he receives half in each case.
He has two lodgings built—one belonging to the Saṅgha and one belonging to an individual—if he builds them using building materials provided from the monastery.
He receives a third share. If he builds a structure or a porch on a site not yet prepared, then half belongs to the Saṅgha outside the wall and half belongs to him.
But if it is built by filling in a large uneven area and providing a path where there was none, the Saṅgha has no ownership over it.

"One choice bed": here the meaning is that I allow one choice bed at the place where building work is being undertaken, or at the place where [the residence] has been obtained by seniority, whichever he desires.

"When he departs once it is finished, it belongs to him alone": when he returns and stays again during the rainy season, it belongs to him alone; however, if he does not return, his pupils and others may not take possession of it.
The discussion on the assignment of building work is concluded.
324. Discussion on the Prohibition Against Using [Furniture] Elsewhere, etc. “*Nātiharantīti*” means they do not use it after having carried it elsewhere.

“*Guttatthāyā*” means for the sake of protecting whatever beds, chairs, and so forth are there; the meaning is that I allow one to carry it elsewhere for that purpose. Therefore, having carried it elsewhere...
For one who uses [the property] as communal enjoyment for the Saṅgha, what is lost is truly lost, and what is worn out is truly worn out.
If it remains sound, once that monastery has been repaired, it must be restored to its original state.

For one who uses it as private enjoyment, what is lost or worn out becomes his personal liability; once it has been repaired, he must indeed give it back. If, from that [private stock], rafters and so forth—

Having taken them, if they are used in another monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, they are considered properly used. However, by those who use them in a private dwelling, either the original value must be paid or they must be restored to their former state.
One who, with a mind of theft, takes beds, chairs, and so forth from an abandoned monastery, is to be dealt with according to the value of the goods as if they were stolen.
If one takes them thinking, "I will give them back at the time of re-inhabitation," and uses them as the property of the Saṅgha...
For one who uses [the property], what is lost is truly lost, and what is worn out is truly worn out.
If it is healthy, it should be restored to its original state. For one who uses it as personal property, what is lost becomes a debt to be repaid.
Furthermore, doors, windows, and so forth, whether installed in a communal dwelling or a private dwelling, must certainly be returned.

"For the sake of compensation" (*phātikammatthāya*) means for the sake of increasing [the value]. In this context, what is permitted as compensation is bedding such as beds and chairs that is equal in value or even more than the original.
"A wheel-shaped rug" (*cakkalika*) refers to one made by wrapping woolen cloth or similar materials into a circular shape.

"With wet feet" (*allehi pādehi*) means with such feet from which water is visible where they have stepped; with such feet, one must not step upon ground that has been plastered or upon a dwelling place (*senāsana*).
If, however, only the moisture of the water is visible and not the water itself, it is permissible.
But a foot-wiping cloth may indeed be stepped upon even with wet feet; it is only impermissible at a place where one must step with washed feet while wearing sandals.
"To wrap with a cloth" means that if there is a wooden plank or a straw mat on a plastered floor or a paved floor—
Or if there is none, the feet should be wrapped with a piece of cloth; if that is unavailable, it is also permissible to spread out leaves.
However, for one who places [the bowl] down without spreading anything out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
But if the resident monks there place it on the ground even when it is not spread out, or use it while their feet are unwashed, it is permissible to use it in that same manner.
"Monks, 'prepared walls' refers to white-washed walls or those decorated with paintings.
It is not only walls; one must likewise not lean against a door, a window, a wooden panel, a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar without having covered it with a robe or some other covering."
“Having washed their feet”: having washed their feet, they feel scrupulous about lying down in a place that should be stepped upon with washed feet.
There is also a reading, “dhotapādaka,” which is a designation for a place to be stepped upon with washed feet.
“Having spread it out”: having spread out either the ground that has been made level, or a floor-covering as bedding, or a bed or chair belonging to the Saṅgha, for oneself...

One must lie down only after having spread out a rug provided by another. If, even while sleeping, any part of the body touches the bed or the bench because the rug has shrunk, there is indeed an offense.
Furthermore, regarding the hair, there is an offense for every single hair.
This same principle applies even to one who does not see [the rug] due to its being used as a covering. As for the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet...
However, it is permissible to touch or step upon it. If it strikes one’s body while someone is carrying out a bed or a chair, there is no offense.
The discussion on the prohibition against using [the robe] for other purposes is finished.
Now begins the discussion on the authorization for communal meals and so forth.
325. "They are unable to provide a meal for the Saṅgha" means they are unable to provide a meal for the entire Saṅgha.
Regarding "a designated meal" (*uddesabhatta*) and so forth, they wish to provide a meal for those monks who have been designated by such an instruction as: "Designate one, two, ...
up to ten monks from the Saṅgha and give [the meal] to them. Others likewise, having delimited the number of monks in that same way...
Having invited them, they wish to prepare a meal for them.

Others, having cut out lots, or others, having fixed a schedule such as "for every half-month," "on the Uposatha day," or "on the first day of the lunar fortnight," wish to prepare a meal for one, two... [and so on]... up to ten monks.
Thus, these meals receive the designation of "designated meal" (*uddesabhatta*) and "invitation meal" (*nimantana*).

Regarding the alms-food: since they might not be able to provide it during a famine, but would be able to provide it again once a good harvest has occurred, the Blessed One included that as well and said:
"I allow you, monks, communal meal (saṅghabhatta) and designated meal (uddesabhatta)," and so forth.

In that regard, there is no such thing as a "standing invitation" (*ṭhitikā*) for a meal provided by the Saṅgha; therefore, one must not say there, "We have been eating here for ten or twelve days today; now, bring monks from elsewhere.
Nor is it even permissible to say, "We did not receive [an invitation] on previous days; please accept us for that now. For that—
It reaches those who have arrived one after another.
The discussion on the authorization for meals for the Saṅgha, etc., is concluded.
The discussion on meals by appointment (*uddesabhatta*).

Regarding the *uddesabhatta* (designated alms) and so forth, this is the procedure: when a king or a royal minister has designated [alms] from the Saṅgha, saying, "Bring so many bhikkhus," one should announce the time and ask for the standing order (*ṭhitikā*).

If there is one, the distribution should begin from that point; if not, it should begin from the seat of the Elder (*therāsana*). The designator should also [consider] those who subsist on alms (*piṇḍapātika*).
It must not be exceeded. However, those who observe the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) will exceed it of their own accord.

If it were distributed in this manner, the indolent elder monks would arrive late; one should not say to them, "Venerable sirs, the distribution for those of twenty years' standing is being given, your turn has passed.
Rather, having set aside the turn and distributed [the requisites] to them, one should afterwards [distribute] according to the turn.
It should be distributed. Having heard that "much *uddesabhatta* has arisen in such-and-such a monastery," even monks from a monastery a *yojana* away may come;
it should be distributed starting from the place where they have arrived one after another.

Even for those who have not yet arrived, but have entered the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*), it must certainly be distributed when their pupils and others receive it. Outside the boundary of the precinct...
They say that one should not include those who are already standing [within the boundary], but it should be included.

However, if they have entered the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) and become connected as one unit—whether at the door of their own monastery or within the monastery itself—the boundary is said to be "extended by way of the assembly" (*parisāvasena vaḍḍhitā*);
therefore, it should be included. Even when the portion has been given to the most junior member of the Sangha, it must still be included for those who arrive later. In the second part:
However, when the Elder’s seat has been occupied, those who arrive later do not receive the first portion; they must receive it from the second portion according to the *vassa* (seniority) list.

In a single monastery, having demarcated one place for the assignment of meals, the assigned meal—wherever it may have been announced within the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*) even if it extends for a league (*gāvuta*)—must be distributed at that very place where the meal was assigned.
He sends one monk to another, saying, "Tomorrow, having designated [the meal] from the Saṅgha, send ten monks.
That matter must be announced to the meal-designator. If he forgets on that day, it must be announced early in the morning on the following day.
If, having forgotten, he remembers while entering for alms, [he must announce it] as far as the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīma).
It does not exceed [the boundary]; rather, it should be determined according to the natural standing of the dining hall itself.

Even if the monks have crossed the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) and are connected in a single line with those remaining within the precinct boundary, provided they do not separate from one another by more than twelve *hattha*, it should be determined according to the natural standing of the hall. For the monks...

However, if such a continuous [boundary] does not exist, one should establish a new *ṭhitika* (boundary marker) at whatever place within the outer *upacāra-sīmā* (proximate boundary) one remembers, and there it should be included.
One who remembers [the boundary] in the sitting hall (*āsanasālā*) inside the village should include it by means of the *ṭhitika* of that sitting hall.
Having remembered it anywhere, it must indeed be included; it is not permissible not to include it. For this is not available on the second day.
If someone has a meal designated for those monks who have seen them going from their own monastery to another monastery,

it should be assigned on the basis of their residence in their own monastery as long as they are within the precincts or connected with those standing at the boundary of the precincts in the manner described.
However, what is given to those standing outside the precincts is [to be considered] "from the Saṅgha."
When it is said, "Venerable sir, assign these many bhikkhus," the assignment should be made to those who have arrived.
In this regard, it should be understood that even those standing at a distance are considered to have arrived provided they remain within twelve cubits of one another in a continuous line.
If they go to a particular monastery and announce [the Uposatha] once they have entered, the assignment should be made according to the established occupancy of that monastery.

Even if someone announces the Sangha’s portion upon seeing monks at a village gate, on a street, at a crossroads, or inside a house, it should be given to those who have entered within the precincts (*upacāra*) of each respective place. And here, the precinct of a house is as follows:
"a single house with a single precinct; a single house with multiple precincts; multiple houses with a single precinct."
This should be understood by way of the phrases "various houses" and "various precincts.
In this context, when a house belonging to a single family has a single common area for use, that space within the boundary of the threshold is called "one precinct.
Any portion of alms-food obtained there reaches everyone who stands within that precinct, even if they are engaged in their alms-round; this is what is meant by "one house with one precinct."

However, when a single house has been built with a wall erected in the middle for the sake of the comfortable living of two wives, and separate doorways and passages have been made, the portion of the alms-food obtained there does not reach the one separated by the wall;
it reaches only those sitting in their respective places. This is called "a single house with different precincts."

However, in a house where many bhikkhus have been invited and they are made to sit in a continuous line starting from inside the house, filling even the neighboring houses, the portion obtained for recitation that arises there accrues to all of them.
This same principle applies even in the case of a residence belonging to various families which, without having a wall in the middle, is used as a single unit with only one entrance. This is so.
“Various houses with a single common area” means this:

when a portion of the recitation (uddesa) arises for monks sitting in various dwellings, even though the monks are visible through openings in the walls, it reaches only those sitting in their respective dwellings; this is called “various houses with separate common areas.”
However, if one receives a meal for recitation at a certain place— such as a village gate, a street, or a crossroads—
and since no other monk is present, he causes it to reach himself, and on the following day receives another [meal] at that very same place,
he must then offer it to whichever other monk he sees, whether junior or senior. If anyone...
There is no [fault]; one may eat after having caused it to be assigned to oneself.
If, while the monks are sitting in the dining hall waiting for their time, someone comes and says, "Give the bowl designated for the Saṅgha;
give the designated bowl; give a bowl designated from the Saṅgha; give a bowl belonging to the Saṅgha," [one may eat].
Or if he says [this], the portion of the assignment (uddesapatta) should be given after having it taken by means of a formal motion (ṭhitikā).
The same rule applies if it is said: “Give a monk designated by the Saṅgha,” “Give a monk designated from the Saṅgha,” or “Give a monk belonging to the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, a pleasant, conscientious, and wise person should be desired as the assigner here; by him, the formal motion should be requested three times.
If there is no one who knows the seniority, it should be taken from the seat of the senior monk. However, if someone says, "I know;
it was obtained by one with ten years of seniority," he should be asked, "Friend, are there other monks with ten years of seniority?
If, upon hearing him, many come forward saying, "We have ten years, we have ten years," [he should say], "It falls to you."
Without saying, "It falls to you," he should say, "All of you be quiet," and have them stand in order.

Having had them stand, he should ask the lay follower, "How many do you require? When the lay follower replies, "So many monks, venerable sir," he should not say, "It falls to you, it falls to you," but rather [assign] the seniority by years and the seasonal period to the most junior of all.
Both the portion of the day and the shadow must be asked about. If, while the shadow is being asked about, another elder arrives, it should be given to him.
However, if after asking about the shadow one says, "It falls to you," and an elder arrives [subsequently], he does not receive it.
For even if one has been sitting or sleeping due to a long conversation, what was taken is rightly taken.
It has been exceeded, even greatly exceeded; for this is indeed a commodity intended for distribution that comes to the one who is present.
In this case, the state of being "present" is to be defined by way of the precincts (*upacāra*). And the precincts consist of the interior enclosure of the assembly hall;
for one standing within that, the gain reaches him.
Someone had eight alms-bowls brought from the assembly hall; he filled seven bowls with choice foods and one bowl with water, and sent them to the assembly hall.
Having received them, they departed without saying anything, placing the bowls in the hands of the monks.
Whatever was obtained by whichever person, that belonged to him alone. But as for the one who received the water, even though it was [the last], it was his.

Setting aside the meal for the resident monks, another designated meal (uddesabhatta) should be requested. Whether that meal obtained is coarse or refined, whether it includes the three robes or not, it belongs to him alone;
for such is his specific distinction of merit. As for water, however, since it is not considered "material food" (āmisa), another designated meal may be received.
But if they come having taken [the requisites] and say, "Venerable sir, please divide all this and consume it," then after everyone has divided and consumed it, water should be drunk.
Having designated [the portion] from the Saṅgha, one should say: "Give to the eight great elders;
give to the middle-ranking [elders]; give to the junior [elders]; give to the novice monks who have completed their years; give to the middle reciters and so forth."
But when someone says, "Give [the food] to my kinsmen who are monks," one should say, "Lay follower, you speak thus,
but it does not reach them by way of their standing [in the order]," and it must be given according to their standing. However, when young novices have received designated meals (*uddesabhatta*),
if there is a festival in the donors' house, they should be told, "Send it to your teachers and preceptors."

However, when in a meal designated for a specific purpose (*uddesabhatta*) the first portion falls to the novices and the subsequent portion to the great elders, the novices do not get to go ahead simply because they received the first portion; they must proceed according to their proper order of seniority.
When it is said, "Having designated [the meal] from the Saṅgha, you come here," if one says, "You will know about me at another time too..."
However, it should be distributed according to the sequence of standing in line (*ṭhitikā*), thinking, "The sequence proceeds in this manner. Furthermore, if after saying,
"Give the bowl designated for the Saṅgha," the bowl is not yet taken, and someone takes the bowl of anyone at all, fills it, and brings it back,
that which has been brought must likewise be distributed according to the sequence of standing in line.
One who has been sent with the instruction, “Bring a bowl for the designated meal,” says, “Venerable sirs, give me one bowl; I shall bring it for the invited meal.
If the monks, knowing that he has come from the house where the designated meal is served, say to him, “Have you not come from such-and-such a house?
he replies, “Yes, venerable sirs; it is not for an invited meal, but for the designated meal.”
He says: "It should be taken by way of standing. However, if one who is told, "Bring a bowl," asks, "Which one shall I bring?
and, being told, "Whichever you prefer," then comes, this is called a "released messenger" (*vissaṭṭhadūta*).
Whether it be the bowl for recitation, the bowl in the regular order, or a personal bowl—whichever he desires, that should be given to him. One fool...
An incompetent person, when sent with the instruction, "Bring the bowl for the recitation," does not know how to speak and remains silent;
he should not be asked, "Whose presence have you come to? or "Whose bowl will you bring?
For if he were so addressed, in accordance with the nature of the question, he might say, "I have come to your presence" or "I will bring your bowl. Thereafter, him—
Other monks, feeling disgusted, would not look at that monk. However, they should be told: "Where are you going? What are you wandering about doing?
When he replies, "I have come for the sake of receiving an alms-bowl," they should give him a bowl after taking one from their own.
There is what is called a "single-pointed" bowl. Indeed, in the house of a king or a royal minister, there are eight very fine [bowls].
Meals for specific invitations were regularly provided; these were treated as meals for solitary wanderers, and the monks ate them separately according to their own seating order.
Some monks, thinking, "They will reach us tomorrow," left after noting their own place in the order.
While they had not yet returned, other visiting monks arrived and sat down in the assembly hall; at that very moment—
The king’s men arrived and said, “Give us the bowls of exquisite food. The visiting monks, not knowing the established rule, accepted them.
At that very moment, monks who knew the rule arrived and asked, “Why are you accepting these?
[They replied,] “It is exquisite food from the royal palace. [They asked,] “From what year onwards? [They replied,] “From such-and-such a year. [They said,] “Do not—”
Having restrained him with the words, "Do not take [it]," one should cause him to take it by means of a standing attendant.

Once he has taken it, those who have arrived—whether they arrive at the time of the distribution of bowls, at the time of the distribution being given, or when the bowls have been filled and brought from the royal palace—and even when the King sends word, saying, "Let only the monks come today," and gives the almsfood directly into the hands of the monks; such is the almsfood thus given.

When they have returned after taking [the food], those monks who know the standing order (ṭhitika) must stop them with the words, "Do not eat," and it should be distributed only according to that standing order. Then,
when the king feeds them and even fills their bowls, whatever has been brought should be distributed according to the standing order.
However, if only a small amount has been placed in the bowls so that they do not go empty-handed, that need not be claimed.
But if they return with empty bowls after having eaten, then whatever was eaten by them becomes their debt—thus said the Elder Mahāsumma.
The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: "In this case, there is no requirement for it to be a debt."
"However, those who do not know the duration [of the meal] should remain seated until those who do know it arrive.
Even so, what has been eaten is well-eaten; now, it should be distributed by means of the bowl-stand.
One bowl belonging to a monk who lacked even the basic requisites was worth a hundred coins and came as an accessory to his set of three robes, along with almsfood. And in the monastery...
They wrote down, "Such was the alms-food received by the sixty-year-old," and set it aside. Then, after the passing of sixty years, another such alms-food arose.
[The question arose: "Should this be assigned to the one who has held the bowl for sixty years, or to the one who has held it for sixty years from the time she began?
It was said, "To the one who has held it for sixty years," for this bhikkhunī had increased [in seniority] only by holding the bowl.
Having eaten one meal designated for instruction (*uddesabhatta*), a novice (*sāmaṇera*) is born; he may again take a bowl [of food] for that meal as the sustenance of a novice.
This, it is said, is called the "one who stands in the interval" (*antarābhaṭṭhaka*).

However, if a novice who has completed his full years of training ordains on this very day, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall receive a meal designated for instruction," his period of standing [as a novice] has passed. For one [who does so],...
If a monk has received a meal for recitation (*uddesabhatta*) in his bowl, and that bowl is not empty, he causes it to be given to another person sitting nearby;

if they take it away with intent to steal, he is liable for the offense. However, if that monk gives it himself, saying, "Give my bowl," he is not liable. Furthermore, if he has no need for that food and says, "Enough..."
If one says something else, such as, “This food is for me; give this bowl to him and have it brought back,” then whatever is brought from there belongs entirely to the owner of the bowl.
If they steal the bowl, it is considered stolen; because the food has already been given away, there is no liability for the value of the bowl.
In a monastery there were ten bhikkhus; of them, nine were alms-food eaters (*piṇḍapātika*) and one was an accepter of invitations.
When it was said, "Give ten portions for the recitation," the alms-food eaters did not wish to take [the portions].

The other bhikkhu took them all, thinking, "They all come to me," and thus the established order (*ṭhitikā*) was not maintained. If he takes them after assigning one to each, the established order is maintained. Having taken them in this manner...
Having had food brought in ten bowls, he says, "Venerable sirs, please show me favor," and gives nine bowls to the alms-collecting monks;
this is called "given by a monk," and it is permissible to accept them.
If that lay follower says, "Venerable sir, you must come to my house," and that monk says to those monks, "Come,..."
“Venerable sir, please be my companions,” he says, and goes to his house. Whatever is obtained there belongs entirely to him;

the others receive only what is given by him. Then, having had them sit right there in the house and having offered the water of hospitality (*dakṣiṇodaka*), they give them rice gruel, hard food, and so forth, saying to that bhikkhu: “Venerable sir, take whatever people give.”
It is permissible for others [to receive] by word alone. Having filled the bowls of those who have finished eating and taken them, they give them for the purpose of departing;
all that belongs to that very bhikkhu, and what is given by him is permissible for the others.
However, if those people are right there in the monastery, that bhikkhu should say: "Venerable sirs, please take alms from me, and [inform] the people."

If they go because they were told, "It is proper to do what the people say," then everything that is eaten there and brought out belongs to that person alone. Furthermore, even if they go because they were not told, "Take my almsfood," but rather because they thought,
"It is proper to do what the people say," and while they are there, one person offers a blessing with a sweet voice—
Having heard [the Dhamma] and having gained confidence in the tranquility of the elders, they give many requisites for ascetics;
this is what is called "a portion not yet assigned" arising through faith in the elders, and therefore it reaches everyone.
One person, having had it assigned from the Saṅgha, takes a bowl received by way of *ṭhitikā* (standing in line) and [fills it] with choice hard and soft foods.
Having filled it and brought it forth, if one gives it saying, "Venerable sir, let the entire Saṅgha consume this," it should be consumed by all after it has been divided.
However, for the owner of the bowl, even if the period [of the meal] has passed, another designated meal (uddesabhatta) should be set aside.
Then, if he says, "First, give all the bowls belonging to the Saṅgha," [they should be given] to a single modest monk.
The bowl belonging to the Sangha should be given back. Having brought it back, when it is said, "Let the entire Sangha consume [the food]," it should be distributed and consumed.

If one person brings rice in a bowl and says, "I give this as an offering to the Sangha," it should be given by making a single portion sufficient for one person's sustenance, rather than giving individual mouthfuls. Then, having brought the rice, if that person does not know how to say anything further—
He remains silent; he should not say, "For whom was this brought for you? To whom do you wish to give it?
For if he were to speak in accordance with the nature of the question, saying, "It was brought for you;
I wish to give it to you," then other monks, feeling disgusted, might even think that they ought to turn their heads and look at him. However, if [he asks], "Where are you going?"...
When asked, "What are you doing as you wander about? he replies, "I have come taking alms-food for recitation. In that case, it should be assigned by standing by one modest bhikkhu.
If what has been brought is abundant and sufficient for everyone, there is no need for assignment by standing;
rather, the bowl should be filled starting from the seat of the senior elder and given out.
When it is said, "Give me a bowl for the Saṅgha," one should accept it according to the standard allowance without asking, "What will you bring?
However, for such fine foods as rice porridge or a meal of savory delicacies that are regularly obtained, a separate allowance should be established;
likewise for rice gruel served with its accompaniments, and for costly or choice fruits.
Regarding solid foods (*khajjaka*): for ordinary meals, rice-gruel, fruits, and solid foods, however, only a single portion (*ṭhitikā*) may be made.
When it is said, "I will bring ghee," only one portion of all types of ghee is permitted; likewise for all types of oil.
But when it is said, "I will bring honey," only one portion of honey is permitted; the same applies to molasses, *laṭṭhi-madhuka*, and so forth.
Regarding medicines: if they offer scents and garlands for the sake of the Saṅgha, it is permissible for a forest-dweller (piṇḍapātika), yet some say it is not permissible.
Because food (āmisa) itself is prohibited, it is permissible; however, because it was given specifically for the Saṅgha, they say it should not be accepted.
The discussion on designated meals (uddesabhatta) is concluded.
The Discussion on Food Offered by Invitation:
If the invitation is for an individual, he is the master himself. But if it is for the Saṅgha, it should be accepted in the same manner as described regarding food designated for a specific purpose.
However, if the messenger here is competent, [one may say]: "Venerable sir, there is food for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus at the royal palace."
If, instead of saying, "Take [it]," he says, "Take alms-food," it is permissible even for those who subsist on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*).

Furthermore, if an incompetent messenger says, "Take the meal," but the competent distributor of meals says, "Venerable sirs, please go [for alms]"—without saying "the meal"—then this too is permissible even for those who subsist on alms-food. [He says,] "The meal is for you in order of seniority."
However, it is not permissible when it is said, "He shall obtain [it].
If the person who has come to invite them enters the dining hall and says, "Give eight bhikkhus," or "Give eight bowls," this is also permissible for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika);
they should say, "You all go together. But if he says, "Give eight bhikkhus..."
If he says, "Take the food, give eight bowls; take the food," it must be given in order.
However, if the one giving does not break the flow and does not say "the food" [at each interval], but simply says, "You two, you two, go on," it is permissible for the alms-collectors.
If he says, "Venerable sir, give your bowl; you come along," [it is also permissible].

However, one should go [to the house], saying, "Very well, lay followers. Even when told by the Sangha, "Go yourselves after we have designated [the portion]," it should be distributed according to the standing order (*ṭhitikā*).

But from a house where one has been invited for a meal, when someone arrives seeking alms, the bowl should be given according to the standing order, in the same manner as described for the designated meal (*uddesabhatta*).
One person, without saying, "A bowl in order from the Sangha," simply says, "Give one bowl."
Having said this, even before the bowls have been distributed, he takes the bowl of anyone [who approaches], fills it, and brings it back; that belongs only to the owner of the bowl.
It should not be taken by way of a standing distribution (*ṭhitikā*), as in the case of a meal offered for recitation (*uddesabhatta*).
Here too, one who comes and stands silently must not be asked, "Whose presence have you come to? or "Whose bowl will you carry?"
For if one were to say, in accordance with the nature of the question, "I have come into your presence;
I shall take your bowl," then that bhikkhu would be held in contempt by the other bhikkhus.
However, when asked, "Where are you going? What are you wandering about doing? if he says, "I have come for the sake of his bowl," [he may take it] in the order of the meal sequence.
Having taken it, the bowl should be given back. Even when told, "Give the bowl for bringing the meal," it should be given only according to the sequence of the meal-stand.
If, after having brought it, one says, "Let the entire Saṅgha eat," it should be eaten after being divided.
For the owner of the bowl, even if their turn has passed, another meal from the sequence should be set aside and given to them.
If one person brings food in a bowl and says, "I give it to the Saṅgha," it should be divided by way of mouthfuls, starting from the point where the food is formed into mouthfuls.
However, if he remains silent, one should not ask, "For whom was this brought?
To whom do you wish to give it? But if he is asked, "Where are you going? What are you wandering about doing? [then he may speak].

If someone says, "Food has been brought for the Saṅgha by me; food has been brought for the Elders by me," it should be accepted and distributed according to the established order of portions (*ālopabhattaṭṭhitikā*).

However, if what has been thus brought is so much that it is sufficient for the entire Saṅgha, it is called "food brought as alms" (*abhihaṭabhikkhā*), which is permissible even for those who live on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*);
in this case, there is no need to ask about the established order of portions, [and distribution begins] starting from the seat of the Elder.
It should be given after filling the bowl.
Suppose a lay follower sends [a message] to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, or to one renowned for his mastery of the scriptures and ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), or to the meal-designator, saying:
"Please come, taking eight bhikkhus with you, for the purpose of receiving our meal. Even if...
If it has been sent by relatives who are attendants, these three persons are not permitted to ask;
rather, having had eight bhikkhus designated from the Saṅgha, one should go with oneself as the ninth. Why?
Because the gain for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha arises depending on these bhikkhus. However, a resident bhikkhu who is not well-known for his mastery of the texts, the dhutaṅgas, and so forth...

He is permitted to ask; therefore, having set forth the preliminary inquiry, "Shall I take [the requisites] from the Saṅgha, or shall I come with those whom I know?", he should act according to what the donors say.
However, when it is said, "Come, taking either those who depend on you or those whom you know," then he may go together with whichever of them so desire.
He is permitted to go. If they send word saying, "Send eight bhikkhus," he must send them from the Saṅgha itself.
If it is possible for him to obtain almsfood in another village, he should go to that other village.
If it is not possible to obtain it, he should enter that very village for alms.
When invited monks are seated in the dining hall, if people come there saying, “Give [alms] into the bowls,” it should not be given by those who were not invited.
It should be said, “These are the invited monks. However, if they say, “You may give as well,” then it is permissible to give.
During festivals and such occasions, people go of their own accord to the monastic cells and meditation halls.
They invite [the Master] together with even a hundred monks who are experts in the Tipiṭaka and preachers of the Dhamma.
At such times, it is appropriate to take along even those who know [the texts], for people who have need of the Great Saṅgha of monks do not go to their individual cells or meditation huts;
rather, they come from the assembly hall and take as many monks as they can, according to their capacity and strength.
However, if the senior monk of the Saṅgha, or one well-known for his mastery of the texts or the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), or the meal-assigner,
or someone else who has spent the rains retreat elsewhere or gone somewhere and is returning to his own place,
and people offer hospitality to this newcomer— then those who know [of his arrival] should take him once and go. But from the time he is bound [to the monastery],...
Once the second round has begun, one must go taking [the robes] from the Saṅgha itself.
If those who have only recently arrived as newcomers go thinking, "We shall see our relatives or supporters," their relatives and supporters there will offer them hospitality.
In this case, however, it is permissible for those who know [the situation] to go taking [the robes].

However, in the case of one who receives excessive invitations such that his own residence and the visiting residences are treated as exactly the same—wherever people prepare meals for the Saṅgha and sit down to eat—the rule is that he must go taking [the meal] from the Saṅgha itself; this is the distinction regarding invitations.
The remainder of all the questions should be understood according to the method already stated concerning meals given by enumeration (*uddesabhatta*). In the *Kurundi*, however...
When it is said, “Give eight great elders,” it is replied, “Only eight great elders should be given. This same principle applies to those of middle standing and so forth.
However, if one says without making a distinction, “Give eight monks,” they should be given from the Saṅgha.
The discussion on meals by invitation is finished.
Regarding the Discourse on the Ticket-Rice:

However, because of the statement, "Monks, I allow you to recite [the schedule] after having tied it to a tally-stick or a tablet and having piled them up," one may use a tally-stick made of heartwood or one made of bamboo, rattan, palm leaves, and so forth.

Or, having inscribed the letters "the ticket-meal for so-and-so" on a strip of cloth and having placed it in a basket or with his robe-possessions, one should heap all the tickets together and mix them repeatedly from bottom to top;
then, if there is a fixed order, the meal-designator endowed with the five factors should begin from that fixed order. If not—
Whatever [tickets] there are, they should be distributed starting from the senior seats.
Even for those who arrive later, they should be given in a continuous sequence, even if they stand far apart, according to the method described for the *uddesabhatta*.
If there are many alms-villages all around the monastery but not many monks, the tickets may also be distributed according to the villages.
When [the alms-food] reaches them, they should be assigned by way of the village alone, saying, "The *salākabhatta* reaches you in such-and-such village. When assigning it in this manner,
even if there are various kinds of sixty *salākabhattas* in each village and all have been assigned, if there are another two or three *salākabhattas* near the village he has reached, those too—
These alone should be given to them; for it is not possible to send another monk on their account.
If many *salāka*-tickets for meals are designated for several villages, they should be given to seven or eight monks.
However, when giving them, one should tie together the tickets for four or five meals and give them as a single unit.

If, after passing that village, there is another village where there is only one *salākabhatta*, and they give it out early in the morning, then having assigned it to one of these monks by means of a formal restriction (*niggaha*), he should be told: "Take that early in the morning and afterwards receive the other meals in the original village.
If, however, before the *salākabhattas* have been received in the original village...

One proceeds with the perception that [the village] has been selected. Having selected the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) in the neighboring village, one should return to the monastery, select the other [tickets], and then go to the original village.
For it is said in the *Kurundi*: "It is not permitted to select the Saṅgha’s share outside the boundary. This is the method.

If, however, there are many bhikkhus, and voting sticks (*salākā*) do not suffice for each individual, they should be distributed by way of streets, or by way of a single house within a street, or by way of families.

And in those streets and so forth where there are many meals, they should be distributed to the many bhikkhus according to the same method prescribed for the village. If voting sticks are unavailable, they may also be distributed by making a formal assignment (*uddisitvā*).
Furthermore, the distributor of voting tickets must know the proper procedure. Having risen early, he should take his bowl and robe,
go to the dining hall, sweep the unswept areas, set out drinking water and water for washing, and—
observing that it is now time for the monks to perform their duties— he should strike the bell.
When the bhikkhus have assembled, the *salākabhatta* (ticket-meal) should first be distributed in the village of Vāra.
One should say: "The ticket reaches you in such-and-such a village named Vāra; go there.
If the village is more than a *gāvuta* away, they will become exhausted traveling that day; therefore, [one should say]: "Tomorrow, in the village of Vāra, for you..."

“...he attains it,” [thinking thus,] it should be distributed this very day. If one who has been sent to Vāragāma does not go and seeks another voting ticket (*salāka*), it should not be given to him.
For if it were given, there would be a loss of merit for faithful people and a cutting off of gains for the Saṅgha;
therefore, on the second or even the third day, no other voting ticket should be given to him, [saying: “Your own place...”
He should be told, “Go and eat. However, if he does not come for three days, a voting ticket (*salāka*) should be issued in the village on this side of the boundary village.
If he does not accept it, from that point onward it is not permitted to give him another voting ticket;
rather, a strict disciplinary measure (*daṇḍakamma*) must be imposed, and he must not be exempted from [the distribution of] sixty or fifty [meals]. In the boundary village...
Having drawn lots, the duty of looking after the monastery (vihāravāra) must be assigned; one should say, "The turn for looking after the monastery falls to you.
To the one in charge of the monastery, two or three ladlefuls of rice gruel and three or four portions of cooked rice should be given, but these should not be given as a fixed, permanent allowance.
For the providers of rice gruel and cooked rice might think, "Only the guardians of the monastery are eating our rice gruel and cooked rice."
They might undergo a change [of mind]; therefore, they should be given to other families.
If those who are in charge of the monastery bring [the food] and give it after it has been prepared, that is good;

if not, one should assign a turn and have their rice-gruel and meal brought. Until then, the distribution of voting tickets for them is merely a preliminary task, according to the seniority of the rains.
Furthermore, those at the designated place are indeed permitted to take another ticket for superior food as well.
For the extra *uttaribhaṅga* meal and the meal for a solitary wanderer, tickets should be given after setting them up separately.
If one who has received a ticket does not receive that meal on that day, it should be drawn again the following day.
He receives only the rice, not the subsequent curry; in this case, he must be invited again. The same rule applies even for a ticket for milk-rice.
However, if he receives only the milk and not the rice, he must not be invited again starting from the time he received the milk.
When two or three meals intended for a single traveler fall to one person during a time of famine, [they are assigned] by the junior member of the Saṅgha.
When it has been obtained, it should be untied and distributed separately; even for one who did not receive the regular ticket for rice, it should be distributed again on the following day.

If the monastery is small and all the bhikkhus share in common, when distributing sugarcane tickets, it is permissible to give them to anyone present and then have them cut during the day to be given to the senior elders and others. As for the ticket for sauce:
Having brought it, after the meal, one should strain it or have molasses prepared and give it even to those who live on alms-food and others.

When newcomers arrive, their status as guests—whether already arrived or yet to come—should be recognized and they should be assigned [a place]. In a large monastery, they should be assigned by establishing a fixed residency.
Even oil-cakes should be brought to a common area, cooked, or smoked, and then given to the elders.
It is permissible. One should proceed exactly according to the method described for the *mahā-āvāsa*.

Even for the tickets for fruit, cakes, medicinal requisites, and scents and garlands, they should be distributed separately by means of individual tickets. Although tickets for medicinal requisites and the like are permitted even for those who are alms-collectors (*piṇḍapātika*), they must not be accepted when obtained by way of such tickets.
They give a ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*) in the measure of a single portion at the head of the line.
Having asked about the seating order (*ṭhitika*), it should be distributed. If there is no seating order, it should be distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder (*therāsana*).
If there are many such meals, two or three should be given to each monk;
if not, having given one to each, when the round has been completed, it should be given again starting from the seat of the senior elder. If, in the meantime...
It is interrupted; therefore, the duration [of its occurrence] must be observed. However, if such food is provided regularly, whoever receives it should be told:

"Whether you receive it today or not, you should take it tomorrow as well. But if one meal is irregular—where on the days it is received one gets as much as desired, yet the days when it is not received are more numerous—then that...
If someone does not receive [their share], they should be told, "You may take it tomorrow.
If someone arrives after the voting sticks (*salākā*) have been distributed, the sticks should not be presented again for them once they have already passed.
Regarding the voting stick: starting from the moment the bell is struck, one receives it as soon as one comes forward and extends one's hand. It is not for anyone else.
Even for one who has arrived and is standing nearby, [the turn] passes by as it passes.

However, if there is another person taking [the ballots] on his behalf, he receives them even if he has not come himself. In a common assembly hall, if it is known that "so-and-so has not arrived," it is permissible to set aside [a ballot] thinking, "This is his ballot.
If they make an agreement that "it must not be given to one who has not arrived," that is contrary to the Dhamma.
For it is when one stands at the edge of the distribution area that the goods to be distributed reach him.
However, if they raise a great clamor, saying, "Give it to those who have not yet arrived," a disciplinary measure must be imposed, and they should be told, "Come and take it.
If five or six voting sticks (salākā) are lost, or if the meal-assigner (bhattuddesaka) does not remember the names of the donors, and if he [the assigner] has lost the voting sticks...
If one has had [the food] assigned to a Mahāthera or to oneself and should say to the bhikkhus, "I have had *salākabhatta* assigned for me in such-and-such a village;
you should eat the *salākabhatta* obtained there," it is permissible.
However, if it was not assigned to the monastery, having received that food in the dining hall (*āsanasālā*) and having had it assigned right there, it is not permissible to eat it.
When it is said, “Starting from today, please accept my *salākabhatta* (ticket-food),” it is not permissible to distribute it there in the dining hall;
rather, it must be brought to the monastery and distributed. However, when it is said, “Starting from tomorrow,” one should inform the distributor of meals:
“Starting from tomorrow, a certain family named so-and-so will provide *salākabhatta*; at the time of taking the tickets...”

“You should go. When, during a famine, they have discontinued the distribution of tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*) and, once a time of plenty has arisen, see something [to offer] and reinstate it by saying, “From today onwards, accept our ticket-meals,” it should be distributed not within the village but having brought it to the monastery.
For this is what is called “ticket-meal” (*salākabhatta*); it is not like the meal given by assignment (*uddesabhatta*), but [is to be taken] only to the monastery.

Since it is given with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), it is not permissible to take it outside the precincts (*upacāra*). However, when it is said, "Starting from tomorrow," it must indeed be taken into the monastery.
A monk who is about to depart and intends to go toward a certain direction finds that the voting-ticket (*salākā*) for the prohibition of entry has already been issued for that region.
Having taken that [ticket] and said to another bhikkhu, "Please take my bowl-ticket," it is permissible for him to go.
However, he must have his ticket taken by that person while still within the boundary of the precinct (upacāra-sīma).
People establish "ticket-food" (salākabhatta) in abandoned monasteries so that those who maintain the Bodhi tree, the cetiya, and other structures may eat.
It is permissible for monks who have stayed in their own respective places to go there early in the morning, perform the duties (*vatta*) there, and eat that meal. If,
after those [monks] have gone having secured it for themselves as a meal for the following day, a visiting monk stays in an abandoned monastery,
performs the duties early in the morning, strikes the bell, secures the ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*) for himself, and [goes to] the dining hall...

He who goes [to receive the meal] is the master of that meal. However, if one goes while the monks are still performing their duties, having merely given two or three strokes with the broom on the floor and struck the bell, thinking, "The *salākabhatta* from the village ahead has reached me," it does not reach him because he has taken it by theft;
but if he performs the duties and causes it to reach him, then it is his.
It belongs only to those monks who arrive later.
If there is a village that is too far away such that the monks do not wish to go regularly,
and the people say, "We will be excluded from merit," then those monks who are of like standing in a monastery near that village should be told:
"Tomorrow you should eat with these monks. However, the voting sticks (salākā) must be distributed every day;
yet they are not properly distributed merely by the striking of a bell or the mere shaking of the basket.
Rather, having taken the basket, the voting sticks should be poured onto a stool, but the basket itself must not be held by its rim.

For if there were a snake or a scorpion there, it would cause pain; therefore, having taken [the bowl] from below and turned the basket away from one's face, the slips should be scattered with the thought, "Even if there is a snake, it will flee from this very place.
Having thus scattered the slips, they should be drawn by means of the village and so forth, according to the method previously described. Furthermore, one [slip] should be for the Great Elder.
Having brought it forward and saying, "The remainder falls to me," he brings it to himself, performs his duties, and pays homage at the cetiya.
When the monks standing in the thought-hall (vitakkamāḷaka) say, "Friends, the voting sticks have been brought forward," he should reply, "Yes, venerable sirs;
you may take the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) in whichever village you go. For in this way, even though they have been brought forward, they are indeed properly brought forward.

When monks go to another monastery for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma throughout the night, they may go without taking voting sticks (*salāka*), thinking, "We shall not take alms there, but will return after wandering for alms in our own alms-resort village";
it is permissible for them to come back to the monastery to eat the bowl-voting-stick meal (*pattasalākabhatta*) intended for the Elder. Now, as for the Great Elder himself...
Thinking, "What shall I do here?", he goes along with them.

When they have arrived at the village for alms-food, having not yet eaten in the monastery where they went, and say, "Venerable sirs, give us your bowls; we shall bring you rice-gruel and other provisions," the bowls must not be given.
If they ask, "Why, venerable sir, do you not give them? one should reply: "The meal intended for those staying in the monastery is for those who reside in the monastery."
[If they say,] "We have stayed in another monastery," [the donor says: "Give it, venerable sirs;
we do not give it to the *pālikā* (the distributor) of the monastery, we give it to you. Accept our alms-food. In this case, it is permissible.
The discussion on *salākabhatta* (tickets for food) is finished.
The Discussion on Fortnightly Meals and the Like:
Regarding the fortnightly meals and so forth, that which is given on specially marked days— namely the fourteenth, the fifteenth, the fifth, and the eighth of the lunar half-month—
to those intent on spiritual practice for the purpose of maintaining mindfulness, is called *pakkhika* (fortnightly).
That follows the same procedure as for *salāka*-tickets; once distributed, it should be consumed.
If there is a large quantity of both *salāka*-ticket food and fortnightly (*pakkhika*) food, and it is to be passed around to everyone, then both types of food should be distributed separately.
If the community of monks is large, one should first distribute the fortnightly food and then distribute the *salāka*-ticket food according to that same order. Regarding the *salāka*-ticket food...
Or, having had [the food] brought in, it should be distributed as a fortnightly meal according to his standing. Those to whom it does not reach should go for alms.

If there are two meals and many [of them], and the monks are weak, and a daily meal known as *salākabhatta* is available, then setting that aside, one should distribute only the fortnightly meal, saying, "Friends, eat the fortnightly meal."
If they give a choice meal for the fortnight, a separate standing place must be assigned. One should not assign the fortnightly meal today [thinking], "It is tomorrow's fortnight.
However, it is permissible if the donors say, "Tomorrow there will be coarse food in our house;
please designate the fortnightly meal for today."
“Uposathika” means that on the half-monthly Uposatha day, having undertaken the Uposatha precepts, whatever one eats oneself is given [to the monks].
“Pāṭipadika” means: “On the Uposatha day many faithful devotees pay honor to the monks;
however, on the first day of the fortnight (pāṭipada), the monks suffer from hunger. What is given on the first day of the fortnight is like a gift during a famine—it is of great fruit.”

Having observed that "a gift given on the second day [of the waxing moon] by those whose virtue is purified through the Uposatha ceremony is of great fruit," one gives the alms-food to be given on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*);
both of these are likewise included under the category of *salākabhatta*.
Thus, these seven types of meals are not permitted for those who practice the alms-round (*piṇḍapātika*); they indeed constitute a breach of the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*).

Furthermore, in the Cīvarakkhandhaka, after Visākhā requested boons, four types of meals were granted—namely, *āgantukabhatta*, *gamikabhatta*, *gilānabhatta*, and *gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta*—all of which are indeed found in the Pāḷi.
Among these, the meal given to newcomers is called "the meal for newcomers" (*āgantukabhatta*). The same method applies to the others. However, if there are also meals for newcomers here...
If there are many guests, one portion must be assigned to each of them; if the meals are insufficient, they should be assigned from the standing supply.
If a single guest arrives first and, having taken all the guest-food for himself, sits down, it belongs to him alone;
those guests who arrive later must consume what has been given by him.
One should take one portion for oneself and give the rest away; this is the superior method.
However, if someone who arrives first does not take their own portion but remains silent, they should take theirs in order along with those who arrive later.
If guests arrive regularly, [the portions should be assigned] on the very day they arrive.
It should be eaten; if others arrive in the interval, it may be eaten for two or three days.
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "It is permissible to eat it for seven days.
Even a resident monk who has gone elsewhere and returned should partake of the guest-food (*āgantuka-bhatta*). But if...
It should be tied up in the monastery and distributed within the monastery. If the monastery is far away, it should be tied up in the assembly hall and distributed in the assembly hall.
However, if the donors say, "In the absence of guests, let the residents also enjoy [it]," then it is permissible.
The same procedure applies to the *gamiyabhatta* (food for those departing). However, this is the distinction:

a guest receives only the guest-food (*āgantukabhatta*), whereas one who is departing receives both the guest-food and the departing-food. Furthermore, even a resident monk who intends to depart is considered one departing and thus receives the departing-food.
Just as with the guest-food, so too with this [departing-food], there are two or three [meals].

It is not permitted for seven days. If one has eaten with the intention, “I will go,” but does not go that day for some reason, it is permissible to eat again on the following day, because of the underlying intention (*saussāhatā*).

For one who has eaten with the intention, “I will go,” even if robbers block the road, or there is water, or it rains, or the caravan does not depart, [it remains permissible] because of the underlying intention.
It may be eaten. Regarding these calamities, it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī* that "it is permissible to eat for two or three days" while observing them.
However, one does not receive permission to eat by making the pretext, "I am going.
As for sick-food, if it suffices for all who are ill, it should be given to all; if not, it should be distributed according to the number of those present.

Having prepared it, it should be given. One who is ill but appears healthy and is able to go into the village, while the other is unable—this latter one is called "one who is seriously ill" (*mahāgilāna*). His sick-meal should be given. There are two types of those who are seriously ill:
one who is successful and well-known, receiving much solid and soft food; and one who is destitute, receiving little because of his lack of gains, and thus [must go] into the village.
"He enters"—to him sick food should be given. Regarding sick food, however, there is no limit of days.
As long as the illness has not subsided, and as long as he cannot survive without consuming suitable food, so long may it be eaten.
But when, even after eating mixed rice-gruel or mixed rice, his illness does not flare up, from that point on it should not be eaten.
Regarding the meal for those attending to the sick: if it is sufficient for all, it should be given to all;

if it is not sufficient, it should be distributed by establishing a fixed portion. Furthermore, this [portion] should be assigned to the primary attendant among two attendants when there is one major illness, and to the attendant of the neglected patient among two major illnesses. As for a family that provides both meals for the sick and meals for those attending to the sick...
In that regard, when food reaches a certain sick person, it must be distributed right there to his attendant as well. There is no daily limit even regarding the food for the sick person's attendant;
as long as the sick person receives it, the attendant receives it too.
If these four types of food are given in this manner—thinking, "The newcomers, those departing, the sick, and the attendants of the sick shall receive my alms"—then [it is properly allotted].

"Let them take [it]," it is permissible even for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika). However, if one has the meal assigned specifically for guests and others, thinking, "Let them take my meal," and it is given in this manner, it is not permissible for alms-collectors.
There are also three other types of meals: the "regular meal" (dhurabhatta), the "hut meal" (kuṭibhatta), and the "turn-based meal" (vārabhatta). Among these, the "regular meal" means...
"Regular meal" (niccabhatta) is said; it is of two kinds: that belonging to the Saṅgha and that belonging to an individual.
Therein, that which has been fixed by saying, "We give a regular meal to the Saṅgha," falls under the category of tickets for meals (salākabhatta).

However, what is given after saying, "Let them take my regular alms," is permissible even for those who live on alms-food (piṇḍapātika). Regarding the individual [meal] as well, "Your regular meal..."
Even if it is said, "I give," it is not permissible for one who is a *piṇḍapātika* (alms-food eater). However, if it is said, "Please accept my regular alms," it is permissible and may be accepted.
Even if, after some days have passed, he later says, "Please accept your regular meal (*dhurabhatta*)," it is permissible because it was properly accepted at the outset.
“Household-food” (*kuṭibhatta*) refers to that which, having had a residence built for the Saṅgha, one has stipulated by saying, “Let those who dwell in our lodgings take food from us alone.
This is of the same category as ticket-food (*salākabhatta*) and may be accepted and eaten.
However, when it is said, “Let those who dwell in our lodgings take almsfood from us alone,” [it is not so].

It is also permissible for those who live on alms-food (piṇḍapātika). However, whatever has been given out of faith in a particular person—either by building a residence for him or by saying, "We give this to you"—belongs to that person alone; when he has gone elsewhere, it should be consumed by his dependents.
What is called "turn-taking food" (vārabhatta) refers to a time of famine when people say, "We shall look after the monks by turns," starting from the primary household.
If it is given, even that which is given under the designation of "alms-food" is permissible for those who subsist on alms.

However, when it is called "food by turn," it falls under the same category as "ticket-food. If they send rice and other provisions, saying, "Let the novices cook and give it," it is permissible for those who subsist on alms.
Thus, these three and the four beginning with "guest-food" make seven.
These, together with the *saṅghabhatta* (food for the Saṅgha) and so forth, constitute fourteen types of meals.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, four other types of meals are also mentioned: *vihārabhatta*, *aṭṭhakabhatta*, *catukkabhatta*, and *guḷhakabhatta*.
Therein, *vihārabhatta* refers to food produced specifically for that monastery.

That was taken as a meal for the Saṅgha. However, because it was received in such a way that even alms-collecting monks (piṇḍapātika) were able to consume it—as was the case at places such as the Tissamahāvihāra and Cittalapabbata—it is permissible for alms-collecting monks to partake of it in such locations.
[They may say: "We give to eight monks; we give to four."

Likewise, when food is given as an "eight-meal" (*aṭṭhakabhatta*) or a "four-meal" (*catukkabhatta*), that too—being given under the designation of "alms-food" (*bhikkhā*)—is permissible for those who live on alms.
When a bowl is filled and covered with an excessive amount of well-prepared rice and cakes, it is called "lump-food" (*guḷhakabhatta*).
These three belong to the same category as "ticket-food" (*salākabhatta*).
There is also another kind called *guḷakabhatta* (ball-rice).

In this case, some people, having arranged for a great hearing of the Dhamma and a festival in honor of the monastery, think, "We are not able to give to the entire Saṅgha," and thus they give balls [of rice] for the purpose of determining the number of monks, saying, "Let two or three hundred monks take our alms-food. This is permissible even for those who subsist on alms-food (*piṇḍapātika*).

Thus, in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*, the distribution of robes has been explained; however, in this *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, both the distribution of lodgings and the distribution of almsfood have been stated.
The distribution of medicinal requisites for the sick should be understood as follows: regarding medicinal substances such as ghee, [there are] kings, royal ministers, and high officials...
Regarding ghee, they may send even a hundred or a thousand jars to the monastery;
having struck the bell, one should fill and give out the vessels starting from the seat of the senior elder (therāsana). This is also permissible for those who live on alms-food (piṇḍapātika).
If the lazy great elders arrive later, one should say: "Venerable sirs, it is being given to those of twenty years' standing; your turn has passed."
It should not be said that it must be given only after setting aside a portion; rather, having given to them [who have arrived], it should later be given from the set-aside portion.
Having heard that much ghee has been obtained in such-and-such a monastery, even monks from a monastery a *yojana* away will come;

it should be given starting from the place where they arrive, one by one as they reach it. Even for those who have not yet reached it, [it should be given] within the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*).
When those who have entered [the boundary] are receiving [alms] from among the pupils and others, it must indeed be given.
If they say, "Give to those standing outside the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*)," it should not be given.

However, if they have entered the precinct boundary and become connected as one unit—whether at the door of their own monastery or within the monastery itself—the boundary is said to have been expanded by way of the assembly; therefore, it must be given.

Even if the gift is given to the newest member of the Saṅgha, it must still be given to those who arrive later.
