However, if the second portion has already been assigned to the senior monk’s seat, the first portion does not reach those who arrive later; from the second portion, it should be distributed according to the number of years of seniority (*vassaggena*).
Whatever is given anywhere after entering the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*) must be divided at the place where the entire assembly is gathered.
In whatever monastery ten bhikkhus reside and ten jars of ghee are given, it should be divided according to each individual jar.
There is one jar of ghee; it should be taken by dividing it among the ten bhikkhus.
If they take it while it remains exactly where it was, thinking, "It falls to our share," it is wrongly taken; wherever it has been moved, it belongs to the Saṅgha. But as for the jar...
Having reflected on this and placed a small amount of ghee in a dish, one should say, "This portion falls to the Great Elder;
the remainder falls to us," and having poured that back into the pot, it is permissible to take as much as desired and depart.
If the ghee is thick, one should make a line and say, "The portion beyond the line falls to the Great Elder; the remainder..."

Even if it is taken [thinking], "It is for us," it is well-taken; and even if there are fewer or more monks than the stated limit, or fewer or more pots of ghee, it should be distributed by this same method.
However, if there is only one monk and only one pot, he should strike the gong and say, "This falls to my share."
It is permissible to take [the portion]. It is also permissible to have even small amounts distributed by saying, "This first portion falls to me;

this is the second portion. This same method applies to butter and so forth as well. However, in the case of clear sesame oil and such liquids where no lines can be established, one should remove it and then distribute it.
This also applies to medicinal items such as ginger and black pepper, as well as the remaining requisites of the monks, such as bowls and cooking pots.
Having thoroughly examined everything according to the method already stated, it should be distributed.
Thus, the wise one, having consulted both the Canon and the Commentary,
should distribute the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha with diligence.
Thus ends the discussion on the distribution of requisites in all its aspects.

When people arrive at the place where requisites are being distributed by those appointed and established as distributors of rice-gruel and so forth, half of the portion must be given to them even without asking for permission;
however, if they are not so appointed, it should be given only after obtaining their consent. By one who has been appointed as a distributor of minor items, [the remainder] should be given...
When a monk is making robe-cloth and says, "Give me a needle," two needles should be given—one long and one short.
There is no need to ask whether it is "unapportioned property belonging to the Saṅgha.
For one who needs a thimble, one thimble; for one wishing to set out upon a journey through a wilderness, a pair of sandals; for one who needs a waistband—
A waistband; for one who has arrived [saying], "My shoulder-strap is worn out," a shoulder-strap should be given.
To one in need of a water-strainer, a water-strainer should be given. To one in need of a water-vessel, a water-vessel should be given.

If there is no cloth, the water-vessel should be given together with a piece of cloth. To one who requests, "I wish to apply the visitor's patch," both a strip of cloth and a half-strip of cloth [should be given].
And a sufficient amount must be given. To one who has come [saying], "The mandala is not enough," one mandala must be given;
two half-mandalas must be given. It should not be given to one who asks for two mandalas.

To one who needs a border for a robe that will fit along with the wind, a sufficient amount for one robe must be given. To a sick person who needs ghee, butter, or the like, one medicinal substance [must be given].
Having made it the measure of a *nāḷi*, the third portion from that should be given.

Having given it in this manner for three days, once the *nāḷi* is full, from the fourth day onward it should be given after asking the Saṅgha. Regarding the lumps of sugar as well, one-third should be given on one day.
When the lumps have been finished in this way over three days, thereafter they should be given after asking the Saṅgha.
The rest is clear in every respect.
The discussion on the fortnightly meal and so forth is concluded.
The commentary on the Khandhaka on Lodgings is finished.
7. The Chapter on Schism in the Sangha (Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka):
The Discourse on the Going-forth of the Śākyas.
330. In the Chapter on Schism in the Sangha, "well-known" means famous; "the Śākyan princes" refers to those [named] Śākyas.
The ten messengers, beginning with Kāḷudāyi, together with their retinues and many other people [were present].

"Among us" (*amhākaṃ*) means "among ourselves"; or it is said to mean "of our family. "I shall instruct you in the matter of household life" means I shall make known what is to be done regarding domestic life.
"Water must be led away" means it must be done in such a way that the water remains level in all places.
"Should be cleared away" means the grass should be pulled out. "The chaff should be removed" means the grain mixed with fine straw should be winnowed of its husks.

"Should be winnowed" means the fine straw should be removed. "You yourself should understand the meaning of household life" means you yourself should know the purpose of living as a householder. "As for me, go forth at your pleasure because of you"—here [is the sense].

The meaning should be understood as follows: having suddenly desired to say, "I shall go forth together with you," out of affection for his companion, yet his heart being dragged back by greed for the glory of kingship, he was unable to say anything more than "I [shall go forth] with you.
(331) *Nippātitā* means "gone out" (*nikkhamitā*). *Mānassino* means "relying on pride"; it is said to mean "dependent on pride."
332. "In whom there are no angers from within": because they have been uprooted by the third path, there are no angers in his mind.
Furthermore, since "existence" (*bhava*) means success and "non-existence" (*vibhava*) means failure; likewise, "existence" means increase and "non-existence" means decrease;
"existence" means eternalism and "non-existence" means annihilationism; "existence" means merit and "non-existence" means demerit; and "non-existence" means... [the text continues].

"Non-existence" (*abhava*) and "existence" (*bhava*) are in meaning one and the same. Therefore, regarding the phrase "one who has transcended both existence and non-existence" (*itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto*):

here, that which is called "existence and non-existence" in its many modes—such as success and failure, increase and decrease, permanence and annihilation, or merit and demerit—is transcended by means of the four paths, according to their respective possibilities and in their various ways. Thus the meaning should be understood. "They do not experience" (*nānubhavanti*) means... [text fragment ends]
They attain [this state]; the intention is that even for the gods, seeing him is difficult to obtain.
333. *Ahimekhalikā* means having bound a snake around her waist. *Ucchaṅge* means on her lap. 334.
*Sammannati* means she honors him. *Yaṃ tumo karissati* means "whatever he will do."
The Discourse on the Renunciation of the Sickly is concluded.
336. Regarding the phrase “of one who swallows spittle”:

here, requisites obtained through wrong livelihood are like spittle, for they must be spat out by the Noble Ones. Because he swallows such requisites, he was called “one who swallows spittle” by the Blessed One.
340. “With a rigid body” means with a motionless body, like a figure made of cloth. 342.

“Indeed, sir, we are known as ‘the King’s kinsmen’” means he spoke thus, exalting himself by way of his status as a royal kinsman, thinking, “The king knows us. “With ears and tail held steady” means having them rendered motionless by binding them.

“For it is painful, O elephant, to approach the Naga” means: O elephant, approaching the Buddha-Naga with a murderous intent—that is, drawing near—is indeed painful. “Of one slain by the Naga” means of one who has killed the Buddha-Naga.
"Drawing back as if recoiling" means that he drew back with his hind feet while facing the Tathāgata. "Unlucky" (*alakkhika*):
here, "he does not perceive" (*na lakkheti*) is *alakkhika*; the meaning is that he does not know, "I am performing an evil deed.
Or, "unworthy of being perceived" (*na lakkhitabbo*) is *alakkhika*; the meaning is that he is not fit to be seen.
343. "Eating in a group" (*tikabhojana*) here refers to food that should be eaten by three people. "I shall prescribe it" means "I shall authorize it.

Regarding "eating in a group," however, one should deal with it according to the rule. The discussion on requesting the five requisites has been stated in the commentary on the *saṅghādisesa* offenses.
"For an eon" (*kappa*) means for the duration of a lifespan. "Brahma merit" means the most excellent merit. "For an eon in heaven" likewise means for the duration of a lifespan.
The Discussion on the Act of Proclamation and so forth is concluded.
344. The Discussion on the Schism of the Saṅgha:

"Then Devadatta, having split the Saṅgha... It is said that he, having thus distributed the voting tickets (*salāka*), went away after performing the Uposatha separately right there; therefore, this was said.
345. "My back is aching" means that it is oppressed by pain due to sitting for a long time. "I will stretch it" means I will extend it.

What is called the "miracle of instruction" (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*) is the teaching of the Dhamma in accordance with another's mind, having known their mind thus: "Such is your thought; even so is your thought."
346. *Mamānukubbanti*: acting in imitation of me. *Kapaṇo*: one who is suffering. *Mahāvarāhassa*: of the great elephant (the Great Nāga). *Mahiṃ vikubbatoti*:
treading upon the earth, tearing up the ground. *Bhisaṃ ghasamānassāti*: while eating lotus roots. *Nadīsu jaggatoti*:
regarding this, it is said that at evening time, that elephant-nāga [would frequent] that lotus pond named "The River."
Having entered [the water], he spent the entire night exhausted; he acts as a fisherman. Therefore it is said:

“while watching over the rivers. (347) *Sutā* means those who hear. *Asandiddho ca akkhātīti* means he explains without doubt, having joined [the words] together by way of their connection (*anusandhi*).

(350) *Āpāyiko* means one who will be reborn in a state of misery (*apāya*). Likewise, *nerayiko* means one bound for hell. *Kappaṭṭho* means one who will remain for an eon (*kappa*). Now, because even a thousand Buddhas would not be able to cure him, he is called *atekiccho*.
“May no one ever in the world”—that is, may no being whatsoever at any time in the world. “Was reborn” (*udapajjatha*) means “you were reborn.

“He stands shining with glory like a flame”—he stands as if blazing with fame. “I have heard that he was Devadatta”—there is also what was heard by the Blessed One, namely, “Devadatta was such as this”;
taking that very [report] as the basis, this was said. “He fell into negligence”—here, *pamādaṃ*.

*Anucināti* means "has practiced"; the meaning is that negligence has not been abandoned. *Āsajja hanti* means having approached with an evil mind, or alternatively, having dried up [the roots of merit].
*Avīcinirayaṃ patto*—this, however, is a past tense form used in the sense of a wish (*āsīsā*). *Bhesma* means terrifying.
The Discussion on the Schism of the Saṅgha is finished.
The Discussion on Upāli’s Questions 351.
“On one side, Upāli, there is one” means one on the side of those who speak according to the Dhamma. “On one side, there are two” means two on the side of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma.
“A fourth proclaims” means that, being the fourth on the side of those who speak contrary to the Dhamma with the intention, “I shall split the Saṅgha,” he proclaims while seeking to win them over.
He proclaims: "The fear of hell is not yours alone; it is ours as well. The path to Avīci is not closed to us.
We are not unwholesome ones who do not fear [the consequences]. For if this were indeed non-Dhamma, non-Vinaya, or the teaching of one who is not a Teacher, we would not accept it.
In such a manner, he proclaims eighteen [points], such as "non-Dhamma is Dhamma."

The meaning is that he makes known the grounds for schism. "He distributes voting tickets" means that after having made such an announcement, he distributes the voting tickets while saying, "Take this; approve this.

The same method applies to cases such as "Upāli, there are two on one side," and so forth. "In this way, Upāli, there is both a dissension in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha"—it is in this way that it occurs; however, the Saṅgha is not actually split by this much alone.
“Upāli, a bhikkhu who is of natural status, belonging to the same community, and standing within the same boundary, causes a schism in the Saṅgha.

Regarding this, one might ask: “In what sense was Devadatta ‘of natural status’? First of all, how could he not be of natural status, given that he caused the king to be killed and committed the shedding of blood?
To this we reply: first, as for the killing of the king, it was because the command [to kill] was not actually carried out.

[It is] not so. "In that case, prince, kill your father and become king; I shall kill the Blessed One and become a Buddha"—such was his command. However, the prince became king first and only later killed his father;
thus, because he failed to carry out the command as given, there was no killing of the king [at that time]. But regarding the shedding of blood, it occurred at that very moment.

The Blessed One did not state that one who causes the shedding of blood is incapable [of spiritual attainment]; nor is it possible to attribute such incapacity to him apart from the word of the Blessed One:
"Monks, one who causes the shedding of blood, if unordained, is not to be ordained; if already ordained, he is to be expelled."
However, this was stated by the Blessed One after the schism in the Saṅgha; therefore, the Saṅgha was split by him while he was still a regular member (pakatatta).
Regarding the eighteen grounds for schism, such as "proclaiming what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma," according to the method of the Suttanta:
first, the ten courses of wholesome action are Dhamma, and the ten courses of unwholesome action are non-Dhamma. Likewise, the four...

The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment— namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path— are called "Dhamma.
[Furthermore,] the three foundations of mindfulness, the three right efforts, the three bases of psychic power, the six faculties, and the six powers...
The eight factors of enlightenment, the ninefold path, the four kinds of clinging, the five hindrances, the seven underlying tendencies, and the eight wrongnesses—this is non-Dhamma (*adhamma*).
In this regard, having taken up any single portion of what is non-Dhamma, one might think: "We shall turn this non-Dhamma into Dhamma."
Thus, by relying on our own teacher’s lineage, [they think], "This will lead to liberation, and we shall become famous in the world.

Speaking of that which is non-Dhamma as "this is Dhamma," they are said to illuminate non-Dhamma as Dhamma. Likewise, by taking one portion from among the categories of Dhamma and saying, "This is non-Dhamma," they are said to illuminate Dhamma as non-Dhamma. According to the method of the Vinaya...
But a legal procedure that is to be carried out after having accused [the person] with a factual basis and having reminded them of it, according to their admission, is called *dhamma*.
A legal procedure that is to be carried out without accusing [the person] with a factual basis, without reminding them of it, and without their admission, is called *adhamma*.
According to the method of the Suttanta, the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, the removal of delusion, restraint, abandonment, and reflective discernment [are *dhamma*].
This is called "discipline" (*vinaya*): the non-disciplining, the lack of restraint, the non-abandoning, and the lack of reflection regarding lust and so forth—this is called "non-discipline.

By way of the method of discipline: the perfection of the subject matter, the perfection of the motion, the perfection of the proclamation, the perfection of the boundary, and the perfection of the assembly—this is called "discipline";
the failure of the subject matter... [and so on] ...the failure of the assembly—this is called "non-discipline."
According to the method of the Suttantas, that which was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata is: "The four foundations of mindfulness... the eightfold path.

That which was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata is: "Three foundations of mindfulness, three right endeavors, three bases of power, six faculties, six powers, eight factors of enlightenment, the ninefold path."
According to the method of the Vinaya, "four *pārājikas*, thirteen *saṅghādisesas*, two *aniyatās*, and thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiyas*"—
this was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata; "three *pārājikas*, fourteen *saṅghādisesas*, three *aniyatās*,
and thirty-one *nissaggiya-pācittiyas*"— this was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata.

According to the method of the Suttantas, it is customary for him to enter the attainment of fruition daily, to enter the attainment of great compassion, to survey the world with the Buddha-eye, to teach the Suttantas by way of specific occasions, and to relate Jātaka stories;
whereas it is not customary for him not to enter the attainment of fruition daily... [and so on] ...or not to relate Jātaka stories.
According to the method of the Vinaya, for one who has been invited, it is customary (*āciṇṇa*) to depart on a journey after spending the rainy-season residence and obtaining permission,
to depart on a journey after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and to exchange greetings first with those who have arrived as guests;
the non-performance of that very custom is called "not customary" (*anāciṇṇa*).
According to the method of the Suttanta, "the four foundations of mindfulness... up to ... the eightfold path"—this is called "prescribed";
"three foundations of mindfulness... up to ... a ninefold path"—this is called "not prescribed. According to the method of the Vinaya, "the four *pārājika* offenses... up to ...
the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* offenses"—this is called "prescribed"; "three *pārājika* offenses... up to ... [is called "not prescribed"].
“The thirty-one offenses entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya)” refers to what is called “not yet promulgated.

“There is no offense for one who does not know, for one whose mind is not intent on theft, for one not intending death, for one not intending to cause [the robe] to be mentioned, and for one not intending to cause it to be released”—the non-offense stated in each respective instance is what is called “no offense. “For one who knows... [and so forth].

An offense described by way of such passages as “of one with a thieving mind,” and so forth, is called an *āpatti* (offense). The five classes of offenses (*pañcāpattikkhandhā*) are called light offenses (*lahukāpatti*);
two classes of offenses are called heavy offenses (*garukāpatti*). Six classes of offenses are called offenses with remainder (*sāvasesāpatti*);
one class of offenses, the *pārājika*, is called an offense without remainder (*anavasesāpatti*). Two classes of offenses are grave offenses (*duṭṭhullāpatti*).
The five classes of offenses are called "non-gross offenses.
Furthermore, in this context, those who describe the kind of teaching mentioned above according to the previous method as "this is non-Dhamma" are said to "proclaim Dhamma as non-Dhamma.
[They proclaim] what is not Vinaya as "this is Vinaya," and so forth... [and they proclaim] a non-gross offense as "a gross offense."
Saying "this is so," they are said to proclaim "a non-gross offense as a gross offense.
Having thus proclaimed "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma" … [and so on] … or "a non-gross offense as a gross offense," and having gained a faction,
the Saṅgha is split by those who perform one of the four types of Saṅgha legal acts separately within a single boundary.
He is called "divided. Therefore it was said: "They draw him away by means of these eighteen grounds," and so forth.
Therein, "draw away" (*apakassanti*) means they pull the assembly toward themselves, disentangle [the group], and lead it off to one side.
"Make manifest" (*avapakāsanti*) means they make it excessively clear; they act in such a way that [the group] becomes completely separated. "Apart" (*āveni*) means separately. Up to this point—

"Upāli, the Saṅgha is split" means that when any one of the eighteen grounds for schism has been illustrated, and by whatever means one has persuaded [the monks] saying, "Take this," or "Approve this," and having had them take voting tickets (*salāka*), the Saṅgha is split once separate *saṅghakamma* (formal acts of the community) have been performed. However, in the *Parivāra*, it says: "By five [factors], Upāli..."
It has been stated, “The Saṅgha is split by means of its aspects,” and so forth;
there is no difference in meaning between that and the definition of schism in the Saṅgha given here. We shall demonstrate the absence of any such difference right there [in that context].
The rest is clear in every respect.
The Discussion on Upāli’s Questions is finished.
The Commentary on the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka is finished.
8. The Vattakkhandhaka (Section on Duties).
357. Regarding the Discussion on the Duties for a Guest:
By the phrase “I shall now enter the monastery,” the vicinity of the boundary (upacārasīma) is indicated.
Therefore, upon reaching the boundary, all duties such as removing one’s sandals must be performed. “Having taken” refers to taking [them] with the sandal-stick.
"Having taken [it]. "Going back" means gathering together. "It should be distributed" means it should be spread out.

"The alms-round should be asked about" means the practice of begging for alms should be asked about in this way: "Is the village for alms-round near or far? Should one go for alms early in the morning or during the day?
"Non-alms-round" refers to a village of those with wrong views, or a village where alms are restricted; where—
If alms are given to one or two [monks], that person also should be asked. Regarding the question about drinking water:
one should ask about both the drinking water and the water for use, such as by asking, "Do they drink only the water from this lotus pond, or do they also use it for bathing and other purposes?
In some places there are wild beasts or non-human beings; therefore—
One should ask: "At what time should one enter? At what time should one leave?
Standing outside means standing outside after giving way to a snake or a non-human being as they exit; one should look out from that position.
"If one is able, it should be cleared" means that if one is capable, the entire monastery should be cleared. By one who is unable [to clear it all], his own...

The dwelling place must be swept. However, for one who is able to clean everything, the detailed explanation regarding the duty of cleaning the monastery shown [here] should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahākhandhaka.
The discussion on the duties of a guest is finished.
359. Discussion on the Duties of a Resident Monk (*āvāsika-vatta*):
Regarding the instruction "the seat should be prepared," and so forth—all of this must be done when an elder has arrived, even if one is occupied with robe-making or new construction work.
When sweeping the *cetiya* courtyard, one should set aside the broom...
He should begin to perform his duties. For a wise newcomer will say, "First, sweep the shrine courtyard.
However, when preparing medicine for the sick, if the patient is not seriously ill, one should perform the duty rather than making medicine.
But for one who is gravely ill, medicine must indeed be prepared. For a wise newcomer...
He will say, “First, prepare some medicine. When asking for drinking water, if he drinks all the water brought once, he must simply ask, “I shall bring more.
Furthermore, he may also be fanned; while fanning, one should fan the soles of his feet once, then the middle of his body once, and then his head once. When told, “Enough,” [one should stop].
Then one should fan him more gently. Again, when he says, "Enough," one should fan him even more gently.
When he says it for the third time, the fan should be set aside. His feet should also be washed; having washed them, if one has one's own oil, they should be anointed with that.
If one does not have any, they should be anointed with what belongs to him. As for the wiping of the sandals—
It should be done according to one’s own preference. For that very reason, it is said here: “If one is able.
Therefore, there is no offense even for one who does not wipe the sandals. When asked, “Where does my lodging reach? the lodging must be assigned;
the meaning is that it should be pointed out thus: “This lodging reaches you. Having struck [the floor]...
However, it is indeed permissible to spread [the cloth] out.
Regarding the duties of a junior: "Water should be pointed out" means one should point it out by saying, "Take this water and drink.
The same method applies to the water for washing as well. The rest is exactly as before. Also, in a large monastery, regarding one who has arrived in one's presence...
A guest is not permitted to fail to perform the duties.
The discussion on the duties of resident monks is finished.
The discussion on the duties of departing monks.
360. Regarding "wooden articles" among the duties for one going on a journey: these refer to beds, chairs, and so forth, as described in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
"Earthenware articles" likewise refers to dye-vessels and all other varieties mentioned therein. Having secured all of these in a fire-shed or some other protected place, one may depart.
It is also permissible to leave them in a sheltered mountain cave (*pabbhāra*). [This concerns] lodgings.

"Should be asked for permission": here, regarding a lodging constructed on a stone surface or upon stone pillars where termites do not infest, there is no offense even for one who does not ask for permission.

The passage beginning with "In the case of four stone supports," etc., is stated for the purpose of showing how a lodging such as a leaf-hut should be prepared in a place where termites arise. Perhaps even the structural members...
“They will know” (seseyyuṃ): this is the benefit when [the bedding] is placed in the open air.
However, in a house that leaks, when grass and lumps of clay fall from above, even the parts of the beds and chairs are destroyed.
The discussion on the duties for one going on a journey is finished.
362. Regarding the discourse on the practice of rejoicing (*anumodanavatta*): "It was successful" means it was accomplished.

"By four or five" means that when the senior of the Saṅgha is seated for the purpose of giving the blessing of rejoicing, one should sit in the row below him; when the junior elders are seated, [one should sit] by the great elder.
And three [monks] should sit below; when the fifth has sat down, four should sit above.
Even if the junior monk below is requested by the senior of the Sangha, the four must still sit starting from the senior of the Sangha.
However, if the monk who offers the thanksgiving says, "Go, venerable sirs, there is no need to wait," [then they may depart].
It is permissible to go. If the Mahāthera says, “Let us go, friend,” and [the other] says, “Go,” it is likewise permissible.

Even if one has formed the intention, “We will wait outside the village,” it is still permissible to go once one has gone outside the village and told one’s own dependents, “You must wait for his arrival. However, if people [are waiting] for oneself...

If one person, such as Rucika, causes the expression of appreciation (*anumodanā*) to be made, there is no offense for that one expressing appreciation, nor does it become a burden for the Great Elder (*mahāthera*).

For the characteristic here is this: while people are engaged in conversation during the seated discourse itself, the Great Elder must be requested [to give the blessing], and he, having been invited by the Great Elder to give the appreciation, must wait [for the occasion]. "One who has defecated" means one in whom feces have arisen.
The meaning is "pressed like a cow.
The discussion on the rules for expressing appreciation is finished.
The discussion on the rules for the dining hall begins.

364. Regarding the procedure for receiving alms-food (*bhattagga-vatta*), it is stated in the commentaries: "Whether it be inside a village or in a monastery, when going to a place where people are serving food, it is permissible to put on one’s robe and fasten the waist-band.
"One should not encroach upon the elder monks" means that one should not sit down by excessively crowding around the elder monks. If [the seat of] the Great Elder...
The seat should be of equal height to the one already occupied. When there are many seats, one should sit after setting aside one or two seats.
Having counted the number of monks, one should not sit on the prepared seats until the senior elder (mahāthera) says, "Sit down.
If the senior elder does not say so, one should say, "Venerable sir, this seat is high. [If he says,] "Sit down," [then one may sit].
When this has been said, one should sit down. However, if he does not speak even when thus requested, there is no offense for the one who sits down;

the offense belongs to the senior elder alone. For it is the junior monk who incurs an offense by sitting on such a seat without asking permission, while the senior elder incurs an offense by not granting permission after having been asked.
"Without spreading the outer robe" means that one should not sit down without having spread out the outer robe.

"With both hands" is said with reference to the water for washing the bowl. However, the *dakṣiṇodaka* (water for the right hand) should be taken after placing the bowl on a stand in front [of oneself].
"Well done" means without making a sound with the water. "An opening for the curry" means that the rice should be taken in such a measure that there is room for the curry.
"Make it equal" applies not only to the ghee and so forth, but also to the rice. Regarding the ghee and so forth...
However, when it is said, "But whatever is small, sufficient for one or two, provide that equally for all," people laugh;
therefore, having taken such a portion once or twice, the remainder should not be taken.
Regarding the statement, "The Elder should not eat yet": this refers to a dining hall where the number of monks is limited, wherein...
This was said with reference to when people wish to give after having served [food] to everyone.
However, regarding a great hall for meals where they eat in one place and water is given in another place, there one may eat as one pleases.
The phrase "not yet water" was said with reference to water for washing the hands. But if one becomes thirsty in the meantime...
Having hung meat from one's neck or having drunk water, one must not wash one's hands.
If people say, "Venerable sir, please wash your bowl and your hands," or if monks say, "Please take some water," it is permissible.
By the phrase "when returning," it is shown that when the Saṅgha has risen from the meal hall and is returning, they should return in this manner.
How so? The entire phrase "by the novices" (navakehi) is to be understood in this way. For in crowded houses, there is no space for the great elders (mahātherā) to exit;
therefore, it was said thus. However, when the novices are returning in this manner, they should stand at the door of the house and proceed in order once the elders have emerged.
But if the great elders are seated at the head of the line, the novices...
In the interior of the house, one must exit in the proper sequence, starting from the senior’s seat.
One should walk in a sparse line so that people can pass between the bodies without being jostled.
The discussion on the rules for the dining hall is concluded.
366. Discussion on the Duties of One Who Goes for Alms:
Regarding "he sets aside his work"—this means he sets aside whatever tool he was using to perform his work, whether it be cotton, a winnowing fan, or a pestle;
or he sets aside whatever position he was in while working, whether standing or sitting. And [he does not do so] "from one who is giving alms."
Whether it be a woman or a man, one must not look up at their face at the time of receiving almsfood.
The discussion on the duties of one who goes for alms is finished.
Now follows the discussion on the duties of a forest-dweller.
368. Regarding the duties of a forest-dweller (*āraññika-vatta*): "One should descend from the lodging" means one should depart from the place of residence.
"Having placed the bowl in its bag": here, if there is no water outside the village, one should perform the meal-duty within the village;
however, if there is water outside the village, one should perform the meal-duty outside the village, wash the bowl, and ensure it is free of water.
It should be placed in a bag.
Regarding "the drinking water should be set out": if there are not enough vessels, one should set out the drinking water itself by treating it as the water for washing;
if no vessel can be obtained, it may even be set out using a bamboo tube. That too—
For one who does not obtain [fire], it should be prepared in such a way that there is a water-pool nearby.
When fire-sticks (*araṇi*) are available, it is permissible even not to make a fire. And just as for a forest-dweller, so too for one traveling through a wilderness, fire-sticks should be desired.
However, for those living in a community, it is permissible even without them. "Nakṣatra" refers specifically to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatrapada*).
The Discussion on the Duties of a Forest-Dweller is finished.
369. Regarding the Duties Concerning Lodgings:
since a "door" is a place of great public traffic, there is a requirement to seek permission regarding it.
The remaining acts, such as giving instructions and so forth, must be performed only after having requested permission. It is also permissible to request permission every day.

Furthermore, if it is said, "Venerable sir, let it be that I have already requested permission," and a senior monk accepts by saying "Very well," or if he himself says, "You may dwell according to your pleasure";
even in this case it is permissible. This is also valid when [the junior] acts through the trust of one who is of like status.
It is indeed proper. One should turn [the seat] toward the elder; that is, one should turn it facing the elder.
One should proceed in exactly the same manner in the dining hall and other such places.
The discussion on the duties regarding lodgings is concluded.
371. The Discussion on the Duties Regarding the Steam-Bath House: "They plaster" means they smooth the ground outside. 373. In the context of the rule regarding rinsing the mouth:
"If there is water"—here, if water is available, [one should go] to a private place.
However, there is no [water] [in the bowl]; one must pour it out with a vessel and rinse. If there is no vessel, it must be poured out with the bowl.
If there is no bowl either, it is said that [the water] is non-existent. If one who has gone forth thinking, "This is too exposed;
there will be other water ahead," finds no water at all, the time for the alms-round arrives; [in such a case], one should wipe [the mouth] with a stick or something similar.
It is permissible to go, to eat, and to offer a blessing of thanksgiving (anumodana). Regarding "in the order of arrival":
in the three locations—the latrine, the urinal, and the bathing place—the order of arrival alone is the standard.
374. Regarding the duties in the latrine: "While chewing a tooth-stick... This applies both to the latrine and to what is not a latrine.
In all cases, there is a prohibition. "Not with a rough stick" means one must not scrape with a split stick, or a harsh one, or a knotted one, or a thorny one, or a hollow one, or a rotten one.
However, there is no offense for one who has entered [the water] without taking up a scraping stick.
"Nor at a water-drinking pool" is said with reference to a place used for the common benefit of all;
for since various people come there one after another, the water must not be left behind.

However, it is permissible in a case where, even in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, a certain spot has been set aside for the regular use of a specific individual, or which is a private place. After drinking a purgative, again and again...
It is indeed permissible even for one who is entering.
"Ūhatā" means "smeared"; the meaning is that it is defiled by excrement on the outside. "Dhovitabbā" means that water should be brought and it should be washed.
If there is water but no vessel, it is said to be "non-existent. If there is a vessel but no water, [it is likewise non-existent].
This too is non-existent. When both are absent, it is indeed non-existent; one should go after wiping [the floor] with a wooden stick or some other object.
The rest is clear throughout.
The discussion on the duties regarding the sauna, etc., is concluded.
The Commentary on the Chapter on the Schedule is finished.
9. The Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha.
Discussion on Requesting the Recitation of the Pātimokkha.
383. In the *Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*: “On a night with a joyful face” (*nandimukhiyā rattiyā*):
even at the time when dawn has risen, the night appears as if it still possesses a joyful face; therefore, he said, “on a night with a joyful face. “Internally rotten” (*antopūti*):

internally rotten due to the state of corruption by defilements within the continuum of one’s own mind. “Leaking” (*avassuta*): leaking by way of the raining down of defilements. “Born of filth” (*kasambukajāta*).
"Corrupted by being crowded with faults. By saying "even to the point of seizing him by the arm," he shows the wonder:

that upon merely hearing the words, "Ānanda, the assembly is impure," that foolish man should have departed; yet instead of departing, that foolish man will wait even until he is seized by the arm. This is truly marvelous.
384. "Not plunging all at once" means it is not deep from the very beginning; the meaning is that it becomes deep gradually.
"The established nature does not overstep its limit" means it does not cross beyond the boundary-limit, which is the trench formed by the receding of the waves.
"It drives against the shore" means it strikes against the edge; the meaning is that it pushes it back. "Penetration of the other [knowledge]" refers to the attainment of Arahatship.
385. "The rain does not leak upon what is covered" means that one who, having committed an offense, conceals it, commits another new offense;
this was said with reference to this. "The rain does not leak upon what is uncovered" means that one who, having committed an offense, discloses it, does not commit another;
this was said with reference to this.
The Discussion on Requesting the Recitation of the Pātimokkha is finished.
The Discussion on Those Worthy to Hear the Pātimokkha (386):
"The Pātimokkha has been set aside"—here, even if it was set aside either before or after [the assembly], it is considered not set aside.
However, that which is placed within the boundary is indeed called "placed. Therefore, in the formula: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me;
today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha," one should set aside [the matter] as long as he is pronouncing the syllable *re*;
for this is the boundary. But when the syllable *yya* has been uttered, one who sets it aside afterwards—
It is said to be "suspended. By one who suspends it before even beginning with the words, "Let my assembly hear me," it is considered suspended beforehand.
The discussion on those worthy of hearing the Pātimokkha is finished.
Now follows the discussion on the suspension of the Pātimokkha as lawful or unlawful.
387. "He suspends the Pātimokkha on account of a groundless failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) that has not been committed":

whether that failure has been committed by that person or not, it is "groundless" (*amūlika*) in the sense that the perception of the one who suspends the Pātimokkha lacks a basis. Regarding "whether committed or uncommitted":
this is stated taking both the committed and the uncommitted together.
"He does not attend to the legitimate unity" means that, out of a desire to disrupt the formal act (*kamma*), when the Saṅgha is performing a formal act, he neither comes nor gives his consent;
yet, being present, he objects. By this, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Thus, even though he is one who has committed an offense, the Pātimokkha is suspended for him. "He recants" means: "It must be done again."
If she objects, saying, “It is *kamma*,” she incurs a *pācittiya* offense for that reopening [of the matter]. Thus, even though she has committed an offense, the Pātimokkha is suspended for her.
The discussion on the suspension of the Pātimokkha—both legitimate and illegitimate—is finished.
**The Discussion on the Suspension of the Dhamma Pātimokkha.** 388.

Regarding the phrase "by whatever modes, by whatever signs, by whatever marks," here the terms "mode" (*ākāra*) and so forth should be understood as referring to the presentation of what is not the Path as the Path, and so on.
Regarding the phrase "by that which was seen, by that which was heard, by that suspicion," here [the term] "seen" (*diṭṭha*)...

And what has been heard is indeed included in the Pāḷi. However, if one should give rise to suspicion based on those things seen and heard, it was with reference to that that it was said: "by that suspicion.
The discussion on the suspension of the legitimate Pātimokkha is concluded.
398. Discussion on Taking Up for Oneself (*Attādāna-aṅga-kathā*).

Regarding the phrase "by one who wishes to take up for oneself": here, when a bhikkhu wishing to purify the Teaching takes up a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) himself, that is called "taking up for oneself.
Regarding the phrase "it is not the right time to take up this taking up for oneself": here, [the reference is to] fear of kings.
Fear of thieves, fear of famine, and the rainy season—this is the improper time; the opposite is the proper time.

"This taking upon oneself is unreal" means this is non-existent: that "this is non-Dhamma or Dhamma," "Dhamma or non-Dhamma," "non-Vinaya or Vinaya," "Vinaya or non-Vinaya," or "a person of bad character is virtuous, or a virtuous person [is of bad character]."
"Of bad morality" means he is one who has taken it up [wrongly]; the opposite should be understood as "true.
Regarding the phrase "this undertaking of self is connected with what is harmful": herein, that which leads to an obstacle to life or an obstacle to the holy life is "connected with what is harmful";
the reverse is called "connected with what is beneficial."

"I shall not obtain monks who are visible and well-disposed"—this was said with reference to times when, due to fear of kings and other such dangers, it is impossible to find monks who can provide support for one's own faction.
However, at other times, when there is safety and an abundance of alms-food, they can be obtained; it is with reference to this that "I shall obtain them" was said.
"There will arise for the Saṅgha, on that account, quarreling"— meaning there will be quarreling, strife, contention, dispute, and even a schism in the Saṅgha,
as occurred among the Kosambakas. "And it will lead to no remorse later"— just as in the case of the Elder Mahākassapa, who,
having rebuked Subhadda who had gone forth in old age, convened the Council of Five Hundred.
It is the subsequent recollection of the Venerable Yasa— who, having restrained ten thousand bhikkhus,
performed the Council of Seven Hundred— and likewise of the Elder Moggaliputtatissa— who, having restrained sixty thousand bhikkhus, performed the Council of One Thousand;
and this leads to the Dispensation becoming as free from defilements as the moon and sun.
The Discussion on the Factors of Self-Appropriation is finished. 399.
Regarding the passage beginning with "by one who is unbroken and unblemished," it refers to anyone at all among householders or those gone forth who has been struck.

If he has performed medical treatments for householders, such as lancing abscesses and so forth, his bodily conduct is perforated like a palm leaf gnawed by termites, and it is "fleshly" because it can be grasped and dragged about anywhere;

its opposite—being unperforated and non-fleshly—should be understood accordingly. As for verbal conduct, however, it is [defiled] by lying, slander, malicious speech, groundless accusations, and so forth.
It is "with gaps and with flaws," while the opposite is "without gaps and without flaws.
"Loving-kindness toward me" refers to the mind of loving-kindness attained through the practice of developing the meditation subject after having severed the hindrances.
"Free from malice" means devoid of resentment; the meaning is that resentment has been destroyed by way of suppression.
"But where, friends, was this said by the Blessed One?"—the meaning is: in which city was this training rule (sikkhāpada) spoken?
The discussion on the qualities to be reflected upon by the accuser is finished.
Now begins the discussion on what should be established by the accuser.
400. Regarding the phrases "I will speak at the proper time" and so forth: one who reproves after having requested an opportunity from another is said to speak at the proper time (*kālena*).

One who reproves in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, at the tip of a voting stick (*salākā*), at the head of a rice-offering (*yāgu*), in a hut for reflection (*vitakkamāḷaka*), on the path to alms-round, or in a dining hall, or at a moment when one is surrounded by attendants, is said to speak at the improper time (*akālena*). Speaking truthfully is called speaking what is factual (*bhūtena*).
[For example: "O elder, you who frequent assemblies, you who wear rag-robes, you who preach the Dhamma—it is fitting..."
When one says, "This belongs to you," while speaking harshly, it is called speaking harshly. However, when one speaks with reference to a specific reason, saying, "Venerable sir, you are elderly;
you are one who moves in assemblies, a wearer of rag-robes, and a preacher of the Dhamma;
this is suitable for you," it is called speaking gently. Speaking with reference to a specific reason is called speaking for the benefit of others. One whose mind is filled with loving-kindness—
"I shall speak without internal ill will; having established a mind of loving-kindness, I shall speak, not with a corrupted mind.
The discussion on what must be established by the accuser is finished.
This concludes the discussion connected to the accuser and the accused.
401. "Having directed the mind inward" means having generated it within one's own mind. "Compassion" (*kāruññatā*) is the state of compassion (*karuṇā*).

By this, he shows both compassion and the preliminary stage to compassion. "Desiring welfare" (*hitesitā*) is the state of seeking welfare. "Sympathizing" (*anukampitā*) is the state of connecting [others] with that welfare.
By these two, he shows both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the preliminary stage to loving-kindness. "Emergence from an offense" (*āpattivuṭṭhānatā*)...
Establishing one in the state of purity after having raised them from an offense;

and performing the formal act (*kamma*) according to their admission, after having charged them with the matter, reminded them of it, and made them admit it—this is called "having the Vinaya as one's primary concern.
These five qualities are those stated in the manner beginning with "compassion" (*kāruññatā*); having brought these five qualities to mind within oneself, another person should be charged.
"In truth and in imperturbability" means both in verbal truth and in the state of being unperturbed. For the one who reproaches must speak the truth and must not give way to anger.
The meaning is that one should neither become angry oneself nor provoke another. The rest is clear throughout.
The discussion connected with the accuser and the accused is finished.
The commentary on the Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha is finished.
10. The Chapter on the Bhikkhunīs:
The Discourse on the Case of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
402. In the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*: Why does [the Buddha] refuse, saying, "Enough, Gotamī, let it not please you"?
Is it not the case that all Buddhas have four assemblies? Certainly they do;

however, it was a blessing that she would protect the going-forth—granted only after she had been exhausted by repeated requests—with the thought, "This has been obtained by us with great difficulty."
Having [formulated the rule], he rejects it because he wishes to permit [the practice]. The discourse on the eight *garudhammas* has been explained in the *Mahāvibhaṅga* itself.
403. "By thieves with jars" means by thieves who steal by lighting a lamp in a jar and searching for goods in another's house using that light.

"The disease called *setaṭṭhika*" refers to a certain kind of parasite that pierces the stalk where it enters the middle of the rice plant; because of being pierced by this, even the milk that has emerged from the top of the rice plant cannot be taken up.
The disease called *mañjiṭṭhikā* is the internal rotting of sugarcane.
By the phrase "a bank for a large pond beforehand," however, he shows this meaning:

just as some water might remain in a large pond even if its bank has not yet been built, whereas that which would not have remained due to the lack of a bank will also remain once the bank has first been constructed.

...would endure; even so, these heavy rules (garudhamma) which have been laid down in anticipation for the sake of non-transgression regarding matters that have not yet arisen—if they had not been laid down, the True Dhamma would have endured for only five hundred years because women have gone forth.
But because they were laid down in anticipation, it will endure for another five hundred years as well. Thus...

It was stated at the outset that he will remain for exactly one thousand years. This "one thousand years" is spoken specifically with reference to those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and who have attained the various analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Beyond that, however, there is another thousand years by way of those whose taints are destroyed through dry-insight (sukkha-vipassaka);
a thousand years by way of non-returners (anāgāmin); a thousand years by way of once-returners (sakadāgāmin); and a thousand years by way of stream-enterers (sotāpanna). Thus...
The true Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-saddhamma) will endure for five thousand years, and the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) will likewise endure for that same length of time.
For there is no realization in the absence of the scriptures, nor is there no realization when the scriptures exist;
however, even after the scriptures have disappeared, their outward signs (liṅga) will continue to prevail for a long time.
The account concerning Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is finished.
Regarding the discourse on the authorization for the higher ordination of bhikkhunīs:
by means of this supplementary rule, "I authorize you, monks, to grant the higher ordination to bhikkhunīs through the monks," [the procedure was established].
The five hundred bhikkhus, having made Mahāpajāpatī the Sākiyan lady their co-resident, conferred full ordination upon her.
Thus, they were all known as those "fully ordained on one side. By means of this exhortation, "O Gotamī," Gotamī attained Arahantship. 409.

"No formal act is performed" means that not even one of the seven kinds of formal acts, such as the act of censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*), is performed. "They ask for forgiveness" means they ask for forgiveness, saying, "We shall not do so again."
410. “I allow you, monks, for the monks to propose a formal act (*kamma*) to the nuns and hand it over to them.

In this context, regarding acts such as censure (*tajjanīya*), one should propose it thus: “This specific formal act is to be performed against her,” and then hand it over by saying, “Now, you yourselves must carry it out.
However, if they perform something other than what was proposed, [it is invalid] for one who deserves a censure act...
They incur the necessity of being dealt with according to the method stated here: "He performs the act of demotion (*niyassakamma*).
411. Regarding the phrase "with muddy water": herein, it is not only with muddy water;

for one who sprinkles with anything—even clear water that has become turbid by mud and the like—it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Monks, that monk is not to be saluted by the Saṅgha of nuns."
"It should be done" means that having assembled in the bhikkhunī’s dwelling place, one should announce three times: "A certain venerable one displays what is offensive to the bhikkhunīs;
does this community approve of the non-paying of respects to this venerable one? By this much, he has been made unworthy of respect.
From that time forward, just as they do not pay respects upon seeing a novice (sāmaṇera), even so [they should not pay respects] upon seeing him.

He is not to be saluted. That bhikkhu, conducting himself properly, having gone to the nuns' quarters, should approach the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual in the monastery itself, sit down on his heels, raise his joined palms, and ask for forgiveness, saying:
"May the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha forgive me. That bhikkhu [should go] into the presence of the bhikkhunīs...
Having arrived, one should say, "This monk asks for your forgiveness. From that point on, he is to be saluted.
This is the summary here; however, we shall explain the details in the *Kammavibhaṅga*.
"They illuminate" means they illuminate by means of what is not the true Dhamma (*asaddhamma*). "They associate with bhikkhunīs" means [they associate] with bhikkhunīs...
They associate with men in an unrighteous manner. The act of making one unworthy of veneration is exactly as described in the previous method.
"Obstruction" means the prevention of entry into the monastery. Regarding the phrase "to suspend the exhortation": here, it should not be suspended by going to the nuns' quarters;
rather, the nuns who have come for the purpose of exhortation should be told: "A certain nun named so-and-so is guilty of an offense; [therefore, do not exhort her]."

“I suspend the exhortation; do not perform the Uposatha together with her. The method for the disciplinary action (daṇḍakamma) regarding the exposure of the body and so forth is exactly as stated before. 413.
“Monks, a bhikkhu must not fail to go for the exhortation of a bhikkhunī,” etc., has already been explained in the commentary on the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.

416. “They bend the ribs”: like young girls of the laity, they bind them with a thick cloth waistband (*kāyabandhana*) for the purpose of bending the ribs. “A single wrap”: that which encircles [the body] once.
"With a bamboo band" means with a band made from soft bamboo strips. "With a cloth band" means with a band of white cloth.

"With a cloth braid" means with a braid made of cloth. "With a cloth cord" means with a cord made of cloth. Regarding "coḷa bands" and so forth, it should be understood that *coḷa* refers to coarse yellowish-brown cloth.
*Aṭṭhillena* means with the bone of the cow’s shank. *Jaghanam* refers to the region of the hips.
*Hatthaṃ koṭṭāpentī* means having had the upper arm ground down, they create decorative patterns with peacock feathers and so forth. *Hatthakoccham* means the back of the hand.
*Pādam* means the lower leg. *Pādakoccham* means the back of the foot.

417. *Mukhalimpanādīni* (lip-sticks for the face, etc. are exactly as described by the method already stated. *Avaṅgaṃ karontī* means they apply collyrium to the eyes, making a downward stroke in the corner of the eye (*avaṅga*).
*Visesakanti* means they make decorative marks (*visesaka*) of various shapes on the cheeks.
*Olokentī* means they open the windows and look out toward the street. *Sāloke tiṭṭhantī* means they stand with the door opened.
They stand showing half their bodies. They dance; they stage theatrical performances. "They set up prostitutes" means they establish courtesans.
"They establish taverns" means they sell liquor. "They establish slaughterhouses" means they sell meat.
"A shop" means they open various kinds of shops for diverse goods. "They employ slaves" means...
Having taken a slave, they have him perform their own work. The same principle applies to female slaves and the rest.
"They sell green and ripe [fruits]" means they sell both the green and the ripe; it is said that they set up a miscellaneous shop.
418. The discussion regarding entirely blue and so forth has already been explained.
419. Regarding the passage beginning, "If, monks, a bhikkhunī should pass away," etc., this is the decision not found in the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya*):

For if any one among the five co-religionists should pass away, [one might think], "After my passing, let my requisites belong to my preceptor (*upajjhāya*), let them belong to my teacher (*ācariya*), let them belong to my co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*), let them belong to my private pupil (*antevāsika*), or let them belong to my mother or my father."
If one says, "Let it be for another, or whoever else [desires it]," it does not belong to them; it belongs to the Saṅgha alone.

For the transfer of property to five persons belonging to the same Dhamma does not take effect, but it does take effect for laypeople. Indeed, if a bhikkhu dies in a bhikkhunī’s dwelling, his requisites belong to the bhikkhus alone. If a bhikkhunī [dies] in a bhikkhu’s dwelling...
If she dies, her requisites belong to the nuns alone.
420. "An old female slave" means a woman who was the wife of a slave during her time as a householder. "Male organ" means the male characteristic;
whether it has been cut off or not cut off, whether it is concealed or unconcealed—if, in this regard...
If, having given rise to the thought, "It is a male organ," one gazes intently [upon it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
421. Regarding that which is said to be "given for one's own use": this refers to what is given after saying, "You alone should use this.
If one gives that to another, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, it is permissible to give it after taking the best portion. If it is unsuitable, [one may give] all of it.
It is permissible to take it away. After having used a robe for one or two days, it is permissible to give it away. The same principle applies to bowls and other requisites.
Regarding the phrase "having had the monks' stored goods accepted by the nuns":
meat that was accepted and kept yesterday, if there is no other person not yet fully ordained (anupasampanna) present today, may be accepted by the monks and then consumed by the nuns.
For what has been accepted by the bhikkhus stands in the place of what has not been accepted by the bhikkhunīs;
and the same principle applies to what has been accepted by the bhikkhunīs regarding the bhikkhus.
426. As they were shifting their seats, they let the time pass; for as they were making one person get up and seating another, they exceeded the mealtime.
Regarding the phrase "according to seniority among the eight bhikkhunīs":
if, while the [first] eight are already seated, another arrives who is more senior than them, she is permitted to sit after making her own junior rise.
However, if one is junior even to those eight—even if she is sixty years old—she is permitted to sit only according to the order of arrival. This applies elsewhere as well.

"In all cases, one must not bypass those according to seniority"—except for the meal hall, in any other place where the four requisites are distributed, one must not take anything by bypassing a senior person on the grounds that "I arrived first";
it is proper only to follow the order of seniority. The discussion regarding the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) has already been explained.
429. By means of the terms "connected with women" and so forth, all vehicles are permitted. "Pāṭaṅki" refers to a cloth-wrapped bundle.
430. Ordination by messenger is permissible for those subject to any of the ten obstacles.
At the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā), whether that nun is standing or lying down in the nuns' quarters, awake or fallen asleep—
She becomes fully ordained (*upasampannā*) immediately. At that very moment, the shadows and other such details must be explained to the messenger nun who has arrived.

431. "Storehouse" (*udosito*) means a warehouse for goods. "Is not sufficient" (*na sammati*) means it does not suffice. "Residence" (*upassaya*) means a house. "Building work" (*navakamma*): the meaning is that I authorize a nun also to perform building work for the sake of the Saṅgha.

432. "Of her who has gone forth" (*tassā pabbajitāya*): at the time she has gone forth. "Until that child reaches the age of discretion" (*viññutaṃ pāpuṇāti*): the meaning is until he is able, by his own nature, to eat, drink, bathe, and adorn himself.
"Except for a house" means excluding merely the act of sleeping in the same house.
This shows that a second bhikkhunī should behave toward that child in the same manner as she would toward another man.
However, the mother is permitted to bathe him, give him drink, feed him, adorn him, and lie down with him while holding him to her breast.

434. "Because she has gone forth" (*vibbhantā*): this shows that because she has gone forth—having donned white robes out of her own preference and consent—she is therefore not a bhikkhunī [in the technical sense] by virtue of having renounced the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*). She does not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) again.

Regarding the statement "when she has returned, she should not be ordained": it means not only that she should not be ordained, but that she does not even receive the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). However, one who has gone forth after taking white robes does receive the mere going-forth.

Regarding the phrase "paying homage" and so forth: the meaning is that when men massage his feet, pay homage, shave his hair, clip his nails, or perform medical treatment for wounds, he does not consent to any of it because he feels remorse. On this point, some teachers say:
"If [the parties] are lustful or infatuated on one side or both sides, it is exactly according to the basis [of the offense]. Some teachers say: [it is according to the basis].

“There is no offense here,” they say. Having thus shown the opinion of the teachers (*ācariyavāda*), it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that this which is specifically permitted is allowable;
that is authoritative. For by the very words, “I allow you, monks, to consent,” that is permissible.
435. “Sitting cross-legged” means sitting having folded the legs crosswise. “Half-cross-legged” means one...
Having folded one leg and assumed the cross-legged posture (*pallaṅka*). Regarding the phrase "open below and covered above":
if there is a hole in the well, but only a wooden plank is visible above in all directions, it is permissible even in such a case.
436. "Rice bran and clay" means both the dregs of rice and clay. The rest here is self-evident.
The Discussion on the Permission for the Higher Ordination of Bhikkhunīs is finished.
The Commentary on the Bhikkhunī-Khandhaka is finished.
11. The Khandhaka on the Five Hundred.
441. Regarding the Discussion on the Minor and Very Minor Training Rules (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada-kathā*):

In the *Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka*, by stating that—with the exception of the four *pārājika* rules—the remainder are "minor and very minor" (*khuddānukhuddaka*), and so forth, [the Buddha] did so as a figurative means (*pariyāya*) to demonstrate that not even a single training rule should be abandoned, but rather all of them must be included.
It has been said: "This, O recluses, is for you" means "this is for the recluses. The particle *vo* is used merely to fill out the meter. 443.

"And this too, friend Ānanda, is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)" was said by the Elders solely as a reproach, meaning "this was badly done by you," and it was not said with reference to a formal offense (*āpatti*).
For they did not fail to know what was an offense and what was not an offense; it was [said] just now...
This has been proclaimed: “The Saṅgha does not lay down what has not been laid down, nor does it abolish what has been laid down.
Confess that *dukkaṭa*. When he says, “Yes, venerable sir, I have done wrong,” he should acknowledge it in this way;
this was said with reference to that *dukkaṭa*, not to the confession of an offense (*āpatti*). But since the Elder [did not do so] out of forgetfulness...

He did not ask out of disrespect; therefore, not perceiving even the state of having committed an offense (*dukkaṭa*) therein, he said, "I do not see that as an offense," and then, showing reverence for the elders, he said, "Nevertheless, with reference to you, Venerable Ones, I acknowledge that offense.
This means: "I confess it just as you say. The same method applies to the remaining four [cases].
In these instances. Whatever else might need to be said here has already been stated in the commentary on the Nidāna (the "Introduction").
The discussion on the minor and lesser training rules is finished.
The commentary on the Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka (the "Chapter on the Five Hundred") is finished.
12. The Chapter on the Seven Hundred: The Discussion on the Ten Bases. 446. Regarding the Chapter on the Seven Hundred:

“By a group of monks” (*bhikkhaggena*) means by a group of monks; the meaning is that having counted the monks, they set aside as many portions of food as there were monks. “Upon the earth” (*mahiyā*) refers to the snowy clouds during the season of snowfall.
447. "Enveloped by ignorance" means covered by ignorance. "Persons" means men. "Delighting in lovely forms" means those who yearn for and take pleasure in what is dear.
"Ignorant" means not knowing. "Dusty" means covered with the dust of passion. "Like deer" means like wild animals.
"With their snares" means together with their nets. "They increase the cemetery" means repeatedly casting down their physical bodies upon the earth.
They increase [their defilements]. Increasing in this way, they take up a terrible renewed existence. 454.
"A wicked deed has been done by us, friend"—the meaning is, "A wicked deed has been committed by us, friend. 455.

"By what dwelling on the plane (*bhūmi-vihāra*), friend?"—here, "plane" (*bhūmi*) is a term of endearment. It is said that the Venerable Sabbakāmī, wishing to speak kindly, addressed the newly ordained monks in this way. "By a dwelling like a raft (*kullaka-vihāra*)" means by a superficial dwelling.
457. Regarding the *Suttavibhaṅga* of Sāvatthī: how is it that something is prohibited in the *Suttavibhaṅga*?
For there, having stated, "What is called 'storing' (*sannidhi*) is what was received today and [eaten] on the following day," it further states the offense:
"If one who is storing eats or consumes either soft food or hard food while perceiving the other as not storing, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Thus the offense is defined.

By speaking thus, it is rejected. Regarding this, some think: "For it has been said, 'Whatever monk [eats] fresh food or soft food that has been stored,' yet this salt, because it is a life-long requisite, does not fall into the state of being stored.
Furthermore, even when one receives non-salted food and consumes it together with that [salt], that [food] is indeed received on that very day."

"Therefore, because of the statement: ‘Monks, that which is for life-long use, if received on that very day, is allowable at the proper time, but not allowable at the improper time,’ there must be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) here. They should be told:

“According to your own opinion, there should not even be an offense of wrong-doing, for in this case it is not something for life-long use received on that day; it is only something for the duration of the day.”
That was accepted at the proper time, and it was not consumed at an improper time.

Or, if you were to think that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) based on the statement, "It is not allowable at an improper time," then for one who consumes at an improper time food that is a mixture of lifetime-allowable (*yāvajīvika*) and time-allowable (*yāvakālika*), there would be no offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for eating at an improper time.
Therefore, one should not grasp merely the literal expression; the underlying meaning must be investigated.

This is the meaning here: if that which is received on that very day—namely, what is for life’s duration—is mixed with what is for the time being, it falls into the category of what is for the time being.

Therefore, by this training rule, "Whatever monk should eat hard food or soft food at an improper time," it is allowable at the proper time and not allowable at an improper time. Here, "it is not allowable" does not mean...

In this case, a *dukkaṭa* offense occurs merely by the utterance [of the words]. Just as food received on that very day for life-long use (*yāvajīvika*) is not allowable at an improper time when its flavor has been mixed with food to be consumed at the proper time (*yāvakālika*), and it entails the *pācittiya* offense of eating at an improper time;

so too, even food received today is not allowable on the following day when its flavor has been mixed with food to be consumed at the proper time, and it entails the *pācittiya* offense of eating what has been stored (*sannidhi*).

Even one who does not know that "this has been stored up" is not exempt from the offense. For this has been stated: "If one eats or consumes fresh or cooked food while perceiving it as not being stored up when it is actually stored up, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Therefore, to the question "Where was this prohibited?", the answer is: "This pure explanation is found in the Suttavibhaṅga at Sāvatthī."
"Connected with the Uposatha at Rājagaha": this was said with reference to the rule, "Monks, two Uposatha halls should not be authorized in a single residence;
whoever should authorize them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing for transgressing the Vinaya," it refers to the Vinaya rule:
"Monks, two Uposatha halls should not be authorized in a single residence."
In the case of excessive [action], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding the phrase "in the Campeyyaka section of the Vinaya":

this is stated with reference to the Vinaya topic that appears in the Campeyya Khandhaka, beginning with the words, "Monks, if an act is performed by an incomplete assembly in a manner contrary to the Dhamma, it is not a legal act and should not be done. Regarding the phrase "for some, it is permissible":

this is stated with reference to a practice that is in accordance with the Dhamma. Regarding the phrase "an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) in the case of cutting": [this is found] in the Suttavibhaṅga.
For it is stated: "A sitting mat (nisīdana) is called 'with a border'"; therefore, over and above two Sugata-spans, only a border of one span is permitted.
For one who makes it that size without a border, this very rule applies:
"If he exceeds that, it is an offense of expiation involving cutting. Therefore, when asked, "What does he incur? [the answer follows].
“[If there is] cutting, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya),” he said. The meaning is that one incurs the offense of expiation as stated in the training rule (sikkhāpada) on cutting.
The rest is clear in all respects.
The Discussion of the Ten Bases is concluded.
The commentary on the Khandhaka in seven hundred [sections] of the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the exposition of the Vinaya, is completed.
It has been explained as comprised of two sections and divided into twenty-two parts.
The Khandhakas in the Teaching have abandoned the suffering of the five aggregates.
May this commentary upon them— just as it was accomplished without obstacle—
likewise fulfill the auspicious hopes of all living beings.
The Commentary on the Cūḷavagga is finished.
